requests.user: {"question":"apa gagasan utama buku ini?","book":"Discourses","examinedBefore":400,"totalWindows":957,"previousNotes":[{"text":"Tesis utama buku: hanya penggunaan yang benar atas penampakan (right use of appearances) yang berada dalam kuasa kita; fakultas rasional adalah satu-satunya yang dapat mengkontemplasi dirinya sendiri dan menilai fakultas lain. Segala hal lain (tubuh, harta, orang tercinta) di luar kuasa kita; manusia menderita karena terikat pada banyak hal eksternal.","source_ids":["S3","S5","S6"]},{"text":"Kunci ketenangan: selalu membedakan apa milikku dan bukan milikku. Contoh: Lateranus mengulurkan leher dengan tenang; Agrippinus tetap makan setelah dijatuhi hukuman pengasingan.","source_ids":["S9","S11","S12"]},{"text":"Menjaga karakter (proper character): yang rasional selalu diterima, yang irasional tak tertanggungkan — karena itu kita butuh disiplin. Yang banyak condong pada daging dan menjadi seperti serigala, singa, atau rubah; sebagian kecil yang mengenali asal ilahiah tidak memiliki pikiran rendah tentang dirinya.","source_ids":["S27","S29"]},{"text":"Kemajuan (progres) bukan menguasai banyak buku filsafat, tetapi melatih desire dan aversion agar tidak gagal memperoleh yang diinginkan atau jatuh pada yang dihindari; bukti kemajuan adalah keadaan kemauan yang bebas, setia, dan sederhana dalam tindakan sehari-hari. Tragedi adalah gambaran gejolak orang yang menghargai hal eksternal.","source_ids":["S32","S36","S37"]},{"text":"Gagasan utama: manusia adalah makhluk rasional, kerabat/kepunyaan Tuhan; tujuan hidup adalah menggunakan akal dengan benar — memahami penggunaan penampakan, bukan sekadar memakainya seperti hewan. Alam berakhir pada kontemplasi dan hidup sesuai alam; memulai dan berakhir seperti hewan adalah memalukan.","source_ids":["S48","S49"]},{"text":"Providence: dari segala yang ada dan terjadi mudah memuji providensi bila memiliki dua hal — kemampuan melihat kegunaan segala hal dan watak bersyukur. Kesesuaian struktur dunia (mata, cahaya, warna) membuktikan Sang Pencipta.","source_ids":["S46","S47"]},{"text":"Kesulitan hidup adalah sarana latihan kebajikan: seperti Hercules membutuhkan singa dan hydra, manusia diberi kebesaran jiwa, keberanian, dan ketahanan untuk menanggung apa pun yang terjadi; mengeluh dan menyalahkan dewa adalah kekufuran akibat jiwa yang hina.","source_ids":["S52","S53"]},{"text":"Kekerasan kepalaan (menolak kebenaran yang jelas) ada dua macam: pada akal dan pada rasa malu. Orang yang melihat kontradiksi tetapi tidak berubah lebih buruk dari orang yang tidak melihat — akalnya tidak hilang melainkan dibinatangkan; itu bukan kekuatan budi.","source_ids":["S42","S43"]},{"text":"Logika dan argumen dialektis adalah kewajiban hidup: cukup tidak hanya mengetahui prinsip membedakan benar-salah, tetapi harus ada kemahiran seperti membedakan drachma asli-palsu. Namun bila premis berubah makna, kita boleh menarik persetujuan dari konsekuensinya.","source_ids":["S57","S60"]},{"text":"Kerabat dengan Tuhan: jangan menyebut diri warga Athena melainkan warga dunia (kosmopolites); komunitas tertinggi adalah manusia dan Tuhan. Contoh Socrates yang memilih mati daripada meninggalkan tugas yang Tuhan tempatkan; tubuh dan harta bukan kekuatan tiran atas kita.","source_ids":["S72","S78"]},{"text":"Gagasan utama: manusia berkerabat dengan Tuhan sehingga memiliki dari dalam dirinya sendiri hal-hal terpenting (kemuliaan jiwa); orang penakut dan hina hanyalah 'mayat dan segayung darah', dan tidak ada orang yang membuat orang lain sengsara—yang benar-benar berharga tidak diperoleh dari orang lain (tanah, uang, jabatan).","source_ids":["S81"]},{"text":"Epictetus mengkritik mereka yang mengejar jabatan di Roma: orang tua yang bersumpah akan hidup tenang setelah pengasingan langsung melupakan segalanya begitu menerima surat dari Caesar. Manusia memang dibuat untuk bekerja, tetapi pekerjaan yang benar adalah mempelajari administrasi dunia dan siapa diri kita, bukan urusan biji gandum dan tanah.","source_ids":["S84","S86"]},{"text":"Dialog tentang kasih sayang alami: meninggalkan anak yang sakit bukanlah tindakan penyayang—kasih sayang harus konsisten dengan rasio; yang keduanya penyayang dan rasional itulah yang benar dan baik. Kita butuh kriteria (bukan sekadar 'semua orang melakukannya') untuk menilai baik-buruk, seperti penglihatan untuk warna.","source_ids":["S92","S93","S94"]},{"text":"Sebab segala tindakan adalah will/opini (dogma) kita sendiri, bukan hal luar: bukan kematian Patroklus yang membuat Achilles meratap, tetapi pilihannya. Kematian, pengasingan, atau rasa sakit tidak menyebabkan kita berbuat apa pun; kita harus membuang opini salah seperti membuang tumor, dan hanya memeriksa opini, bukan tanah, budak, atau kuda.","source_ids":["S96","S97","S98"]},{"text":"Kebahagiaan (contentment): manusia harus meneliti pendapat tentang para dewa lalu menundukkan pikirannya kepada Yang mengatur semuanya seperti warga yang taat pada hukum. Kebebasan adalah belajar menginginkan segala sesuatu terjadi sebagaimana terjadi; yang tidak menerima hukumannya adalah menjadi dirinya sendiri—di mana ia berada dengan tidak rela, di situ ia dipenjara (Socrates tidak dipenjara karena ada dengan rela).","source_ids":["S103","S104","S107"]},{"text":"Tuhan mengawasi segala hal: jiwa kita adalah bagian dan potongan dari Tuhan, dan setiap manusia diberi penjaga (daimon) yang tidak pernah tidur; kita harus bersumpah kepada Tuhan—tidak pernah membangkang, tidak mencela apa yang diberikan, dan tidak dengan enggan melakukan atau menderita apa yang perlu—sumpah yang menghormati diri sendiri, bukan Caesar.","source_ids":["S115","S117","S118"]},{"text":"Filosofi tidak menjanjikan hal eksternal apa pun; materinya adalah hidup orang itu sendiri. Angka saudara marah bukan wilayahnya — ia hanya menjamin bagian penguasa (governing part) selalu sesuai alam. Kebenaran besar tidak terbentuk tiba-tiba, seperti buah ara butuh waktu matang.","source_ids":["S121","S123"]},{"text":"Providence terlihat bahkan dalam hal kecil: susu dari rumput, keju dari susu, rambut dagu sebagai tanda pembeda pria-wanita. Hymn kepada Tuhan harus dinyanyikan terus — Epictetus menyebut dirinya makhluk rasional yang tugasnya memuji Tuhan; 'jika aku burungNightangle aku menyanyi seperti nightangle, tetapi aku makhluk rasional, maka aku memuji Tuhan.'","source_ids":["S127","S128","S129"]},{"text":"Seni logis diperlukan karena akal menganalisis fakultas lain dan harus menganalisis dirinya sendiri; tanpa kriteria (seperti modius untuk gandum) tidak ada pengukuran akurat. Kita tidak butuh Chrysippus karena dirinya, tetapi untuk memahami kehendak alam.","source_ids":["S133","S136"]},{"text":"Kebebasan will terbukti: tak ada yang bisa memaksa assent pada yang palsu atau menghalangi assent pada yang benar. Yang memaksa bukan yang diletakkan di depan (ketakutan akan mati), melainkan opini kita sendiri — will memaksa will. Jika memilih, kita bebas, tidak menyalahkan siapa pun; segala jadi sesuai kehendak kita dan Tuhan.","source_ids":["S137","S138"]},{"text":"Jangan marah pada kesalahan orang lain: pelaku salah adalah yang keliru tentang baik-buruk, seperti buta — layak dikasihani bukan dibenci. Kita marah karena menghargai hal yang dicuri; jangan menghargai pakaian, tak akan marah pada pencuri. Latih diri dari hal kecil (sakit kepala tanpa 'alas!') menuju yang besar.","source_ids":["S141","S143","S145"]},{"text":"Tiran hanya menguasai tubuh (kaki, leher), tidak akan (will). Yang membuat orang takut bukan tiran dan pengawalnya, melainkan opini sendiri. Manusia yang ditunjuk Caesar jadi tukang sepatunya langsung tampak bijak di mata orang — nilai yang salah. Bakat dirinya mencakup memikirkan diri sendiri, dan karena manusia rasional tak bisa memperoleh kepentingannya sendiri tanpa berkontribusi pada kepentingan bersama, mementingkan diri tidak kontrasosial.","source_ids":["S151","S152","S154"]},{"text":"Akal sendiri berasal dari penampakan (system of appearances) sehingga bisa mengkhawati dirinya sendiri; tugas pertama filosof adalah memeriksa penampakan tanpa menerima tanpa ujian. Doktrin filosof sangat singkat: tujuan manusia mengikuti para dewa, dan baik adalah penggunaan penampakan yang tepat; kata-kata panjang hanya perlu menjelaskan apa Tuhan, penampakan, dan alam.","source_ids":["S158","S160"]},{"text":"Kritik terhadap Epicurus: kendati mengakui manusia bersifat sosial, ia menempatkan kebaikan pada 'kulitnya' sehingga menyarankan orang bijak tidak membesarkan anak—padahal begitu anak lahir, sayang padanya di luar kuasa kita; bahkan domba dan serigala tidak meninggalkan anaknya. Orang bijak seharusnya terlibat urusan publik, bukan memperlakukan manusia seperti sekawanan lalat.","source_ids":["S174","S175"]},{"text":"Kesulitan adalah lawan sparring dari Tuhan: seperti pelatih gulat mencocokkan kita dengan pemuda tangguh agar menjadi juara Olimpiade. Diogenes adalah penembak ronda teladan—melaporkan kematian bukan jahat, ketenaran gemuruh orang gila, hidup telanjang dan tidur di tanah lebih baik, dengan bukti ketenangan dan kebebasannya sendiri; penembak ronda penakut yang lapor musuh dekat hanya layak disuruh pulang.","source_ids":["S178","S179"]},{"text":"Hidup seperti berperan: manusia hanya boleh membawa yang miliknya (kirimannya), bukan kemudi atau dayung kapal—hal luar boleh dicabut satu per satu (toga, tubuh) tanpa takut. Harta seperti tempat tidur di penginapan; tragedi hanya terjadi pada orang kaya dan raja, orang miskin tidak punya peran tragis; bila permainan tidak menyenangkan, 'aku tidak bermain lagi'—pintu terbuka.","source_ids":["S180","S181","S182"]},{"text":"Perintah Zeus sudah cukup: jaga apa milikmu (integritas, rasa malu yang baik), jangan menginginkan milik orang lain; bila memegangnya tidak perlu arahan lain. Hidup itu permainan Saturnalia: patuh raja yang ditunjuk agar permainan tidak kacau, tetapi tidak ada yang memaksa kita berpikir menderita—seperti hipotesis logika, boleh menyanggupi 'sial', tetapi Zeus melarang menganggap diri hina.","source_ids":["S186","S187","S188"]},{"text":"Kita yang menghimpit diri sendiri lewat opini: ingin duduk di tempat senator menghimpit; hinaan hanya efektif lewat kelemahan orang yang dihinakan—jika mendengar seperti batu, tidak ada untungnya. Yang dijaga itulah yang diserang: bila menaruh hormat pada tubuh atau harta kecil, di situlah kita jadi budak. Socrates selalu satu wajah karena mempraktikkan kebebasan tanpa hambatan.","source_ids":["S189","S190","S191","S192"]},{"text":"Hukum hidup mendahului hukum hipotesis logis: bertindak sesuai alam adalah hukum dasar; filsuf melatih teori dulu (lebih mudah) baru urusan hidup yang lebih sulit. Awal filsafat adalah menyadari kelemahan fakultas penuntun—yang tak bisa menelan sepotong pun membeli seluruh jilid lalu memuntahkannya; orang membaca argumen hipotetis hanya untuk dipuji orang senatori (contoh: pengeluh punya 1,5 juta denarii yang membuat Epaphroditus tercengang, bukan mentertawakan).","source_ids":["S195","S196","S199"]},{"text":"Empat cara penampakan muncul; tugas orang terdidik menilai dengan benar. Ramuan melawan kebiasaan adalah kebiasaan yang berlawanan; melawan penampakan menipu adalah prekognisi yang bersih; melawan kematian—ia perlu dan bukan kejahatan, jadi tanpa rasa takut. Ketiadaan kesalehan lahir karena piety dan kepentingan pribadi dianggap terpisah.","source_ids":["S202","S205"]},{"text":"Jangan marah kepada orang lain: jiwa hanya menyetujui yang tampak benar (Plato: jiwa kehilangan kebenaran dengan tak rela); Medea terlilit karena mengira balas dendam lebih menguntungkan. Orang sesat pada fakultas tertinggi patut dikasihani seperti orang buta, bukan dibenci. Segala tindakan diukur oleh penampakan.","source_ids":["S210","S212","S213"]},{"text":"Iliad hanyalah penampakan dan penggunaannya: pembakaran Troya tidak lebih dahsyat dari sarang bangau yang terbakar—bedanya manusia memiliki kejujuran, kemoderatan, kesetiaan, kecerdasan. Kehancuran sejati adalah kehancuran opini benar: Alexander hancur saat kehilangan karakter, Achilles saat marah dan lupa tugasnya.","source_ids":["S214","S216","S217"]},{"text":"Esensi Baik adalah kemauan; hal luar hanya bahan bagi kemauan. Hukum Allah: ambil kebaikan dari dirimu sendiri. Tirani hanya mengancam tubuh; tidak ada yang lebih kuat daripada kemauan kecuali kemauan sendiri—sepuluh orang lebih kuat dalam mengekang, tetapi tidak dalam opini yang benar.","source_ids":["S222","S224"]},{"text":"Socrates menafsir ulang: yang dibawa ke penjara hanyalah 'tubuh miskinnya'; 'Anytus dan Melitus dapat membunuhku, tetapi tidak menyakitiku.' Kesulitan adalah ujian pembelajaran: seperti atlet yang ingin lawan berat, orang terdidik harus menunjukkan ajarannya dalam praktik, bukan argumen kecil di sudut sekolah; jadilah saksi Allah bahwa yang eksternal bukan baik atau jahat.","source_ids":["S226","S232","S235"]},{"text":"Pelayan yang baik menghormati semua orang sesuai 'relasi': ayah, saudara, keabadian—mengingat bahwa adalah watak dewata mempertahankan diri dari mimpi dan kecenderungan; putusan orang yang belum terdidik tentang kesalehan tidak lebih penting daripada seorang musisi yang salah menilai tali lyre. Hamba yang lari menikmati teater dengan ketakutan; membebaskan diri dari 'majikan' (kematian, kesenangan, sakit) menghapus seluruh ketakutan.","source_ids":["S236","S238","S239"]},{"text":"Sikap yang harus disiapkan dalam kesulitan: saat menghadapi orang besar, ingat ada yang melihat dari atas; pengasingan, penjara, mati, aib tetap hal indiferen yang tak berubah — hanya hal di luar kemauan yang 'tak ada bagiku'; Baik adalah kemauan sebagaimana mestinya dan penggunaan penampakan; tujuan hidup adalah mengikuti Tuhan. YAng begitu belajar akan berani karena tahu semua persiapan gelar-gelar kuasa 'bukanlah apa-apa'.","source_ids":["S243","S244"]},{"text":"Percaya diri dan kehati-hatian tidak bertentangan bila diterapkan pada objek berbeda: kehati-hatian pada hal dalam kemauan (satu-satunya jahat), keberanian pada hal di luar kemauan. Manusia terbalik seperti rusa yang takut pada bulu pemburu lalu lari ke jaring: takut pada kematian, sakit, aib (hal luar) tetapi gegabah pada tipu, nafsu, aib tindakan (hal will). Bukan kematian yang menakutkan, melainkan ketakutan pada kematian.","source_ids":["S247","S248","S249"]},{"text":"Kematian dan sakit adalah 'topeng tragedi': putar dan periksa — tidak menggigit; pintu selalu terbuka bila tak tertahankan. Kebebasan sejati adalah milik yang terdidik: hidup tanpa kesalahan, takut, duka, dan gejolak adalah bebas; budak yang dibebaskan di pengadilan tetap tak bebas bila uang, kekasih, atau tiran jadi majikannya. Socrates menulis untuk menguji dirinya sendiri dalam praktik, bukan karya-karya kosong; pamer sejati pemuda terdidik adalah 'sajikan kematian, penjara, siksaan — aku tak kecewa dan tak jatuh'.","source_ids":["S252","S254","S257","S258"]},{"text":"Ketenangan dalam perkara (contoh: ke pengadilan): bila tujuannya mempertahankan will sesuai alam, aman penuh — tak ada yang menguasainya; bila ingin mempertahankan hal luar, siaplah jadi budak penuh (berlutut, menangis). Socrates seumur hidup bersiap menghadapi sidang karena tak pernah berbuat zalim. Minta 'saran untuk setiap kejadian' seperti orang buta huruf minta tahu nama apa yang akan ditulis; latihan membuat siap untuk semua, dan yang mengejar hal luar pasti terombang-ambing pada kehendak majikannya.","source_ids":["S262","S263","S264","S267"]},{"text":"Magnanimitas konsisten dengan kehati-hatian lewat analogi meja judi: keping dan dadanya indiferen, tetapi penggunaan lemparan harus cermat — hal luar tak milik kita, will milik kita; gunakan hal luar dengan hati-hati karena penggunaannya bukan indiferen, sambil tetap tenang karena materinya indiferen. Seperti pelayaran: pilih kapten, pelaut, waktu; datang badai, tugas kita selesai — bila kapal tenggelam, lakukan satu-satunya yang bisa: tidak tenggelam.","source_ids":["S279","S280"]},{"text":"Manusia dibentuk untuk kesetiaan (fidelity); perusaknya meruntuhkan ciri khas manusia: kesopanan, kesucian, hubungan tetangga, persahabatan, komunitas — jadilah serigala atau kera, dan layak dibuang seperti peralatan rusak ke tumpukan kotoran. Argumen 'wanita memang bersifat umum secara alam' dibantah dengan analogi: babi dan teater juga umum bagi semua, tetapi setelah dibagikan, mencuri porsi orang lain adalah perampokan.","source_ids":["S274","S276"]},{"text":"Metafora permainan bola: keahlian ada pada melempar dan menangkap, bukan pada bola itu sendiri — bola (hal eksternal) harus dianggap tak berharga. Socrates bermain bola di pengadilannya: omongannya yang menyenangkan pada Anytus adalah lemparan; bolanya adalah hidup, belenggu, racun. Kita harus mengerahkan seluruh keahlian pada materi eksternal tanpa menghargai materinya, seperti tukang tenun yang mengerjakan wol apa pun yang diterimanya.","source_ids":["S282","S283"]},{"text":"Foot analogy: manusia adalah bagian dari keseluruhan, bukan makhluk terpisah — kaki yang menjejak lumpur atau dipotong demi tubuh masih sesuai alam sebagai kaki; manusia yang sakit, miskin, atau mati muda tetap sesuai alam sebagai bagian dari negara yang pertama (dewa dan manusia). Hidup seperti satu jam dalam sehari: hadir lalu lewat; bagaimana cara berlalunya tak penting.","source_ids":["S281","S285"]},{"text":"Hal indiferen vs penilaiannya: proposisi hipotetis indiferen, tetapi penilaian tentangnya tidak (pengetahuan, opini, atau kekelirian); hidup indiferen, penggunaannya tidak. Maka jangan lalai karenanya, tetapi juga jangan tunduk pada materi. Ingatlah pembagian milikku/bukan milikku — jangan mengklaim milik orang lain (misal: hasil pembicaraan dengan orang lain bukan tanggung jawabmu).","source_ids":["S289","S293"]},{"text":"Kematian itu kutukan bila dihindari: padi yang tidak pernah dipanen adalah kutukan; manusia yang tidak mati seperti tidak matang. Chrysantas menuruti terompet mundur daripada kehendaknya sendiri, sedangkan kita meratap menyebutnya 'keadaan' — padahal semua cara menuju Hades setara, bahkan jalan tiran lebih singkat daripada demam.","source_ids":["S290","S291"]},{"text":"Ramalan/divinasi sering dipakai karena pengecut — ketakutan pada masa depan — hingga melalaikan kewajiban (contoh: perempuan mengirim bantuan ke Gratilla yang diasingkan meski risiko disita Domitian). Konsultasi dengan Tuhan harus tanpa desire/aversion, seperti bertanya arah jalan kepada penumpang atau memakai mata; yang sejati adalah ramal internal dalam diri yang tanda baik-buruk.","source_ids":["S297","S298","S300"]},{"text":"Hakikat Baik: Tuhan bermanfaat, maka Baik ada di mana hakikat Tuhan ada — yaitu nalar benar dan kecerdasan dalam makhluk rasional, bukan pada tumbuhan atau hewan. Manusia adalah bagian terpisah dari dewa, 'membawa Tuhan di dalam dirinya' dan merusaknya dengan pikiran kotor; Tuhan menitipkan diri kita pada diri kita sendiri seperti titipan — jaganya agar sederhana, setia, bebas gejolak. Orang bijak mati dan sakit 'sebagaimana layaknya dewa'.","source_ids":["S303","S305","S307"]},{"text":"Kritik filsuf yang hanya bicara: menempatkan doktrin seperti roti di gudang, bukan yang telah dicerna menjadi daging dan tulang — hanya muncul bila kebisingan atau tawa mengganggu. Gagasan harus dipraktikkan setelah dipelajari; yang gagal memenuhi janji watak manusia (rasional) lalu menambahkan profesi filsuf seperti orang tak mampu mengangkat beban 10 pon mencoba mengangkat batu Ajax. Analogi: disebut Yahudi bukan dengan nama melainkan dengan pemilihan dan afek yang nyata.","source_ids":["S314","S316","S317"]},{"text":"Man adalah warga dunia yang rasional, yang tugasnya adalah bertindak sesuai dengan konstitusi alam dan tatanan ilahi (S321, S322). Karakter yang baik adalah tidak menganggap apa pun menguntungkan bagi diri sendiri dan bertindak sesuai peran (S321).","source_ids":["S321"]},{"text":"Kerusakan sejati bagi manusia bukanlah kehilangan harta atau tubuh, melainkan hilangnya karakter (seperti kesopanan atau ketenangan) yang merupakan bagian dari kehendak (will) (S324, S326).","source_ids":["S324","S326"]},{"text":"Filsafat dimulai dari kesadaran akan kelemahan diri dan ketidakmampuan untuk secara sempurna menyesuaikan prasangka bawaan (seperti baik/buruk) dengan kasus nyata. Tujuannya adalah menemukan aturan (kanonos) yang melampaui sekadar 'tampakan' atau 'perasaan' (S330, S333).","source_ids":["S330","S333"]},{"text":"Kecemasan (anxiety) muncul karena manusia menginginkan hal-hal yang berada di luar kekuasaannya (seperti pujian atau kehendak Caesar). Kepercayaan sejati hanya ada dalam penguasaan keadaan internal (keinginan dan keengganannya) (S347, S348).","source_ids":["S347","S348"]},{"text":"Tujuan praktis filsafat adalah menyesuaikan kehendak (will) dengan apa yang terjadi, sehingga seseorang dapat menjalani hidup tanpa ketakutan atau gangguan, baik dalam urusan pribadi maupun sosial (S358, S359).","source_ids":["S358","S359"]},{"text":"Langkah awal dalam filsafat adalah mempelajari providensi Tuhan dan berusaha meniru sifat-sifat ilahi (seperti kesetiaan dan kebebasan) dalam tindakan dan perkataan (S360).","source_ids":["S360"]}],"sources":[{"id":"S401","chapter":"XVIII: How We Should Struggle Against Appearances","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"XVIII"},{"id":"S402","chapter":"XVIII: How We Should Struggle Against Appearances","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"How We Should Struggle Against Appearances"},{"id":"S403","chapter":"XVIII: How We Should Struggle Against Appearances","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running. If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write. But when you shall not have read for thirty days in succession, but have done something else, you will know the consequence. In the same way, if you shall have lain down ten days, get up and attempt to make a long walk, and you will see how your legs are weakened. Generally then if you would make anything a habit, do it; if you would not make it a habit, do not do it, but accustom yourself to do something else in place of it."},{"id":"S404","chapter":"XVIII: How We Should Struggle Against Appearances","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"So it is with respect to the affections of the soul: when you have been angry, you must know that not only has this evil befallen you, but that you have also increased the habit, and in a manner thrown fuel upon fire. When you have been overcome in sexual intercourse with a person, do not reckon this single defeat only, but reckon that you have also nurtured, increased your incontinence. For it is impossible for habits and faculties, some of them not to be produced, when they did not exist before, and others not be increased and strengthened by corresponding acts."},{"id":"S405","chapter":"XVIII: How We Should Struggle Against Appearances","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"In this manner certainly, as philosophers say, also diseases of the mind grow up. For when you have once desired money, if reason be applied to lead to a perception of the evil, the desire is stopped, and the ruling faculty of our mind is restored to the original authority. But if you apply no means of cure, it no longer returns to the same state, but being again excited by the corresponding appearance, it is inflamed to desire quicker than before: and when this takes place continually, it is henceforth hardened (made callous), and the disease of the mind confirms the love of money. For he who has had a fever, and has been relieved from it, is not in the same state that he was before, unless he has been completely cured. Something of the kind happens also in diseases of the soul. Certain traces and blisters are left in it, and unless a man shall completely efface them, when he is again lashed on the same places, the lash will produce not blisters (weals) but sores. If then you wish not to be of an angry temper, do not feed the habit: throw nothing on it which will increase it: at first keep quiet, and count the days on which you have not been angry. I used to be in passion every da"},{"id":"S406","chapter":"XVIII: How We Should Struggle Against Appearances","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"y; now every second day; then every third, then every fourth. But if you have intermitted thirty days, make a sacrifice to God. For the habit at first begins to be weakened, and then is completely destroyed. “I have not been vexed today, nor the day after, nor yet on any succeeding day during two or three months; but I took care when some exciting things happened.” Be assured that you are in a good way. Today when I saw a handsome person, I did not say to myself, “I wish I could lie with her,” and happy is her husband; for he who says this says, “Happy is her adulterer also.” Nor do I picture the rest to my mind: the woman present, and stripping herself and lying down by my side. I stroke my head and say, “Well done, Epictetus, you have solved a fine little sophism, much finer than that which is called the master sophism.” And if even the woman is willing, and gives signs, and sends messages, and if she also fondle me and come close to me, and I should abstain and be victorious, that would be a sophism beyond that which is named the Liar, and the Quiescent. Over such a victory as this a man may justly be proud; not for proposing the master sophism."},{"id":"S407","chapter":"XVIII: How We Should Struggle Against Appearances","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"How then shall this be done? Be willing at length to be approved by yourself, be willing to appear beautiful to God, desire to be in purity with your own pure self and with God. Then when any such appearance visits you, Plato says, “Have recourse to expiations, go a suppliant to the temples of the averting deities. It is even sufficient if you resort to the society of noble and just men, and compare yourself with them, whether you find one who is living or dead.” Go to Socrates and see him lying down with Alcibiades, and mocking his beauty: consider what a victory he at last found that he had gained over himself; what an Olympian victory; in what number he stood from Hercules; so that, by the Gods, one may justly salute him, “Hail, wondrous man, you who have conquered not these sorry boxers and pancratiasts, nor yet those who are like them, the gladiators.” By placing these objects on the other side you will conquer the appearance: you will not be drawn away by it. But in the first place be not hurried away by the rapidity of the appearance, but say, “Appearances, wait for me a little: let me see who you are, and what you are about: let me put you to the test.” And then do not allo"},{"id":"S408","chapter":"XVIII: How We Should Struggle Against Appearances","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"w the appearance to lead you on and draw lively pictures of the things which will follow; for if you do, it will carry you off wherever it pleases. But rather bring in to oppose it some other beautiful and noble appearance and cast out this base appearance. And if you are accustomed to be exercised in this way, you will see what shoulders, what sinews, what strength you have. But now it is only trifling words, and nothing more."},{"id":"S409","chapter":"XVIII: How We Should Struggle Against Appearances","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"This is the true athlete, the man who exercises himself against such appearances. Stay, wretch, do not be carried way. Great is the combat, divine is the work; it is for kingship, for freedom, for happiness, for freedom from perturbation. Remember God: call on him as a helper and protector, as men at sea call on the Dioscuri in a storm. For what is a greater storm than that which comes from appearances which are violent and drive away the reason? For the storm itself, what else is it but an appearance? For take away the fear of death, and suppose as many thunders and lightnings as you please, and you will know what calm and serenity there is in the ruling faculty. But if you have once been defeated and say that you will conquer hereafter, and then say the same again, be assured that you will at last be in so wretched a condition and so weak that you will not even know afterwards that you are doing wrong, but you will even begin to make apologies (defenses) for your wrongdoing, and then you will confirm the saying of Hesiod to be true,"},{"id":"S410","chapter":"XVIII: How We Should Struggle Against Appearances","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"With constant ills the dilatory strives."},{"id":"S411","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"XIX"},{"id":"S412","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words"},{"id":"S413","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"The argument called the ruling argument (ὁ κυριεύων λόγος) appears to have been proposed from such principles as these. There is in fact a common contradiction between one another in these three propositions, each two being in contradiction to the third. The propositions are: that everything past must of necessity be true; that an impossibility does not follow a possibility; and that a thing is possible which neither is nor will be true. Diodorus, observing this contradiction, employed the probative force of the first two for the demonstration of this proposition: That nothing is possible which is not true and never will be. Now another will hold these two: That something is possible which is neither true nor ever will be, and, That an impossibility does not follow a possibility. But he will not allow that everything which is past is necessarily true, as the followers of Cleanthes seem to think, and Antipater copiously defended them. But others maintain the other two propositions: That a thing is possible which is neither true nor will be true, and, That everything which is past is necessarily true; but then they will maintain that an impossibility can follow a possibility. But it "},{"id":"S414","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"is impossible to maintain these three propositions, because of their common contradiction."},{"id":"S415","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"If then any man should ask me, “which of these propositions do you maintain?” I will answer him that I do not know, but I have received this story: that Diodorus maintained one opinion, the followers of Panthoides, I think, and Cleanthes maintained another opinion, and those of Chrysippus a third. “What then is your opinion?” I was not made for this purpose, to examine the appearances that occur to me, and to compare what others say and to form an opinion of my own on the thing. Therefore I differ not at all from the grammarian. Who was Hector’s father? Priam. Who were his brothers? Alexander and Deiphobus. Who was their mother? Hecuba. —I have heard this story. From whom? From Homer. And Hellanicus also, I think, writes about the same things, and perhaps others like him. And what further have I about the ruling argument? Nothing. But, if I am a vain man, especially at a banquet, I surprise the guests by enumerating those who have written on these matters. Both Chrysippus has written wonderfully in his first book about Possibilities, and Cleanthes has written specially on the subject, and Archedemus. Antipater also has written not only in his work about Possibilities, but also sepa"},{"id":"S416","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"rately in his work on the ruling argument. “Have you not read the work?” I have not read it. “Read.” And what profit will a man have from it? he will be more trifling and impertinent than he is now; for what else have you gained by reading it? What opinion have you formed on this subject? none; but you will tell us of Helen and Priam, and the island of Calypso which never was and never will be. And in this matter indeed it is of no great importance if you retain the story, but have formed no opinion of your own. But in matters of morality (Ethic) this happens to us much more than in these things of which we are speaking."},{"id":"S417","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"“Speak to me about good and evil.” Listen:"},{"id":"S418","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"The wind from Ilium to Ciconian shores\nBrought me."},{"id":"S419","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"— Odyssey, ix 39."},{"id":"S420","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"Of things some are good, some are bad, and others are indifferent. The good then are the virtues and the things which partake of the virtues: the bad are the vices, and the things which partake of them; and the indifferent are the things which lie between the virtues and the vices: wealth, health, life, death, pleasure, pain. “Whence do you know this?” Hellanicus says it in his Egyptian history; for what difference does it make to say this, or to say that Diogenes has it in his Ethic, or Chrysippus or Cleanthes? Have you then examined any of these things and formed an opinion of your own? Show how you are used to behave in a storm on shipboard? Do you remember this division (distinction of things), when the sail rattles and a man, who knows nothing of times and seasons, stands by you when you are screaming and says, “Tell me, I ask you by the Gods, what you were saying just now: Is it a vice to suffer shipwreck: does it participate in vice?” Will you not take up a stick and lay it on his head? “What have we to do with you, man? we are perishing and you come to mock us?” But if Caesar send for you to answer a charge, do you remember the distinction? If when you are going in pale and"},{"id":"S421","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":" trembling, a person should come up to you and say, “Why do you tremble, man? what is the matter about which you are engaged? Does Caesar who sits within give virtue and vice to those who go in to him?” You reply: “Why do you also mock me and add to my present sorrows?” “Still tell me, philosopher, tell me why you tremble? Is it not death of which you run the risk, or a prison, or pain of the body, or banishment, or disgrace? What else is there? Is there any vice or anything which partakes of vice? What then did you use to say of these things?” “What have you to do with me, man? my own evils are enough for me.” And you say right. Your own evils are enough for you, your baseness, your cowardice, your boasting which you showed when you sat in the school. Why did you decorate yourself with what belonged to others? Why did you call yourself a Stoic?"},{"id":"S422","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":"Observe yourselves thus in your actions, and you will find to what sect you belong. You will find that most of you are Epicureans, a few Peripatetics, and those feeble. For wherein will you show that you really consider virtue equal to everything else or even superior? But show me a Stoic, if you can. Where or how? But you can show me an endless number who utter small arguments of the Stoics. For do the same persons repeat the Epicurean opinions any worse? And the Peripatetic, do they not handle them also with equal accuracy? Who then is a Stoic? As we call a statue Phidiac, which is fashioned according to the art of Phidias; so show me a man who is fashioned according to the doctrines which he utters. Show me a man who is sick and happy, in danger and happy, dying and happy, in exile and happy, in disgrace and happy. Show him: I desire, by the gods, to see a Stoic. You cannot show me one fashioned so; but show me at least one who is forming, who has shown a tendency to be a Stoic. Do me this favor: do not grudge an old man seeing a sight which I have not seen yet. Do you think that you must show me the Zeus of Phidias or the Athena, a work of ivory and gold? Let any of you show me"},{"id":"S423","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":" a human soul ready to think as God does, and not to blame either God or man, ready not to be disappointed about anything, not to consider himself damaged by anything, not to be angry, not to be envious, not to be jealous; and why should I not say it direct? desirous from a man to become a god, and in this poor mortal body thinking of his fellowship with Zeus. Show me the man. But you cannot. Why then do you delude yourselves and cheat others? and why do you put on a guise which does not belong to you, and walk about being thieves and pilferers of these names and things which do not belong to you?"},{"id":"S424","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":9,"paragraphEnd":9,"text":"And now I am your teacher, and you are instructed in my school. And I have this purpose, to make you free from restraint, compulsion, hindrance, to make you free, prosperous, happy, looking to God in everything small and great. And you are here to learn and practice these things. Why then do you not finish the work, if you also have such a purpose as you ought to have, and if I in addition to the purpose also have such qualification as I ought to have? What is that which is wanting? When I see an artificer and material lying by him, I expect the work. Here then is the artificer, here the material; what is it that we want? Is not the thing one that can be taught? It is. Is it not then in our power? The only thing of all that is in our power. Neither wealth is in our power, nor health, nor reputation, nor in a word anything else except the right use of appearances. This (right use) is by nature free from restraint, this alone is free from impediment. Why then do you not finish the work? Tell me the reason. For it is either through my fault that you do not finish it, or through your own fault, or through the nature of the thing. The thing itself is possible, and the only thing in our "},{"id":"S425","chapter":"XIX: Against Those Who Embrace Philosophical Opinions Only in Words","paragraphStart":9,"paragraphEnd":9,"text":"power. It remains then that the fault is either in me or in you, or, what is nearer the truth, in both. Well then, are you willing that we begin at last to bring such a purpose into this school, and to take no notice of the past? Let us only make a beginning. Trust to me, and you will see."},{"id":"S426","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"XX"},{"id":"S427","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"Against the Epicureans and Academics"},{"id":"S428","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"The propositions which are true and evident are of necessity used even by those who contradict them: and a man might perhaps consider it to be the greatest proof of a thing being evident that it is found to be necessary even for him who denies it to make use of it at the same time. For instance, if a man should deny that there is anything universally true, it is plain that he must make the contradictory negation, that nothing is universally true. What, wretch, do you not admit even this? For what else is this than to affirm that whatever is universally affirmed is false? Again if a man should come forward and say: “Know that there is nothing that can be known, but all things are incapable of sure evidence;” or if another say, “Believe me and you will be the better for it, that a man ought not to believe anything;” or again, if another should say, “Learn from me, man, that it is not possible to learn anything; I tell you this and will teach you, if you choose.” Now in what respect do these differ from those? Whom shall I name? Those who call themselves Academics? “Men, agree [with us] that no man agrees [with another]: believe us that no man believes anybody.”"},{"id":"S429","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"Thus Epicurus also, when he designs to destroy the natural fellowship of mankind, at the same time makes use of that which he destroys. For what does he say? “Be not deceived, men, nor be led astray, nor be mistaken: there is no natural fellowship among rational animals; believe me. But those who say otherwise, deceive you and seduce you by false reasons.” —What is this to you? Permit us to be deceived. Will you fare worse, if all the rest of us are persuaded that there is a natural fellowship among us, and that it ought by all means to be preserved? Nay, it will be much better and safer for you. Man, why do you trouble yourself about us? Why do you keep awake for us? Why do you light your lamp? Why do you rise early? Why do you write so many books, that no one of us may be deceived about the gods and believe that they take care of men; or that no one may suppose the nature of good to be other than pleasure? For if this is so, lie down and sleep, and lead the life of a worm, of which you judged yourself worthy: eat and drink, and enjoy women, and ease yourself, and snore. And what is it to you, how the rest shall think about these things, whether right or wrong? For what have we to"},{"id":"S430","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":" do with you? You take care of sheep because they supply us with wool and milk, and last of all with their flesh. Would it not be a desirable thing if men could be lulled and enchanted by the Stoics, and sleep and present themselves to you and to those like you to be shorn and milked? For this you ought to say to your brother Epicureans: but ought you not to conceal it from others, and particularly before everything to persuade them, that we are by nature adapted for fellowship, that temperance is a good thing; in order that all things may be secured for you? Or ought we to maintain this fellowship with some and not with others? With whom then ought we to maintain it? With such as on their part also maintain it, or with such as violate this fellowship? And who violate it more than you who establish such doctrines?"},{"id":"S431","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"What then was it that waked Epicurus from his sleepiness, and compelled him to write what he did write? What else was it than that which is the strongest thing in men: nature, which draws a man to her own will though he be unwilling and complaining? For since, she says, you think that there is no community among mankind, write this opinion and leave it for others, and break your sleep to do this, and by your own practice condemn your own opinions. Shall we then say that Orestes was agitated by the Erinyes (Furies) and roused from his deep sleep, and did not more savage Erinyes and Pains rouse Epicurus from his sleep and not allow him to rest, but compelled him to make known his own evils, as madness and wine did the Galli (the priests of Cybele)? So strong and invincible is man’s nature: For how can a vine be moved not in the manner of a vine, but in the manner of an olive tree? or on the other hand how can an olive tree be moved not in the manner of an olive tree, but in the manner of a vine? It is impossible: it cannot be conceived. Neither then is it possible for a man completely to lose the movements (affects) of a man; and even those who are deprived of their genital members a"},{"id":"S432","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"re not able to deprive themselves of man’s desires. Thus Epicurus also mutilated all the offices of a man, and of a father of a family, and of a citizen and of a friend, but he did not mutilate human desires, for he could not; not more than the lazy Academics can cast away or blind their own senses, though they have tried with all their might to do it. What a shame is this: when a man has received from nature measures and rules for the knowing of truth, and does not strive to add to these measures and rules and to improve them, but just the contrary, endeavors to take away and destroy whatever enables us to discern the truth?"},{"id":"S433","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"What say you philosopher? piety and sanctity, what do you think that they are? “If you like, I will demonstrate that they are good things.” Well, demonstrate it that our citizens may be turned and honor the deity and may no longer be negligent about things of the highest value. “Have you then the demonstrations?” I have, and I am thankful. “Since then you are well pleased with them, hear the contrary: That there are no Gods, and, if there are, they take no care of men, nor is there any fellowship between us and them; and that this piety and sanctity which is talked of among most men is the lying of boasters and sophists, or certainly of legislators for the purpose of terrifying and checking wrongdoers.” Well done, philosopher, you have done something for our citizens, you have brought back all the young men to contempt of things divine. “What then, does not this satisfy you? Learn now, that justice is nothing, that modesty is folly, that a father is nothing, a son nothing.” Well done, philosopher, persist, persuade the young men, that we may have more with the same opinions as you and who say the same as you. From such principles as these have grown our well constituted states; by "},{"id":"S434","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"these was Sparta founded: Lycurgus fixed these opinions in the Spartans by his laws and education, that neither is the servile condition more base than honorable, nor the condition of free men more honorable than base, and that those who died at Thermopylae died from these opinions; and through what other opinions did the Athenians leave their city? Then those who talk thus, marry and beget children, and employ themselves in public affairs and make themselves priests and interpreters. Of whom? of gods who do not exist: and they consult the Pythian priestess that they may hear lies, and they report the oracles to others. Monstrous impudence and imposture."},{"id":"S435","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"Man what are you doing? are you refuting yourself every day; and will you not give up these frigid attempts? When you eat, where do you carry your hand to? to your mouth or to your eye? when you wash yourself, what do you go into? do you ever call a pot a dish, or a ladle a spit? If I were a slave of any of these men, even if I must be flayed by him daily, I would rack him. If he said, “Boy, throw some olive oil into the bath,” I would take pickle sauce and pour it down on his head. “What is this?” he would say. An appearance was presented to me, I swear by your genius, which could not be distinguished from oil and was exactly like it. “Here give me the barley drink (tisane),” he says. I would fill and carry him a dish of sharp sauce. “Did I not ask for the barley drink?” Yes, mister: “this is the barley drink?” Take it and smell; take it and taste. How do you know then if our senses deceive us? —If I had three or four fellow-slaves of the same opinion, I should force him to hang himself through passion or to change his mind. But now they mock us by using all the things which nature gives, and in words destroying them."},{"id":"S436","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"Grateful indeed are men and modest, who, if they do nothing else, are daily eating bread and yet are shameless enough to say, we do not know if there is a Demeter or her daughter Persephone or a Pluto; not to mention that they are enjoying the night and the day, the seasons of the year, and the stars, and the sea and the land and the cooperation of mankind, and yet they are not moved in any degree by these things to turn their attention to them; but they only seek to belch out their little problem (matter for discussion), and when they have exercised their stomach to go off to the bath. But what they shall say, and about what things or to what persons, and what their hearers shall learn from this talk, they care not even in the least degree, nor do they care if any generous youth after hearing such talk should suffer any harm from it, nor after he has suffered harm should lose all the seeds of his generous nature; nor if we should give an adulterer help towards being shameless in his acts; nor if a public peculator should lay hold of some cunning excuse from these doctrines; nor if another who neglects his parents should be confirmed in his audacity by this teaching. —What then in "},{"id":"S437","chapter":"XX: Against the Epicureans and Academics","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"your opinion is good or bad? This or that? —Why then should a man say any more in reply to such persons as these, or give them any reason or listen to any reason from them, or try to convince them? By Zeus one might much sooner expect to make catamites change their mind than those who are become so deaf and blind to their own evils."},{"id":"S438","chapter":"XXI: Of Inconsistency","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"XXI"},{"id":"S439","chapter":"XXI: Of Inconsistency","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"Of Inconsistency"},{"id":"S440","chapter":"XXI: Of Inconsistency","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"Some things men readily confess, and other things they do not. No one then will confess that he is a fool or without understanding; but quite the contrary you will hear all men saying, “I wish that I had fortune equal to my understanding.” But men readily confess that they are timid, and they say: “I am rather timid, I confess; but as to other respects you will not find me to be foolish.” A man will not readily confess that he is intemperate; and that he is unjust, he will not confess at all. He will by no means confess that he is envious or a busybody. Most men will confess that they are compassionate. What then is the reason? —The chief thing (the ruling thing) is inconsistency and confusion in the things which relate to good and evil. But different men have different reasons; and generally what they imagine to be base, they do not confess at all. But they suppose timidity to be a characteristic of a good disposition, and compassion also; but silliness to be the absolute characteristic of a slave. And they do not at all admit (confess) the things which are offenses against society. But in the case of most errors for this reason chiefly they are induced to confess them, because th"}],"newWindowIds":["S401","S402","S403","S404","S405","S406","S407","S408","S409","S410","S411","S412","S413","S414","S415","S416","S417","S418","S419","S420","S421","S422","S423","S424","S425","S426","S427","S428","S429","S430","S431","S432","S433","S434","S435","S436","S437","S438","S439","S440"]}

Segala hal lain (tubuh, harta, orang tercinta) di luar kuasa kita; manusia menderita karena terikat pada banyak hal eksternal.","source_ids":["S3","S5","S6"]},{"text":"Kunci ketenangan: selalu membedakan apa milikku dan bukan milikku. Namun bila premis berubah makna, kita boleh menarik persetujuan dari konsekuensinya.","source_ids":["S57","S60"]},{"text":"Kerabat dengan Tuhan: jangan menyebut diri warga Athena melainkan warga dunia (kosmopolites); komunitas tertinggi adalah manusia dan Tuhan. Manusia memang dibuat untuk bekerja, tetapi pekerjaan yang benar adalah mempelajari administrasi dunia dan siapa diri kita, bukan urusan biji gandum dan tanah.","source_ids":["S84","S86"]},{"text":"Dialog tentang kasih sayang alami: meninggalkan anak yang sakit bukanlah tindakan penyayang—kasih sayang harus konsisten dengan rasio; yang keduanya penyayang dan rasional itulah yang benar dan baik. Kita butuh kriteria (bukan sekadar 'semua orang melakukannya') untuk menilai baik-buruk, seperti penglihatan untuk warna.","source_ids":["S92","S93","S94"]},{"text":"Sebab segala tindakan adalah will/opini (dogma) kita sendiri, bukan hal luar: bukan kematian Patroklus yang membuat Achilles meratap, tetapi pilihannya. Kebebasan adalah belajar menginginkan segala sesuatu terjadi sebagaimana terjadi; yang tidak menerima hukumannya adalah menjadi dirinya sendiri—di mana ia berada dengan tidak rela, di situ ia dipenjara (Socrates tidak dipenjara karena ada dengan rela).","source_ids":["S103","S104","S107"]},{"text":"Tuhan mengawasi segala hal: jiwa kita adalah bagian dan potongan dari Tuhan, dan setiap manusia diberi penjaga (daimon) yang tidak pernah tidur; kita harus bersumpah kepada Tuhan—tidak pernah membangkang, tidak mencela apa yang diberikan, dan tidak dengan enggan melakukan atau menderita apa yang perlu—sumpah yang menghormati diri sendiri, bukan Caesar.","source_ids":["S115","S117","S118"]},{"text":"Filosofi tidak menjanjikan hal eksternal apa pun; materinya adalah hidup orang itu sendiri. Kebenaran besar tidak terbentuk tiba-tiba, seperti buah ara butuh waktu matang.","source_ids":["S121","S123"]},{"text":"Providence terlihat bahkan dalam hal kecil: susu dari rumput, keju dari susu, rambut dagu sebagai tanda pembeda pria-wanita.
