requests.user: {"question":"apa gagasan utama buku ini?","book":"Discourses","examinedBefore":440,"totalWindows":957,"previousNotes":[{"text":"Tesis utama buku: hanya penggunaan yang benar atas penampakan (right use of appearances) yang berada dalam kuasa kita; fakultas rasional adalah satu-satunya yang dapat mengkontemplasi dirinya sendiri dan menilai fakultas lain. Segala hal lain (tubuh, harta, orang tercinta) di luar kuasa kita; manusia menderita karena terikat pada banyak hal eksternal.","source_ids":["S3","S5","S6"]},{"text":"Kunci ketenangan: selalu membedakan apa milikku dan bukan milikku. Kematian, penjara, pengasingan harus dihadapi tanpa ratapan — tubuh bisa dibelenggu, tetapi kemauan (will) tidak bisa ditaklukkan bahkan oleh Zeus. Contoh: Lateranus mengulurkan leher dengan tenang; Agrippinus tetap makan setelah dijatuhi hukuman pengasingan.","source_ids":["S9","S11","S12"]},{"text":"Menjaga karakter (proper character): yang rasional selalu diterima, yang irasional tak tertanggungkan — karena itu kita butuh disiplin. Agrippinus menolak ikut tontonan Nero: ia ingin menjadi 'ungu' pada jubah, bukan sekadar satu benang biasa; Priscus Helvidius tetap bersuara di senat meski Vespasian mengancam mati — tugas kaisar membunuh, tugasnya mati tanpa takut.","source_ids":["S15","S18","S19"]},{"text":"Allah adalah bapa semua manusia: manusia memiliki kekerabatan ganda — tubuh bersama hewan, nalar bersama dewa. Yang banyak condong pada daging dan menjadi seperti serigala, singa, atau rubah; sebagian kecil yang mengenali asal ilahiah tidak memiliki pikiran rendah tentang dirinya.","source_ids":["S27","S29"]},{"text":"Kemajuan (progres) bukan menguasai banyak buku filsafat, tetapi melatih desire dan aversion agar tidak gagal memperoleh yang diinginkan atau jatuh pada yang dihindari; bukti kemajuan adalah keadaan kemauan yang bebas, setia, dan sederhana dalam tindakan sehari-hari. Tragedi adalah gambaran gejolak orang yang menghargai hal eksternal.","source_ids":["S32","S36","S37"]},{"text":"Gagasan utama: manusia adalah makhluk rasional, kerabat/kepunyaan Tuhan; tujuan hidup adalah menggunakan akal dengan benar — memahami penggunaan penampakan, bukan sekadar memakainya seperti hewan. Alam berakhir pada kontemplasi dan hidup sesuai alam; memulai dan berakhir seperti hewan adalah memalukan.","source_ids":["S48","S49"]},{"text":"Providence: dari segala yang ada dan terjadi mudah memuji providensi bila memiliki dua hal — kemampuan melihat kegunaan segala hal dan watak bersyukur. Kesesuaian struktur dunia (mata, cahaya, warna) membuktikan Sang Pencipta.","source_ids":["S46","S47"]},{"text":"Kesulitan hidup adalah sarana latihan kebajikan: seperti Hercules membutuhkan singa dan hydra, manusia diberi kebesaran jiwa, keberanian, dan ketahanan untuk menanggung apa pun yang terjadi; mengeluh dan menyalahkan dewa adalah kekufuran akibat jiwa yang hina.","source_ids":["S52","S53"]},{"text":"Kekerasan kepalaan (menolak kebenaran yang jelas) ada dua macam: pada akal dan pada rasa malu. Orang yang melihat kontradiksi tetapi tidak berubah lebih buruk dari orang yang tidak melihat — akalnya tidak hilang melainkan dibinatangkan; itu bukan kekuatan budi.","source_ids":["S42","S43"]},{"text":"Logika dan argumen dialektis adalah kewajiban hidup: cukup tidak hanya mengetahui prinsip membedakan benar-salah, tetapi harus ada kemahiran seperti membedakan drachma asli-palsu. Namun bila premis berubah makna, kita boleh menarik persetujuan dari konsekuensinya.","source_ids":["S57","S60"]},{"text":"Kerabat dengan Tuhan: jangan menyebut diri warga Athena melainkan warga dunia (kosmopolites); komunitas tertinggi adalah manusia dan Tuhan. Contoh Socrates yang memilih mati daripada meninggalkan tugas yang Tuhan tempatkan; tubuh dan harta bukan kekuatan tiran atas kita.","source_ids":["S72","S78"]},{"text":"Gagasan utama: manusia berkerabat dengan Tuhan sehingga memiliki dari dalam dirinya sendiri hal-hal terpenting (kemuliaan jiwa); orang penakut dan hina hanyalah 'mayat dan segayung darah', dan tidak ada orang yang membuat orang lain sengsara—yang benar-benar berharga tidak diperoleh dari orang lain (tanah, uang, jabatan).","source_ids":["S81"]},{"text":"Epictetus mengkritik mereka yang mengejar jabatan di Roma: orang tua yang bersumpah akan hidup tenang setelah pengasingan langsung melupakan segalanya begitu menerima surat dari Caesar. Manusia memang dibuat untuk bekerja, tetapi pekerjaan yang benar adalah mempelajari administrasi dunia dan siapa diri kita, bukan urusan biji gandum dan tanah.","source_ids":["S84","S86"]},{"text":"Dialog tentang kasih sayang alami: meninggalkan anak yang sakit bukanlah tindakan penyayang—kasih sayang harus konsisten dengan rasio; yang keduanya penyayang dan rasional itulah yang benar dan baik. Kita butuh kriteria (bukan sekadar 'semua orang melakukannya') untuk menilai baik-buruk, seperti penglihatan untuk warna.","source_ids":["S92","S93","S94"]},{"text":"Sebab segala tindakan adalah will/opini (dogma) kita sendiri, bukan hal luar: bukan kematian Patroklus yang membuat Achilles meratap, tetapi pilihannya. Kematian, pengasingan, atau rasa sakit tidak menyebabkan kita berbuat apa pun; kita harus membuang opini salah seperti membuang tumor, dan hanya memeriksa opini, bukan tanah, budak, atau kuda.","source_ids":["S96","S97","S98"]},{"text":"Kebahagiaan (contentment): manusia harus meneliti pendapat tentang para dewa lalu menundukkan pikirannya kepada Yang mengatur semuanya seperti warga yang taat pada hukum. Kebebasan adalah belajar menginginkan segala sesuatu terjadi sebagaimana terjadi; yang tidak menerima hukumannya adalah menjadi dirinya sendiri—di mana ia berada dengan tidak rela, di situ ia dipenjara (Socrates tidak dipenjara karena ada dengan rela).","source_ids":["S103","S104","S107"]},{"text":"Tuhan mengawasi segala hal: jiwa kita adalah bagian dan potongan dari Tuhan, dan setiap manusia diberi penjaga (daimon) yang tidak pernah tidur; kita harus bersumpah kepada Tuhan—tidak pernah membangkang, tidak mencela apa yang diberikan, dan tidak dengan enggan melakukan atau menderita apa yang perlu—sumpah yang menghormati diri sendiri, bukan Caesar.","source_ids":["S115","S117","S118"]},{"text":"Filosofi tidak menjanjikan hal eksternal apa pun; materinya adalah hidup orang itu sendiri. Angka saudara marah bukan wilayahnya — ia hanya menjamin bagian penguasa (governing part) selalu sesuai alam. Kebenaran besar tidak terbentuk tiba-tiba, seperti buah ara butuh waktu matang.","source_ids":["S121","S123"]},{"text":"Providence terlihat bahkan dalam hal kecil: susu dari rumput, keju dari susu, rambut dagu sebagai tanda pembeda pria-wanita. Hymn kepada Tuhan harus dinyanyikan terus — Epictetus menyebut dirinya makhluk rasional yang tugasnya memuji Tuhan; 'jika aku burungNightangle aku menyanyi seperti nightangle, tetapi aku makhluk rasional, maka aku memuji Tuhan.'","source_ids":["S127","S128","S129"]},{"text":"Seni logis diperlukan karena akal menganalisis fakultas lain dan harus menganalisis dirinya sendiri; tanpa kriteria (seperti modius untuk gandum) tidak ada pengukuran akurat. Kita tidak butuh Chrysippus karena dirinya, tetapi untuk memahami kehendak alam.","source_ids":["S133","S136"]},{"text":"Kebebasan will terbukti: tak ada yang bisa memaksa assent pada yang palsu atau menghalangi assent pada yang benar. Yang memaksa bukan yang diletakkan di depan (ketakutan akan mati), melainkan opini kita sendiri — will memaksa will. Jika memilih, kita bebas, tidak menyalahkan siapa pun; segala jadi sesuai kehendak kita dan Tuhan.","source_ids":["S137","S138"]},{"text":"Jangan marah pada kesalahan orang lain: pelaku salah adalah yang keliru tentang baik-buruk, seperti buta — layak dikasihani bukan dibenci. Kita marah karena menghargai hal yang dicuri; jangan menghargai pakaian, tak akan marah pada pencuri. Latih diri dari hal kecil (sakit kepala tanpa 'alas!') menuju yang besar.","source_ids":["S141","S143","S145"]},{"text":"Tiran hanya menguasai tubuh (kaki, leher), tidak akan (will). Yang membuat orang takut bukan tiran dan pengawalnya, melainkan opini sendiri. Manusia yang ditunjuk Caesar jadi tukang sepatunya langsung tampak bijak di mata orang — nilai yang salah. Bakat dirinya mencakup memikirkan diri sendiri, dan karena manusia rasional tak bisa memperoleh kepentingannya sendiri tanpa berkontribusi pada kepentingan bersama, mementingkan diri tidak kontrasosial.","source_ids":["S151","S152","S154"]},{"text":"Akal sendiri berasal dari penampakan (system of appearances) sehingga bisa mengkhawati dirinya sendiri; tugas pertama filosof adalah memeriksa penampakan tanpa menerima tanpa ujian. Doktrin filosof sangat singkat: tujuan manusia mengikuti para dewa, dan baik adalah penggunaan penampakan yang tepat; kata-kata panjang hanya perlu menjelaskan apa Tuhan, penampakan, dan alam.","source_ids":["S158","S160"]},{"text":"Kritik terhadap Epicurus: kendati mengakui manusia bersifat sosial, ia menempatkan kebaikan pada 'kulitnya' sehingga menyarankan orang bijak tidak membesarkan anak—padahal begitu anak lahir, sayang padanya di luar kuasa kita; bahkan domba dan serigala tidak meninggalkan anaknya. Orang bijak seharusnya terlibat urusan publik, bukan memperlakukan manusia seperti sekawanan lalat.","source_ids":["S174","S175"]},{"text":"Kesulitan adalah lawan sparring dari Tuhan: seperti pelatih gulat mencocokkan kita dengan pemuda tangguh agar menjadi juara Olimpiade. Diogenes adalah penembak ronda teladan—melaporkan kematian bukan jahat, ketenaran gemuruh orang gila, hidup telanjang dan tidur di tanah lebih baik, dengan bukti ketenangan dan kebebasannya sendiri; penembak ronda penakut yang lapor musuh dekat hanya layak disuruh pulang.","source_ids":["S178","S179"]},{"text":"Hidup seperti berperan: manusia hanya boleh membawa yang miliknya (kirimannya), bukan kemudi atau dayung kapal—hal luar boleh dicabut satu per satu (toga, tubuh) tanpa takut. Harta seperti tempat tidur di penginapan; tragedi hanya terjadi pada orang kaya dan raja, orang miskin tidak punya peran tragis; bila permainan tidak menyenangkan, 'aku tidak bermain lagi'—pintu terbuka.","source_ids":["S180","S181","S182"]},{"text":"Perintah Zeus sudah cukup: jaga apa milikmu (integritas, rasa malu yang baik), jangan menginginkan milik orang lain; bila memegangnya tidak perlu arahan lain. Hidup itu permainan Saturnalia: patuh raja yang ditunjuk agar permainan tidak kacau, tetapi tidak ada yang memaksa kita berpikir menderita—seperti hipotesis logika, boleh menyanggupi 'sial', tetapi Zeus melarang menganggap diri hina.","source_ids":["S186","S187","S188"]},{"text":"Kita yang menghimpit diri sendiri lewat opini: ingin duduk di tempat senator menghimpit; hinaan hanya efektif lewat kelemahan orang yang dihinakan—jika mendengar seperti batu, tidak ada untungnya. Yang dijaga itulah yang diserang: bila menaruh hormat pada tubuh atau harta kecil, di situlah kita jadi budak. Socrates selalu satu wajah karena mempraktikkan kebebasan tanpa hambatan.","source_ids":["S189","S190","S191","S192"]},{"text":"Hukum hidup mendahului hukum hipotesis logis: bertindak sesuai alam adalah hukum dasar; filsuf melatih teori dulu (lebih mudah) baru urusan hidup yang lebih sulit. Awal filsafat adalah menyadari kelemahan fakultas penuntun—yang tak bisa menelan sepotong pun membeli seluruh jilid lalu memuntahkannya; orang membaca argumen hipotetis hanya untuk dipuji orang senatori (contoh: pengeluh punya 1,5 juta denarii yang membuat Epaphroditus tercengang, bukan mentertawakan).","source_ids":["S195","S196","S199"]},{"text":"Empat cara penampakan muncul; tugas orang terdidik menilai dengan benar. Ramuan melawan kebiasaan adalah kebiasaan yang berlawanan; melawan penampakan menipu adalah prekognisi yang bersih; melawan kematian—ia perlu dan bukan kejahatan, jadi tanpa rasa takut. Ketiadaan kesalehan lahir karena piety dan kepentingan pribadi dianggap terpisah.","source_ids":["S202","S205"]},{"text":"Jangan marah kepada orang lain: jiwa hanya menyetujui yang tampak benar (Plato: jiwa kehilangan kebenaran dengan tak rela); Medea terlilit karena mengira balas dendam lebih menguntungkan. Orang sesat pada fakultas tertinggi patut dikasihani seperti orang buta, bukan dibenci. Segala tindakan diukur oleh penampakan.","source_ids":["S210","S212","S213"]},{"text":"Iliad hanyalah penampakan dan penggunaannya: pembakaran Troya tidak lebih dahsyat dari sarang bangau yang terbakar—bedanya manusia memiliki kejujuran, kemoderatan, kesetiaan, kecerdasan. Kehancuran sejati adalah kehancuran opini benar: Alexander hancur saat kehilangan karakter, Achilles saat marah dan lupa tugasnya.","source_ids":["S214","S216","S217"]},{"text":"Esensi Baik adalah kemauan; hal luar hanya bahan bagi kemauan. Hukum Allah: ambil kebaikan dari dirimu sendiri. Tirani hanya mengancam tubuh; tidak ada yang lebih kuat daripada kemauan kecuali kemauan sendiri—sepuluh orang lebih kuat dalam mengekang, tetapi tidak dalam opini yang benar.","source_ids":["S222","S224"]},{"text":"Socrates menafsir ulang: yang dibawa ke penjara hanyalah 'tubuh miskinnya'; 'Anytus dan Melitus dapat membunuhku, tetapi tidak menyakitiku.' Kesulitan adalah ujian pembelajaran: seperti atlet yang ingin lawan berat, orang terdidik harus menunjukkan ajarannya dalam praktik, bukan argumen kecil di sudut sekolah; jadilah saksi Allah bahwa yang eksternal bukan baik atau jahat.","source_ids":["S226","S232","S235"]},{"text":"Pelayan yang baik menghormati semua orang sesuai 'relasi': ayah, saudara, keabadian—mengingat bahwa adalah watak dewata mempertahankan diri dari mimpi dan kecenderungan; putusan orang yang belum terdidik tentang kesalehan tidak lebih penting daripada seorang musisi yang salah menilai tali lyre. Hamba yang lari menikmati teater dengan ketakutan; membebaskan diri dari 'majikan' (kematian, kesenangan, sakit) menghapus seluruh ketakutan.","source_ids":["S236","S238","S239"]},{"text":"Sikap yang harus disiapkan dalam kesulitan: saat menghadapi orang besar, ingat ada yang melihat dari atas; pengasingan, penjara, mati, aib tetap hal indiferen yang tak berubah — hanya hal di luar kemauan yang 'tak ada bagiku'; Baik adalah kemauan sebagaimana mestinya dan penggunaan penampakan; tujuan hidup adalah mengikuti Tuhan. YAng begitu belajar akan berani karena tahu semua persiapan gelar-gelar kuasa 'bukanlah apa-apa'.","source_ids":["S243","S244"]},{"text":"Percaya diri dan kehati-hatian tidak bertentangan bila diterapkan pada objek berbeda: kehati-hatian pada hal dalam kemauan (satu-satunya jahat), keberanian pada hal di luar kemauan. Manusia terbalik seperti rusa yang takut pada bulu pemburu lalu lari ke jaring: takut pada kematian, sakit, aib (hal luar) tetapi gegabah pada tipu, nafsu, aib tindakan (hal will). Bukan kematian yang menakutkan, melainkan ketakutan pada kematian.","source_ids":["S247","S248","S249"]},{"text":"Kematian dan sakit adalah 'topeng tragedi': putar dan periksa — tidak menggigit; pintu selalu terbuka bila tak tertahankan. Kebebasan sejati adalah milik yang terdidik: hidup tanpa kesalahan, takut, duka, dan gejolak adalah bebas; budak yang dibebaskan di pengadilan tetap tak bebas bila uang, kekasih, atau tiran jadi majikannya. Socrates menulis untuk menguji dirinya sendiri dalam praktik, bukan karya-karya kosong; pamer sejati pemuda terdidik adalah 'sajikan kematian, penjara, siksaan — aku tak kecewa dan tak jatuh'.","source_ids":["S252","S254","S257","S258"]},{"text":"Ketenangan dalam perkara (contoh: ke pengadilan): bila tujuannya mempertahankan will sesuai alam, aman penuh — tak ada yang menguasainya; bila ingin mempertahankan hal luar, siaplah jadi budak penuh (berlutut, menangis). Socrates seumur hidup bersiap menghadapi sidang karena tak pernah berbuat zalim. Minta 'saran untuk setiap kejadian' seperti orang buta huruf minta tahu nama apa yang akan ditulis; latihan membuat siap untuk semua, dan yang mengejar hal luar pasti terombang-ambing pada kehendak majikannya.","source_ids":["S262","S263","S264","S267"]},{"text":"Magnanimitas konsisten dengan kehati-hatian lewat analogi meja judi: keping dan dadanya indiferen, tetapi penggunaan lemparan harus cermat — hal luar tak milik kita, will milik kita; gunakan hal luar dengan hati-hati karena penggunaannya bukan indiferen, sambil tetap tenang karena materinya indiferen. Seperti pelayaran: pilih kapten, pelaut, waktu; datang badai, tugas kita selesai — bila kapal tenggelam, lakukan satu-satunya yang bisa: tidak tenggelam.","source_ids":["S279","S280"]},{"text":"Manusia dibentuk untuk kesetiaan (fidelity); perusaknya meruntuhkan ciri khas manusia: kesopanan, kesucian, hubungan tetangga, persahabatan, komunitas — jadilah serigala atau kera, dan layak dibuang seperti peralatan rusak ke tumpukan kotoran. Argumen 'wanita memang bersifat umum secara alam' dibantah dengan analogi: babi dan teater juga umum bagi semua, tetapi setelah dibagikan, mencuri porsi orang lain adalah perampokan.","source_ids":["S274","S276"]},{"text":"Metafora permainan bola: keahlian ada pada melempar dan menangkap, bukan pada bola itu sendiri — bola (hal eksternal) harus dianggap tak berharga. Socrates bermain bola di pengadilannya: omongannya yang menyenangkan pada Anytus adalah lemparan; bolanya adalah hidup, belenggu, racun. Kita harus mengerahkan seluruh keahlian pada materi eksternal tanpa menghargai materinya, seperti tukang tenun yang mengerjakan wol apa pun yang diterimanya.","source_ids":["S282","S283"]},{"text":"Foot analogy: manusia adalah bagian dari keseluruhan, bukan makhluk terpisah — kaki yang menjejak lumpur atau dipotong demi tubuh masih sesuai alam sebagai kaki; manusia yang sakit, miskin, atau mati muda tetap sesuai alam sebagai bagian dari negara yang pertama (dewa dan manusia). Hidup seperti satu jam dalam sehari: hadir lalu lewat; bagaimana cara berlalunya tak penting.","source_ids":["S281","S285"]},{"text":"Hal indiferen vs penilaiannya: proposisi hipotetis indiferen, tetapi penilaian tentangnya tidak (pengetahuan, opini, atau kekelirian); hidup indiferen, penggunaannya tidak. Maka jangan lalai karenanya, tetapi juga jangan tunduk pada materi. Ingatlah pembagian milikku/bukan milikku — jangan mengklaim milik orang lain (misal: hasil pembicaraan dengan orang lain bukan tanggung jawabmu).","source_ids":["S289","S293"]},{"text":"Kematian itu kutukan bila dihindari: padi yang tidak pernah dipanen adalah kutukan; manusia yang tidak mati seperti tidak matang. Chrysantas menuruti terompet mundur daripada kehendaknya sendiri, sedangkan kita meratap menyebutnya 'keadaan' — padahal semua cara menuju Hades setara, bahkan jalan tiran lebih singkat daripada demam.","source_ids":["S290","S291"]},{"text":"Ramalan/divinasi sering dipakai karena pengecut — ketakutan pada masa depan — hingga melalaikan kewajiban (contoh: perempuan mengirim bantuan ke Gratilla yang diasingkan meski risiko disita Domitian). Konsultasi dengan Tuhan harus tanpa desire/aversion, seperti bertanya arah jalan kepada penumpang atau memakai mata; yang sejati adalah ramal internal dalam diri yang tanda baik-buruk.","source_ids":["S297","S298","S300"]},{"text":"Hakikat Baik: Tuhan bermanfaat, maka Baik ada di mana hakikat Tuhan ada — yaitu nalar benar dan kecerdasan dalam makhluk rasional, bukan pada tumbuhan atau hewan. Manusia adalah bagian terpisah dari dewa, 'membawa Tuhan di dalam dirinya' dan merusaknya dengan pikiran kotor; Tuhan menitipkan diri kita pada diri kita sendiri seperti titipan — jaganya agar sederhana, setia, bebas gejolak. Orang bijak mati dan sakit 'sebagaimana layaknya dewa'.","source_ids":["S303","S305","S307"]},{"text":"Kritik filsuf yang hanya bicara: menempatkan doktrin seperti roti di gudang, bukan yang telah dicerna menjadi daging dan tulang — hanya muncul bila kebisingan atau tawa mengganggu. Gagasan harus dipraktikkan setelah dipelajari; yang gagal memenuhi janji watak manusia (rasional) lalu menambahkan profesi filsuf seperti orang tak mampu mengangkat beban 10 pon mencoba mengangkat batu Ajax. Analogi: disebut Yahudi bukan dengan nama melainkan dengan pemilihan dan afek yang nyata.","source_ids":["S314","S316","S317"]},{"text":"Man adalah warga dunia yang rasional, yang tugasnya adalah bertindak sesuai dengan konstitusi alam dan tatanan ilahi (S321, S322). Karakter yang baik adalah tidak menganggap apa pun menguntungkan bagi diri sendiri dan bertindak sesuai peran (S321).","source_ids":["S321"]},{"text":"Kerusakan sejati bagi manusia bukanlah kehilangan harta atau tubuh, melainkan hilangnya karakter (seperti kesopanan atau ketenangan) yang merupakan bagian dari kehendak (will) (S324, S326).","source_ids":["S324","S326"]},{"text":"Filsafat dimulai dari kesadaran akan kelemahan diri dan ketidakmampuan untuk secara sempurna menyesuaikan prasangka bawaan (seperti baik/buruk) dengan kasus nyata. Tujuannya adalah menemukan aturan (kanonos) yang melampaui sekadar 'tampakan' atau 'perasaan' (S330, S333).","source_ids":["S330","S333"]},{"text":"Kecemasan (anxiety) muncul karena manusia menginginkan hal-hal yang berada di luar kekuasaannya (seperti pujian atau kehendak Caesar). Kepercayaan sejati hanya ada dalam penguasaan keadaan internal (keinginan dan keengganannya) (S347, S348).","source_ids":["S347","S348"]},{"text":"Tujuan praktis filsafat adalah menyesuaikan kehendak (will) dengan apa yang terjadi, sehingga seseorang dapat menjalani hidup tanpa ketakutan atau gangguan, baik dalam urusan pribadi maupun sosial (S358, S359).","source_ids":["S358","S359"]},{"text":"Langkah awal dalam filsafat adalah mempelajari providensi Tuhan dan berusaha meniru sifat-sifat ilahi (seperti kesetiaan dan kebebasan) dalam tindakan dan perkataan (S360).","source_ids":["S360"]}],"sources":[{"id":"S441","chapter":"XXI: Of Inconsistency","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"ey imagine that there is something involuntary in them as in timidity and compassion; and if a man confess that he is in any respect intemperate, he alleges love (or passion) as an excuse for what is involuntary. But men do not imagine injustice to be at all involuntary. There is also in jealousy, as they suppose, something involuntary; and for this reason they confess to jealousy also."},{"id":"S442","chapter":"XXI: Of Inconsistency","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"Living then among such men, who are so confused, so ignorant of what they say, and of the evils which they have or have not, and why they have them, or how they shall be relieved of them, I think it is worth the trouble for a man to watch constantly (and to ask) whether I also am one of them, what imagination I have about myself, how I conduct myself, whether I conduct myself as a prudent man, whether I conduct myself as a temperate man, whether I ever say this: that I have been taught to be prepared for everything that may happen. Have I the consciousness which a man who knows nothing ought to have, that I know nothing? Do I go to my teacher as men go to oracles, prepared to obey? or do I like a snivelling boy go to my school to learn history and understand the books which I did not understand before, and, if it should happen so, to explain them also to others? —Man, you have had a fight in the house with a poor slave, you have turned the family upside down, you have frightened the neighbours, and you come to me as if you were a wise man, and you take your seat and judge how I have explained some word, and how I have babbled whatever came into my head. You come full of envy, and h"},{"id":"S443","chapter":"XXI: Of Inconsistency","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"umbled, because you bring nothing from home; and you sit during the discussion thinking of nothing else than how your father is disposed towards you and your brother. “What are they saying about me there? now they think that I am improving, and are saying, ‘He will return with all knowledge.’ I wish I could learn everything before I return: but much labor is necessary, and no one sends me anything, and the baths at Nicopolis are dirty; everything is bad at home, and bad here.”"},{"id":"S444","chapter":"XXI: Of Inconsistency","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"Then they say, no one gains any profit from the school. —Why, who comes to the school? who comes for the purpose of being improved? who comes to present his opinions to be purified? who comes to learn what he is in want of? Why do you wonder then if you carry back from the school the very things which you bring into it? For you come not to lay aside (your principles) or to correct them or to receive other principles in place of them. By no means, nor anything like it. You rather look to this: whether you possess already that for which you come. You wish to prattle about theorems? What then? Do you not become greater triflers? Do not your little theorems give you some opportunity of display? You solve sophistical syllogisms. Do you not examine the assumptions of the syllogism named the Liar? Do you not examine hypothetical syllogisms? Why then are you still vexed if you receive the things for which you come to the school? “Yes; but if my child die or my brother, or if I must die or be racked, what good will these things do me?” —Well, did you come for this? for this do you sit by my side? did you ever for this light your lamp or keep awake? or, when you went out to the walking place"},{"id":"S445","chapter":"XXI: Of Inconsistency","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":", did you ever propose any appearance that had been presented to you instead of a syllogism, and did you and your friends discuss it together? Where and when? Then you say, “Theorems are useless.” To whom? To such as make a bad use of them. For eye-salves are not useless to those who use them as they ought and when they ought. Fomentations are not useless. Dumbbells are not useless; but they are useless to some, useful to others. If you ask me now if syllogisms are useful, I will tell you that they are useful, and if you choose, I will prove it. —“How then will they in any way be useful to me?” Man, did you ask if they are useful to you, or did you ask generally? Let him who is suffering from dysentery ask me if vinegar is useful; I will say that it is useful. —“Will it then be useful to me?” —I will say: no. Seek first for the discharge to be stopped and the ulcers to be closed. And do you, O men, first cure the ulcers and stop the discharge; be tranquil in your mind, bring it free from distraction into the school, and you will know what power reason has."},{"id":"S446","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"XXII"},{"id":"S447","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"On Friendship"},{"id":"S448","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"What a man applies himself to earnestly, that he naturally loves. Do men then apply themselves earnestly to the things which are bad? By no means. Well, do they apply themselves to things which in no way concern themselves? not to these either. It remains then that they employ themselves earnestly only about things which are good; and if they are earnestly employed about things, they love such things also. Whoever then understands what is good, can also know how to love: but he who cannot distinguish good from bad, and things which are neither good nor bad from both, how can he possess the power of loving? To love then is only in the power of the wise."},{"id":"S449","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"How is this? a man may say, “I am foolish, and yet I love my child.” —I am surprised indeed that you have begun by making the admission that you are foolish. For what are you deficient in? Can you not make use of your senses? do you not distinguish appearances? do you not use food which is suitable for your body, and clothing and habitation? Why then do you admit that you are foolish? It is in truth because you are often disturbed by appearances and perplexed, and their power of persuasion often conquers you; and sometimes you think these things to be good, and then the same things to be bad, and lastly neither good nor bad; and in short you grieve, fear, envy, are disturbed, you are changed. This is the reason why you confess that you are foolish. And are you not changeable in love? But wealth, and pleasure, and in a word things themselves, do you sometimes think them to be good, and sometimes bad? and do you not think the same men at one time to be good, at another time bad? and have you not at one time a friendly feeling towards them, and at another time the feeling of an enemy? and do you not at one time praise them, and at another time blame them? “Yes; I have these feelings a"},{"id":"S450","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"lso.” Well then, do you think that he who has been deceived about a man is his friend? “Certainly not.” And he who has selected a man as his friend and is of a changeable disposition, has he good will towards him? “He has not.” And he who now abuses a man, and afterwards admires him? “This man also has no good will to the other.” Well then, did you never see little dogs caressing and playing with one another, so that you might say, there is nothing more friendly? but that you may know what friendship is, throw a bit of flesh among them, and you will learn. Throw between yourself and your son a little estate, and you will know how soon he will wish to bury you and how soon you wish your son to die. Then you will change your tone and say, what a son I have brought up! He has long been wishing to bury me. Throw a smart girl between you; and do you the old man love her, and the young one will love her too. If a little fame intervene or dangers, it will be just the same. You will utter the words of the father of Admetus!"},{"id":"S451","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"Life gives you pleasure: and why not your father?"},{"id":"S452","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"Do you think that Admetus did not love his own child when he was little? that he was not in agony when the child had a fever? that he did not often say, “I wish I had the fever instead of the child?” then when the test (the thing) came and was near, see what words they utter. Were not Eteocles and Polynices from the same mother and from the same father? Were they not brought up together; had they not lived together, drunk together, slept together, and often kissed one another? So that if any man, I think, had seen them, he would have ridiculed the philosophers for the paradoxes which they utter about friendship. But when a quarrel rose between them about the royal power, as between dogs about a bit of meat, see what they say:"},{"id":"S453","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"Such are the wishes that they utter."},{"id":"S454","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"For universally, be not deceived, every animal is attached to nothing so much as to its own interest. Whatever then appears to it an impediment to this interest, whether this be a brother, or a father, or a child, or beloved, or lover, it hates, spurns, curses: for its nature is to love nothing so much as its own interest; this is father, and brother and kinsman, and country, and God. When then the gods appear to us to be an impediment to this, we abuse them and throw down their statues and burn their temples, as Alexander ordered the temples of Aesculapius to be burned when his dear friend died."},{"id":"S455","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":"For this reason if a man put in the same place his interest, sanctity, goodness, and country, and parents, and friends, all these are secured: but if he puts in one place his interest, in another his friends, and his country and his kinsmen and justice itself, all these give way being borne down by the weight of interest. For where the I and the Mine are placed, to that place of necessity the animal inclines: if in the flesh, there is the ruling power: if in the will, it is there: and if it is in externals, it is there. If then I am there where my will is, then only shall I be a friend such as I ought to be, and son, and father; for this will be my interest, to maintain the character of fidelity, of modesty, of patience, of abstinence, of active cooperation, of observing my relations (towards all). But if I put myself in one place, and honesty in another, then the doctrine of Epicurus becomes strong, which asserts either that there is no honesty or it is that which opinion holds to be honest (virtuous)."},{"id":"S456","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":9,"paragraphEnd":9,"text":"It was through this ignorance that the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians quarrelled, and the Thebans with both; and the great king quarrelled with Hellas, and the Macedonians with both; and the Romans with the Getae. And still earlier the Trojan war happened for these reasons. Alexander was the guest of Menelaus; and if any man had seen their friendly disposition, he would not have believed anyone who said that they were not friends. But there was cast between them (as between dogs) a bit of meat, a handsome woman, and about her war arose. And now when you see brothers to be friends appearing to have one mind, do not conclude from this anything about their friendship, not even if they swear it and say that it is impossible for them to be separated from one another. For the ruling principle of a bad man cannot be trusted; it is insecure, has no certain rule by which it is directed, and is overpowered at different times by different appearances. But examine, not what other men examine —if they are born of the same parents and brought up together, and under the same pedagogue —but examine this only, wherein they place their interest, whether in externals or in the will. If in externals"},{"id":"S457","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":9,"paragraphEnd":9,"text":", do not name them friends, no more than name them trustworthy or constant, or brave or free: do not name them even men, if you have any judgment. For that is not a principle of human nature which makes them bite one another, and abuse one another, and occupy deserted places or public places, as if they were mountains, and in the courts of justice display the acts of robbers; nor yet that which makes them intemperate and adulterers and corrupters, nor that which makes them do whatever else men do against one another through this one opinion only, that of placing themselves and their interests in the things which are not within the power of their will. But if you hear that in truth these men think the good to be only there, where will is, and where there is a right use of appearances, no longer trouble yourself whether they are father or son, or brothers, or have associated a long time and are companions, but when you have ascertained this only, confidently declare that they are friends, as you declare that they are faithful, that they are just. For where else is friendship than where there is fidelity, and modesty, where there is a communion of honest things and of nothing else?"},{"id":"S458","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":10,"paragraphEnd":10,"text":"But you may say, “such a one treated me with regard so long; and did he not love me?” How do you know, slave, if he did not regard you in the same way as he wipes his shoes with a sponge, or as he takes care of his beast? How do you know, when you have ceased to be useful as a vessel, he will not throw you away like a broken platter? “But this woman is my wife, and we have lived together so long.” And how long did Eriphyle live with Amphiaraus, and was the mother of children and of many? But a necklace came between them: and what is a necklace? It is the opinion about such things. That was the bestial principle, that was the thing which broke asunder the friendship between husband and wife, that which did not allow the woman to be a wife nor the mother to be a mother. And let every man among you who has seriously resolved either to be a friend himself or to have another for his friend, cut out these opinions, hate them, drive them from his soul. And thus first of all he will not reproach himself, he will not be at variance with himself, he will not change his mind, he will not torture himself. In the next place, to another also, who is like himself, he will be altogether and comple"},{"id":"S459","chapter":"XXII: On Friendship","paragraphStart":10,"paragraphEnd":10,"text":"tely a friend. But he will bear with the man who is unlike himself, he will be kind to him, gentle, ready to pardon on account of his ignorance, on account of his being mistaken in things of the greatest importance; but he will be harsh to no man, being well convinced of Plato’s doctrine that every mind is deprived of truth unwillingly. If you cannot do this, yet you can do in all other respects as friends do —drink together, and lodge together, and sail together —and you may be born of the same parents —for snakes also are —but neither will they be friends nor you, so long as you retain these bestial and cursed opinions."},{"id":"S460","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"XXIII"},{"id":"S461","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"On the Power of Speaking"},{"id":"S462","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"Every man will read a book with more pleasure, or even with more ease, if it is written in fairer characters. Therefore every man will also listen more readily to what is spoken, if it is signified by appropriate and becoming words. We must not say then that there is no faculty of expression: for this affirmation is the characteristic of an impious and also of a timid man. Of an impious man, because he undervalues the gifts which come from God, just as if he would take away the commodity of the power of vision, or of hearing, or of seeing. Has then God given you eyes to no purpose? and to no purpose has he infused into them a spirit so strong and of such skillful contrivance as to reach a long way and to fashion the forms of things which are seen? What messenger is so swift and vigilant? And to no purpose has he made the interjacent atmosphere so efficacious and elastic that the vision penetrates through the atmosphere which is in a manner moved? And to no purpose has he made light, without the presence of which there would be no use in any other thing?"},{"id":"S463","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"Man, be neither ungrateful for these gifts nor yet forget the things which are superior to them. But indeed for the power of seeing and hearing, and indeed for life itself, and for the things which contribute to support it, for the fruits which are dry, and for wine and oil give thanks to God. But remember that he has given you something else better than all these: I mean the power of using them, proving them and estimating the value of each. For what is that which gives information about each of these powers, what each of them is worth? Is it each faculty itself? Did you ever hear the faculty of vision saying anything about itself? or the faculty of hearing? or wheat, or barley, or a horse or a dog? No; but they are appointed as ministers and slaves to serve the faculty which has the power of making use of the appearances of things. And if you inquire what is the value of each thing, of whom do you inquire? who answers you? How then can any other faculty be more powerful than this, which uses the rest as ministers and itself proves each and pronounces about them? for which of them knows what itself is, and what is its own value? which of them knows when it ought to employ itself a"},{"id":"S464","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"nd when not? what faculty is it which opens and closes the eyes, and turns them away from objects to which it ought not to apply them and does apply them to other objects? Is it the faculty of vision? No; but it is the faculty of the will. What is that faculty which closes and opens the ears? what is that by which they are curious and inquisitive, or on the contrary unmoved by what is said? is it the faculty of hearing? It is no other than the faculty of the will. Will this faculty then, seeing that it is amidst all the other faculties which are blind and dumb and unable to see anything else except the very acts for which they are appointed in order to minister to this (faculty) and serve it, but this faculty alone sees sharp and sees what is the value of each of the rest; will this faculty declare to us that anything else is the best, or that itself is? And what else does the eye do when it is opened than see? But whether we ought to look on the wife of a certain person, and in what manner, who tells us? The faculty of the will. And whether we ought to believe what is said or not to believe it, and if we do believe, whether we ought to be moved by it or not, who tells us? Is it no"},{"id":"S465","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"t the faculty of the will? But this faculty of speaking and of ornamenting words, if there is indeed any such peculiar faculty, what else does it do, when there happens to be discourse about a thing, than to ornament the words and arrange them as hairdressers do the hair? But whether it is better to speak or to be silent, and better to speak in this way or that way, and whether this is becoming or not becoming, and the season for each and the use, what else tells us than the faculty of the will? Would you have it then to come forward and condemn itself?"},{"id":"S466","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"What then? it (the will) says, if the fact is so, can that which ministers be superior to that to which it ministers, can the horse be superior to the rider, or the dog to the huntsman, or the instrument to the musician, or the servants to the king? What is that which makes use of the rest? The will. What takes care of all? The will. What destroys the whole man, at one time by hunger, at another time by hanging, and at another time by a precipice? The will. Then is anything stronger in men than this? and how is it possible that the things which are subject to restraint are stronger than that which is not? What things are naturally formed to hinder the faculty of vision? Both will and things which do not depend on the faculty of the will. It is the same with the faculty of hearing, with the faculty of speaking in like manner. But what has a natural power of hindering the will? Nothing which is independent of the will; but only the will itself, when it is perverted. Therefore this (the will) is alone vice or alone virtue."},{"id":"S467","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"Then being so great a faculty and set over all the rest, let it (the will) come forward and tell us that the most excellent of all things is the flesh. Not even if the flesh itself declared that it is the most excellent, would any person bear that it should say this. But what is it, Epicurus, which pronounces this, which wrote about the End (purpose) of our Being, which wrote on the Nature of Things, which wrote about the Canon (rule of truth), which led you to wear a beard, which wrote when it was dying that it was spending the last and a happy day? Was this the flesh or the will? Then do you admit that you possess anything superior to this (the will)? and are you not mad? are you in fact so blind and deaf?"},{"id":"S468","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"What then? does any man despise the other faculties? I hope not. Does any man say that there is no use or excellence in the speaking faculty? I hope not. That would be foolish, impious, ungrateful towards God. But a man renders to each thing its due value. For there is some use even in an ass, but not so much as in an ox: there is also use in a dog, but not so much as in a slave: there is also some use in a slave, but not so much as in citizens: there is also some use in citizens, but not so much as in magistrates. Not indeed because some things are superior, must we undervalue the use which other things have. There is a certain value in the power of speaking, but it is not so great as the power of the will. When then I speak thus, let no man think that I ask you to neglect the power of speaking, for neither do I ask you to neglect the eyes, nor the ears nor the hands nor the feet, nor clothing nor shoes. But if you ask me what then is the most excellent of all things, what must I say? I cannot say the power of speaking, but the power of the will, when it is right (ὀρθὴ). For it is this which uses the other (the power of speaking), and all the other faculties both small and great. "},{"id":"S469","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"For when this faculty of the will is set right, a man who is not good becomes good: but when it fails, a man becomes bad. It is through this that we are unfortunate, that we are fortunate, that we blame one another, are pleased with one another. In a word, it is this which if we neglect it makes unhappiness, and if we carefully look after it, makes happiness."},{"id":"S470","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"But to take away the faculty of speaking and to say that there is no such faculty in reality, is the act not only of an ungrateful man towards those who gave it, but also of a cowardly man: for such a person seems to me to fear, if there is any faculty of this kind, that we shall not be able to despise it. Such also are those who say that there is no difference between beauty and ugliness. Then it would happen that a man would be affected in the same way if he saw Thersites and if he saw Achilles; in the same way, if he saw Helen and any other woman. But these are foolish and clownish notions, and the notions of men who know not the nature of each thing, but are afraid, if a man shall see the difference, that he shall immediately be seized and carried off vanquished. But this is the great matter; to leave to each thing the power (faculty) which it has, and leaving to it this power to see what is the worth of the power, and to learn what is the most excellent of all things, and to pursue this always, to be diligent about this, considering all other things of secondary value compared with this, but yet, as far as we can, not neglecting all those other things. For we must take care of"},{"id":"S471","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":" the eyes also, not as if they were the most excellent thing, but we must take care of them on account of the most excellent thing, because it will not be in its true natural condition, if it does not rightly use the other faculties, and prefer some things to others."},{"id":"S472","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":"What then is usually done? Men generally act as a traveller would do on his way to his own country, when he enters a good inn, and being pleased with it should remain there. Man, you have forgotten your purpose: you were not travelling to this inn, but you were passing through it. “But this is a pleasant inn.” And how many other inns are pleasant? and how many meadows are pleasant? yet only for passing through. But your purpose is this, to return to your country, to relieve your kinsmen of anxiety, to discharge the duties of a citizen, to marry, to beget children, to fill the usual magistracies. For you are not come to select more pleasant places, but to live in these where you were born and of which you were made a citizen. Something of the kind takes place in the matter which we are considering. Since by the aid of speech and such communication as you receive here you must advance to perfection, and purge your will and correct the faculty which makes use of the appearances of things; and since it is necessary also for the teaching (delivery) of theorems to be effected by a certain mode of expression and with a certain variety and sharpness, some persons captivated by these very t"},{"id":"S473","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":"hings abide in them, one captivated by the expression, another by syllogisms, another again by sophisms, and still another by some other inn (πανδοκείου) of the kind; and there they stay and waste away as if they were among Sirens."},{"id":"S474","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":9,"paragraphEnd":9,"text":"Man, your purpose (business) was to make yourself capable of using comformably to nature the appearances presented to you, in your desires not to be frustrated, in your aversion from things not to fall into that which you would avoid, never to have no luck (as one may say), nor ever to have bad luck, to be free, not hindered, not compelled, conforming yourself to the administration of Zeus, obeying it, well satisfied with this, blaming no one, charging no one with fault, able from your whole soul to utter these verses"},{"id":"S475","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":10,"paragraphEnd":10,"text":"Lead me, O Zeus, and thou too Destiny."},{"id":"S476","chapter":"XXIII: On the Power of Speaking","paragraphStart":11,"paragraphEnd":11,"text":"Then having this purpose before you, if some little form of expression pleases you, if some theorems please you, do you abide among them and choose to dwell there, forgetting the things at home, and do you say, “These things are fine?” Who says that they are not fine? but only as being a way home, as inns are. For what hinders you from being an unfortunate man, even if you speak like Demosthenes? and what prevents you, if you can resolve syllogisms like Chrysippus, from being wretched, from sorrowing, from envying, in a word, from being disturbed, from being unhappy? Nothing. You see then that these were inns, worth nothing; and that the purpose before you was something else. When I speak thus to some persons, they think that I am rejecting care about speaking or care about theorems. But I am not rejecting this care, but I am rejecting the abiding about these things incessantly and putting our hopes in them. If a man by this teaching does harm to those who listen to him, reckon me too among those who do this harm: for I am not able, when I see one thing which is most excellent and supreme, to say that another is so, in order to please you."},{"id":"S477","chapter":"XXIV: To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"XXIV"},{"id":"S478","chapter":"XXIV: To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him"},{"id":"S479","chapter":"XXIV: To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"A certain person said to him (Epictetus): “Frequently I desired to hear you and came to you, and you never gave me any answer: and now, if it is possible, I entreat you to say something to me.” Do you think, said Epictetus, that as there is an art in anything else, so there is also an art in speaking, and that he who has the art, will speak skillfully, and he who has not, will speak unskillfully? “I do think so.” He then who by speaking receives benefit himself, and is able to benefit others, will speak skillfully: but he who is rather damaged by speaking and does damage to others, will he be unskilled in this art of speaking? And you may find that some are damaged and others benefited by speaking. And are all who hear benefited by what they hear? Or will you find that among them also some are benefited and some damaged? “There are both among these also,” he said. In this case also then those who hear skillfully are benefited, and those who hear unskillfully are damaged? He admitted this. Is there then a skill in hearing also, as there is in speaking? “It seems so.” If you choose, consider the matter in this way also. The practice of music, to whom does it belong? To a musician. An"},{"id":"S480","chapter":"XXIV: To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"d the proper making of a statue, to whom do you think that it belongs? To a statuary. And the looking at a statue skillfully, does this appear to you to require the aid of no art? “This also requires the aid of art.” Then if speaking properly is the business of the skillful man, do you see that to hear also with benefit is the business of the skillful man? Now as to speaking and hearing perfectly, and usefully, let us for the present, if you please, say no more, for both of us are a long way from everything of the kind. But I think that every man will allow this: that he who is going to hear philosophers requires some amount of practice in hearing. Is it not so?"}],"newWindowIds":["S441","S442","S443","S444","S445","S446","S447","S448","S449","S450","S451","S452","S453","S454","S455","S456","S457","S458","S459","S460","S461","S462","S463","S464","S465","S466","S467","S468","S469","S470","S471","S472","S473","S474","S475","S476","S477","S478","S479","S480"]}
requests.raw: {"notes":[{"text":"Inkonsistensi moral: orang menganggap ketakutan, kasih sayang, cemburu, dan nafsu 'tidak disengaja' untuk membenarkan diri, tetapi ketidakadilan dianggap disengaja. Menghadapi murid yang datang ke sekolah hanya untuk menguasai syllogisme sambil bertengkar dengan budak di rumah; mereka membawa pulang persis yang mereka bawa—teorema tidak berguna bagi yang salah guna, seperti cuka tidak berguna bagi penderita disentri sebelum luka disembuhkan. Alasan mesti dibawa ke sekolah tenang dan bebas distraksi.","source_ids":["S441","S444","S445"]},{"text":"Persahabatan: hanya orang bijak yang mampu mencintai, karena cinta memerlukan pengetahuan tentang Baik. Setiap makhluk terikat pada kepentingannya sendiri; bila kepentingan diletakkan pada hal eksternal, saudara atau ayah pun bisa jadi musuh—seperti anjing yang bertengkar saat sepotong daging dilempar di antara mereka (Eteocles-Polynices, Alexander membakar kuil Aesculapius). Persahabatan sejati ada hanya bila kepentingan diletakkan pada will dan penggunaan penampakan yang benar.","source_ids":["S448","S454","S455"]},{"text":"Uji persahabatan: jangan percaya pada sumpah atau lahir dari orang tua sama—periksa di mana kepentingan orang itu diletakkan (hal luar atau will). 'Kamu menemani saya lama—tahu kamu tidak ia memperlakukanmu seperti membasuh sepatu dengan spons?'; kalung Eriphyle (opini tentang barang) merusak pernikahan Amphiaraus. Yang menempatkan diri pada will akan menjadi teman sejati dan memaafkan yang berbeda karena kebodohan (doktrin Plato: jiwa dirampas kebenaran dengan tak rela).","source_ids":["S456","S458","S459"]},{"text":"Kekuatan berbicara adalah hadiah Tuhan; menyangkalnya tidak syukur dan pengecut. Namun fakultas will adalah yang tertinggi: ia menggunakan semua fakultas lain sebagai pelayan, menilai nilai setiap fakultas, membuka-tutup mata dan telinga; hanya will sendiri yang bisa menghambat will—maka will itulah satu-satunya kebajikan atau kejahatan. Kritik Epicurus yang memposisikan daging sebagai yang terutama padahal daging tidak bisa menulis tentang tujuan hidup.","source_ids":["S462","S464","S466","S467"]},{"text":"Kekuatan bicara dan teorema hanyalah 'penginapan' di jalan pulang: jangan berhenti dan tinggal di sana seperti pelancong yang lupa tujuannya, terpikat pada ungkapan, syllogisme, atau sophisme seperti di antara Sirens. Tujuan sejati: menggunakan penampakan sesuai alam, desire tidak frustrasi, bebas, taat pada administrasi Zeus, tanpa menyalahkan siapa pun ('Lead me, O Zeus, and thou too Destiny'). Bicara seperti Demosthenes atau memecahkan syllogisme seperti Chrysippus tidak mencegah kecelakaan.","source_ids":["S472","S474","S476"]},{"text":"Ada juga seni mendengar: sebagaimana mendengar musik milik musisi dan menilai patung memerlukan seni, mendengar filsuf dengan bermanfaat memerlukan latihan khusus; tidak semua pendengar teruntung—yang mendengar terampil teruntung, yang tidak terampil merugi.","source_ids":["S479","S480"]}]}
