requests.user: {"question":"apa gagasan utama buku ini?","book":"Discourses","examinedBefore":480,"totalWindows":957,"previousNotes":[{"text":"Tesis utama buku: hanya penggunaan yang benar atas penampakan (right use of appearances) yang berada dalam kuasa kita; fakultas rasional adalah satu-satunya yang dapat mengkontemplasi dirinya sendiri dan menilai fakultas lain. Segala hal lain (tubuh, harta, orang tercinta) di luar kuasa kita; manusia menderita karena terikat pada banyak hal eksternal.","source_ids":["S3","S5","S6"]},{"text":"Kunci ketenangan: selalu membedakan apa milikku dan bukan milikku. Kematian, penjara, pengasingan harus dihadapi tanpa ratapan — tubuh bisa dibelenggu, tetapi kemauan (will) tidak bisa ditaklukkan bahkan oleh Zeus. Contoh: Lateranus mengulurkan leher dengan tenang; Agrippinus tetap makan setelah dijatuhi hukuman pengasingan.","source_ids":["S9","S11","S12"]},{"text":"Menjaga karakter (proper character): yang rasional selalu diterima, yang irasional tak tertanggungkan — karena itu kita butuh disiplin. Agrippinus menolak ikut tontonan Nero: ia ingin menjadi 'ungu' pada jubah, bukan sekadar satu benang biasa; Priscus Helvidius tetap bersuara di senat meski Vespasian mengancam mati — tugas kaisar membunuh, tugasnya mati tanpa takut.","source_ids":["S15","S18","S19"]},{"text":"Allah adalah bapa semua manusia: manusia memiliki kekerabatan ganda — tubuh bersama hewan, nalar bersama dewa. Yang banyak condong pada daging dan menjadi seperti serigala, singa, atau rubah; sebagian kecil yang mengenali asal ilahiah tidak memiliki pikiran rendah tentang dirinya.","source_ids":["S27","S29"]},{"text":"Kemajuan (progres) bukan menguasai banyak buku filsafat, tetapi melatih desire dan aversion agar tidak gagal memperoleh yang diinginkan atau jatuh pada yang dihindari; bukti kemajuan adalah keadaan kemauan yang bebas, setia, dan sederhana dalam tindakan sehari-hari. Tragedi adalah gambaran gejolak orang yang menghargai hal eksternal.","source_ids":["S32","S36","S37"]},{"text":"Gagasan utama: manusia adalah makhluk rasional, kerabat/kepunyaan Tuhan; tujuan hidup adalah menggunakan akal dengan benar — memahami penggunaan penampakan, bukan sekadar memakainya seperti hewan. Alam berakhir pada kontemplasi dan hidup sesuai alam; memulai dan berakhir seperti hewan adalah memalukan.","source_ids":["S48","S49"]},{"text":"Providence: dari segala yang ada dan terjadi mudah memuji providensi bila memiliki dua hal — kemampuan melihat kegunaan segala hal dan watak bersyukur. Kesesuaian struktur dunia (mata, cahaya, warna) membuktikan Sang Pencipta.","source_ids":["S46","S47"]},{"text":"Kesulitan hidup adalah sarana latihan kebajikan: seperti Hercules membutuhkan singa dan hydra, manusia diberi kebesaran jiwa, keberanian, dan ketahanan untuk menanggung apa pun yang terjadi; mengeluh dan menyalahkan dewa adalah kekufuran akibat jiwa yang hina.","source_ids":["S52","S53"]},{"text":"Kekerasan kepalaan (menolak kebenaran yang jelas) ada dua macam: pada akal dan pada rasa malu. Orang yang melihat kontradiksi tetapi tidak berubah lebih buruk dari orang yang tidak melihat — akalnya tidak hilang melainkan dibinatangkan; itu bukan kekuatan budi.","source_ids":["S42","S43"]},{"text":"Logika dan argumen dialektis adalah kewajiban hidup: cukup tidak hanya mengetahui prinsip membedakan benar-salah, tetapi harus ada kemahiran seperti membedakan drachma asli-palsu. Namun bila premis berubah makna, kita boleh menarik persetujuan dari konsekuensinya.","source_ids":["S57","S60"]},{"text":"Kerabat dengan Tuhan: jangan menyebut diri warga Athena melainkan warga dunia (kosmopolites); komunitas tertinggi adalah manusia dan Tuhan. Contoh Socrates yang memilih mati daripada meninggalkan tugas yang Tuhan tempatkan; tubuh dan harta bukan kekuatan tiran atas kita.","source_ids":["S72","S78"]},{"text":"Gagasan utama: manusia berkerabat dengan Tuhan sehingga memiliki dari dalam dirinya sendiri hal-hal terpenting (kemuliaan jiwa); orang penakut dan hina hanyalah 'mayat dan segayung darah', dan tidak ada orang yang membuat orang lain sengsara—yang benar-benar berharga tidak diperoleh dari orang lain (tanah, uang, jabatan).","source_ids":["S81"]},{"text":"Epictetus mengkritik mereka yang mengejar jabatan di Roma: orang tua yang bersumpah akan hidup tenang setelah pengasingan langsung melupakan segalanya begitu menerima surat dari Caesar. Manusia memang dibuat untuk bekerja, tetapi pekerjaan yang benar adalah mempelajari administrasi dunia dan siapa diri kita, bukan urusan biji gandum dan tanah.","source_ids":["S84","S86"]},{"text":"Dialog tentang kasih sayang alami: meninggalkan anak yang sakit bukanlah tindakan penyayang—kasih sayang harus konsisten dengan rasio; yang keduanya penyayang dan rasional itulah yang benar dan baik. Kita butuh kriteria (bukan sekadar 'semua orang melakukannya') untuk menilai baik-buruk, seperti penglihatan untuk warna.","source_ids":["S92","S93","S94"]},{"text":"Sebab segala tindakan adalah will/opini (dogma) kita sendiri, bukan hal luar: bukan kematian Patroklus yang membuat Achilles meratap, tetapi pilihannya. Kematian, pengasingan, atau rasa sakit tidak menyebabkan kita berbuat apa pun; kita harus membuang opini salah seperti membuang tumor, dan hanya memeriksa opini, bukan tanah, budak, atau kuda.","source_ids":["S96","S97","S98"]},{"text":"Kebahagiaan (contentment): manusia harus meneliti pendapat tentang para dewa lalu menundukkan pikirannya kepada Yang mengatur semuanya seperti warga yang taat pada hukum. Kebebasan adalah belajar menginginkan segala sesuatu terjadi sebagaimana terjadi; yang tidak menerima hukumannya adalah menjadi dirinya sendiri—di mana ia berada dengan tidak rela, di situ ia dipenjara (Socrates tidak dipenjara karena ada dengan rela).","source_ids":["S103","S104","S107"]},{"text":"Tuhan mengawasi segala hal: jiwa kita adalah bagian dan potongan dari Tuhan, dan setiap manusia diberi penjaga (daimon) yang tidak pernah tidur; kita harus bersumpah kepada Tuhan—tidak pernah membangkang, tidak mencela apa yang diberikan, dan tidak dengan enggan melakukan atau menderita apa yang perlu—sumpah yang menghormati diri sendiri, bukan Caesar.","source_ids":["S115","S117","S118"]},{"text":"Filosofi tidak menjanjikan hal eksternal apa pun; materinya adalah hidup orang itu sendiri. Angka saudara marah bukan wilayahnya — ia hanya menjamin bagian penguasa (governing part) selalu sesuai alam. Kebenaran besar tidak terbentuk tiba-tiba, seperti buah ara butuh waktu matang.","source_ids":["S121","S123"]},{"text":"Providence terlihat bahkan dalam hal kecil: susu dari rumput, keju dari susu, rambut dagu sebagai tanda pembeda pria-wanita. Hymn kepada Tuhan harus dinyanyikan terus — Epictetus menyebut dirinya makhluk rasional yang tugasnya memuji Tuhan; 'jika aku burungNightangle aku menyanyi seperti nightangle, tetapi aku makhluk rasional, maka aku memuji Tuhan.'","source_ids":["S127","S128","S129"]},{"text":"Seni logis diperlukan karena akal menganalisis fakultas lain dan harus menganalisis dirinya sendiri; tanpa kriteria (seperti modius untuk gandum) tidak ada pengukuran akurat. Kita tidak butuh Chrysippus karena dirinya, tetapi untuk memahami kehendak alam.","source_ids":["S133","S136"]},{"text":"Kebebasan will terbukti: tak ada yang bisa memaksa assent pada yang palsu atau menghalangi assent pada yang benar. Yang memaksa bukan yang diletakkan di depan (ketakutan akan mati), melainkan opini kita sendiri — will memaksa will. Jika memilih, kita bebas, tidak menyalahkan siapa pun; segala jadi sesuai kehendak kita dan Tuhan.","source_ids":["S137","S138"]},{"text":"Jangan marah pada kesalahan orang lain: pelaku salah adalah yang keliru tentang baik-buruk, seperti buta — layak dikasihani bukan dibenci. Kita marah karena menghargai hal yang dicuri; jangan menghargai pakaian, tak akan marah pada pencuri. Latih diri dari hal kecil (sakit kepala tanpa 'alas!') menuju yang besar.","source_ids":["S141","S143","S145"]},{"text":"Tiran hanya menguasai tubuh (kaki, leher), tidak akan (will). Yang membuat orang takut bukan tiran dan pengawalnya, melainkan opini sendiri. Manusia yang ditunjuk Caesar jadi tukang sepatunya langsung tampak bijak di mata orang — nilai yang salah. Bakat dirinya mencakup memikirkan diri sendiri, dan karena manusia rasional tak bisa memperoleh kepentingannya sendiri tanpa berkontribusi pada kepentingan bersama, mementingkan diri tidak kontrasosial.","source_ids":["S151","S152","S154"]},{"text":"Akal sendiri berasal dari penampakan (system of appearances) sehingga bisa mengkhawati dirinya sendiri; tugas pertama filosof adalah memeriksa penampakan tanpa menerima tanpa ujian. Doktrin filosof sangat singkat: tujuan manusia mengikuti para dewa, dan baik adalah penggunaan penampakan yang tepat; kata-kata panjang hanya perlu menjelaskan apa Tuhan, penampakan, dan alam.","source_ids":["S158","S160"]},{"text":"Kritik terhadap Epicurus: kendati mengakui manusia bersifat sosial, ia menempatkan kebaikan pada 'kulitnya' sehingga menyarankan orang bijak tidak membesarkan anak—padahal begitu anak lahir, sayang padanya di luar kuasa kita; bahkan domba dan serigala tidak meninggalkan anaknya. Orang bijak seharusnya terlibat urusan publik, bukan memperlakukan manusia seperti sekawanan lalat.","source_ids":["S174","S175"]},{"text":"Kesulitan adalah lawan sparring dari Tuhan: seperti pelatih gulat mencocokkan kita dengan pemuda tangguh agar menjadi juara Olimpiade. Diogenes adalah penembak ronda teladan—melaporkan kematian bukan jahat, ketenaran gemuruh orang gila, hidup telanjang dan tidur di tanah lebih baik, dengan bukti ketenangan dan kebebasannya sendiri; penembak ronda penakut yang lapor musuh dekat hanya layak disuruh pulang.","source_ids":["S178","S179"]},{"text":"Hidup seperti berperan: manusia hanya boleh membawa yang miliknya (kirimannya), bukan kemudi atau dayung kapal—hal luar boleh dicabut satu per satu (toga, tubuh) tanpa takut. Harta seperti tempat tidur di penginapan; tragedi hanya terjadi pada orang kaya dan raja, orang miskin tidak punya peran tragis; bila permainan tidak menyenangkan, 'aku tidak bermain lagi'—pintu terbuka.","source_ids":["S180","S181","S182"]},{"text":"Perintah Zeus sudah cukup: jaga apa milikmu (integritas, rasa malu yang baik), jangan menginginkan milik orang lain; bila memegangnya tidak perlu arahan lain. Hidup itu permainan Saturnalia: patuh raja yang ditunjuk agar permainan tidak kacau, tetapi tidak ada yang memaksa kita berpikir menderita—seperti hipotesis logika, boleh menyanggupi 'sial', tetapi Zeus melarang menganggap diri hina.","source_ids":["S186","S187","S188"]},{"text":"Kita yang menghimpit diri sendiri lewat opini: ingin duduk di tempat senator menghimpit; hinaan hanya efektif lewat kelemahan orang yang dihinakan—jika mendengar seperti batu, tidak ada untungnya. Yang dijaga itulah yang diserang: bila menaruh hormat pada tubuh atau harta kecil, di situlah kita jadi budak. Socrates selalu satu wajah karena mempraktikkan kebebasan tanpa hambatan.","source_ids":["S189","S190","S191","S192"]},{"text":"Hukum hidup mendahului hukum hipotesis logis: bertindak sesuai alam adalah hukum dasar; filsuf melatih teori dulu (lebih mudah) baru urusan hidup yang lebih sulit. Awal filsafat adalah menyadari kelemahan fakultas penuntun—yang tak bisa menelan sepotong pun membeli seluruh jilid lalu memuntahkannya; orang membaca argumen hipotetis hanya untuk dipuji orang senatori (contoh: pengeluh punya 1,5 juta denarii yang membuat Epaphroditus tercengang, bukan mentertawakan).","source_ids":["S195","S196","S199"]},{"text":"Empat cara penampakan muncul; tugas orang terdidik menilai dengan benar. Ramuan melawan kebiasaan adalah kebiasaan yang berlawanan; melawan penampakan menipu adalah prekognisi yang bersih; melawan kematian—ia perlu dan bukan kejahatan, jadi tanpa rasa takut. Ketiadaan kesalehan lahir karena piety dan kepentingan pribadi dianggap terpisah.","source_ids":["S202","S205"]},{"text":"Jangan marah kepada orang lain: jiwa hanya menyetujui yang tampak benar (Plato: jiwa kehilangan kebenaran dengan tak rela); Medea terlilit karena mengira balas dendam lebih menguntungkan. Orang sesat pada fakultas tertinggi patut dikasihani seperti orang buta, bukan dibenci. Segala tindakan diukur oleh penampakan.","source_ids":["S210","S212","S213"]},{"text":"Iliad hanyalah penampakan dan penggunaannya: pembakaran Troya tidak lebih dahsyat dari sarang bangau yang terbakar—bedanya manusia memiliki kejujuran, kemoderatan, kesetiaan, kecerdasan. Kehancuran sejati adalah kehancuran opini benar: Alexander hancur saat kehilangan karakter, Achilles saat marah dan lupa tugasnya.","source_ids":["S214","S216","S217"]},{"text":"Esensi Baik adalah kemauan; hal luar hanya bahan bagi kemauan. Hukum Allah: ambil kebaikan dari dirimu sendiri. Tirani hanya mengancam tubuh; tidak ada yang lebih kuat daripada kemauan kecuali kemauan sendiri—sepuluh orang lebih kuat dalam mengekang, tetapi tidak dalam opini yang benar.","source_ids":["S222","S224"]},{"text":"Socrates menafsir ulang: yang dibawa ke penjara hanyalah 'tubuh miskinnya'; 'Anytus dan Melitus dapat membunuhku, tetapi tidak menyakitiku.' Kesulitan adalah ujian pembelajaran: seperti atlet yang ingin lawan berat, orang terdidik harus menunjukkan ajarannya dalam praktik, bukan argumen kecil di sudut sekolah; jadilah saksi Allah bahwa yang eksternal bukan baik atau jahat.","source_ids":["S226","S232","S235"]},{"text":"Pelayan yang baik menghormati semua orang sesuai 'relasi': ayah, saudara, keabadian—mengingat bahwa adalah watak dewata mempertahankan diri dari mimpi dan kecenderungan; putusan orang yang belum terdidik tentang kesalehan tidak lebih penting daripada seorang musisi yang salah menilai tali lyre. Hamba yang lari menikmati teater dengan ketakutan; membebaskan diri dari 'majikan' (kematian, kesenangan, sakit) menghapus seluruh ketakutan.","source_ids":["S236","S238","S239"]},{"text":"Sikap yang harus disiapkan dalam kesulitan: saat menghadapi orang besar, ingat ada yang melihat dari atas; pengasingan, penjara, mati, aib tetap hal indiferen yang tak berubah — hanya hal di luar kemauan yang 'tak ada bagiku'; Baik adalah kemauan sebagaimana mestinya dan penggunaan penampakan; tujuan hidup adalah mengikuti Tuhan. YAng begitu belajar akan berani karena tahu semua persiapan gelar-gelar kuasa 'bukanlah apa-apa'.","source_ids":["S243","S244"]},{"text":"Percaya diri dan kehati-hatian tidak bertentangan bila diterapkan pada objek berbeda: kehati-hatian pada hal dalam kemauan (satu-satunya jahat), keberanian pada hal di luar kemauan. Manusia terbalik seperti rusa yang takut pada bulu pemburu lalu lari ke jaring: takut pada kematian, sakit, aib (hal luar) tetapi gegabah pada tipu, nafsu, aib tindakan (hal will). Bukan kematian yang menakutkan, melainkan ketakutan pada kematian.","source_ids":["S247","S248","S249"]},{"text":"Kematian dan sakit adalah 'topeng tragedi': putar dan periksa — tidak menggigit; pintu selalu terbuka bila tak tertahankan. Kebebasan sejati adalah milik yang terdidik: hidup tanpa kesalahan, takut, duka, dan gejolak adalah bebas; budak yang dibebaskan di pengadilan tetap tak bebas bila uang, kekasih, atau tiran jadi majikannya. Socrates menulis untuk menguji dirinya sendiri dalam praktik, bukan karya-karya kosong; pamer sejati pemuda terdidik adalah 'sajikan kematian, penjara, siksaan — aku tak kecewa dan tak jatuh'.","source_ids":["S252","S254","S257","S258"]},{"text":"Ketenangan dalam perkara (contoh: ke pengadilan): bila tujuannya mempertahankan will sesuai alam, aman penuh — tak ada yang menguasainya; bila ingin mempertahankan hal luar, siaplah jadi budak penuh (berlutut, menangis). Socrates seumur hidup bersiap menghadapi sidang karena tak pernah berbuat zalim. Minta 'saran untuk setiap kejadian' seperti orang buta huruf minta tahu nama apa yang akan ditulis; latihan membuat siap untuk semua, dan yang mengejar hal luar pasti terombang-ambing pada kehendak majikannya.","source_ids":["S262","S263","S264","S267"]},{"text":"Magnanimitas konsisten dengan kehati-hatian lewat analogi meja judi: keping dan dadanya indiferen, tetapi penggunaan lemparan harus cermat — hal luar tak milik kita, will milik kita; gunakan hal luar dengan hati-hati karena penggunaannya bukan indiferen, sambil tetap tenang karena materinya indiferen. Seperti pelayaran: pilih kapten, pelaut, waktu; datang badai, tugas kita selesai — bila kapal tenggelam, lakukan satu-satunya yang bisa: tidak tenggelam.","source_ids":["S279","S280"]},{"text":"Manusia dibentuk untuk kesetiaan (fidelity); perusaknya meruntuhkan ciri khas manusia: kesopanan, kesucian, hubungan tetangga, persahabatan, komunitas — jadilah serigala atau kera, dan layak dibuang seperti peralatan rusak ke tumpukan kotoran. Argumen 'wanita memang bersifat umum secara alam' dibantah dengan analogi: babi dan teater juga umum bagi semua, tetapi setelah dibagikan, mencuri porsi orang lain adalah perampokan.","source_ids":["S274","S276"]},{"text":"Metafora permainan bola: keahlian ada pada melempar dan menangkap, bukan pada bola itu sendiri — bola (hal eksternal) harus dianggap tak berharga. Socrates bermain bola di pengadilannya: omongannya yang menyenangkan pada Anytus adalah lemparan; bolanya adalah hidup, belenggu, racun. Kita harus mengerahkan seluruh keahlian pada materi eksternal tanpa menghargai materinya, seperti tukang tenun yang mengerjakan wol apa pun yang diterimanya.","source_ids":["S282","S283"]},{"text":"Foot analogy: manusia adalah bagian dari keseluruhan, bukan makhluk terpisah — kaki yang menjejak lumpur atau dipotong demi tubuh masih sesuai alam sebagai kaki; manusia yang sakit, miskin, atau mati muda tetap sesuai alam sebagai bagian dari negara yang pertama (dewa dan manusia). Hidup seperti satu jam dalam sehari: hadir lalu lewat; bagaimana cara berlalunya tak penting.","source_ids":["S281","S285"]},{"text":"Hal indiferen vs penilaiannya: proposisi hipotetis indiferen, tetapi penilaian tentangnya tidak (pengetahuan, opini, atau kekelirian); hidup indiferen, penggunaannya tidak. Maka jangan lalai karenanya, tetapi juga jangan tunduk pada materi. Ingatlah pembagian milikku/bukan milikku — jangan mengklaim milik orang lain (misal: hasil pembicaraan dengan orang lain bukan tanggung jawabmu).","source_ids":["S289","S293"]},{"text":"Kematian itu kutukan bila dihindari: padi yang tidak pernah dipanen adalah kutukan; manusia yang tidak mati seperti tidak matang. Chrysantas menuruti terompet mundur daripada kehendaknya sendiri, sedangkan kita meratap menyebutnya 'keadaan' — padahal semua cara menuju Hades setara, bahkan jalan tiran lebih singkat daripada demam.","source_ids":["S290","S291"]},{"text":"Ramalan/divinasi sering dipakai karena pengecut — ketakutan pada masa depan — hingga melalaikan kewajiban (contoh: perempuan mengirim bantuan ke Gratilla yang diasingkan meski risiko disita Domitian). Konsultasi dengan Tuhan harus tanpa desire/aversion, seperti bertanya arah jalan kepada penumpang atau memakai mata; yang sejati adalah ramal internal dalam diri yang tanda baik-buruk.","source_ids":["S297","S298","S300"]},{"text":"Hakikat Baik: Tuhan bermanfaat, maka Baik ada di mana hakikat Tuhan ada — yaitu nalar benar dan kecerdasan dalam makhluk rasional, bukan pada tumbuhan atau hewan. Manusia adalah bagian terpisah dari dewa, 'membawa Tuhan di dalam dirinya' dan merusaknya dengan pikiran kotor; Tuhan menitipkan diri kita pada diri kita sendiri seperti titipan — jaganya agar sederhana, setia, bebas gejolak. Orang bijak mati dan sakit 'sebagaimana layaknya dewa'.","source_ids":["S303","S305","S307"]},{"text":"Kritik filsuf yang hanya bicara: menempatkan doktrin seperti roti di gudang, bukan yang telah dicerna menjadi daging dan tulang — hanya muncul bila kebisingan atau tawa mengganggu. Gagasan harus dipraktikkan setelah dipelajari; yang gagal memenuhi janji watak manusia (rasional) lalu menambahkan profesi filsuf seperti orang tak mampu mengangkat beban 10 pon mencoba mengangkat batu Ajax. Analogi: disebut Yahudi bukan dengan nama melainkan dengan pemilihan dan afek yang nyata.","source_ids":["S314","S316","S317"]},{"text":"Man adalah warga dunia yang rasional, yang tugasnya adalah bertindak sesuai dengan konstitusi alam dan tatanan ilahi (S321, S322). Karakter yang baik adalah tidak menganggap apa pun menguntungkan bagi diri sendiri dan bertindak sesuai peran (S321).","source_ids":["S321"]},{"text":"Kerusakan sejati bagi manusia bukanlah kehilangan harta atau tubuh, melainkan hilangnya karakter (seperti kesopanan atau ketenangan) yang merupakan bagian dari kehendak (will) (S324, S326).","source_ids":["S324","S326"]},{"text":"Filsafat dimulai dari kesadaran akan kelemahan diri dan ketidakmampuan untuk secara sempurna menyesuaikan prasangka bawaan (seperti baik/buruk) dengan kasus nyata. Tujuannya adalah menemukan aturan (kanonos) yang melampaui sekadar 'tampakan' atau 'perasaan' (S330, S333).","source_ids":["S330","S333"]},{"text":"Kecemasan (anxiety) muncul karena manusia menginginkan hal-hal yang berada di luar kekuasaannya (seperti pujian atau kehendak Caesar). Kepercayaan sejati hanya ada dalam penguasaan keadaan internal (keinginan dan keengganannya) (S347, S348).","source_ids":["S347","S348"]},{"text":"Tujuan praktis filsafat adalah menyesuaikan kehendak (will) dengan apa yang terjadi, sehingga seseorang dapat menjalani hidup tanpa ketakutan atau gangguan, baik dalam urusan pribadi maupun sosial (S358, S359).","source_ids":["S358","S359"]},{"text":"Langkah awal dalam filsafat adalah mempelajari providensi Tuhan dan berusaha meniru sifat-sifat ilahi (seperti kesetiaan dan kebebasan) dalam tindakan dan perkataan (S360).","source_ids":["S360"]},{"text":"Membedakan 'menggunakan' dan 'memahami': orang banyak memakai kata baik-buruk seperti buta huruf memakai tulisan atau hewan memakai penampakan. Seseorang yang kaya, punya keluarga dan teman Caesar, tetapi tak tahu apa itu Tuhan, manusia, baik dan jahat — bahkan tak tahu tentang dirinya sendiri. Kebenaran seperti cermin atau dokter: bukan penghinaan, meski orang mengeluh dihina bila dikatakan keinginannya menyala dan opiniannya gegabah.","source_ids":["S361","S362"]},{"text":"Mayoritas manusia seperti hewan di pasar: hanya sibuk dengan 'pakan' (harta, tanah, budak, jabatan). Sedikit yang datang untuk memperhatikan tatanan dunia — siapa yang mengaturnya, apa relasi kita dengan pengatur itu — dan karena itu ditertawakan banyak orang, seperti penonton ditertawakan pedagang di pasar.","source_ids":["S363","S364"]},{"text":"Kekerasan kepalaan pada keputusan bukanlah keteguhan: yang tetap dipegang hanyalah keputusan yang benar, seperti otot yang sehat, bukan kejang orang gila. Contoh teman yang memutuskan mati kelaparan tanpa alasan; jiwa sakit yang menambah keputusan gegabah jadi tak terbantu — 'orang bodoh tak bisa diyakinkan maupun dipecahkan'.","source_ids":["S367","S368","S370"]},{"text":"Baik ada di kemauan, jahat di kemauan, keduanya tidak ada di luar kemauan — tetapi kita tak pernah berlatih memberi jawaban benar di luar sekolah (ketika uang ditunjukkan: uang bukan baik). Rhetorician dan pemain lute gemetar di atas panggung karena tak dilatih tentang pujian dan cemoohan; ketakutan dan kecemasan bukan pekerjaan orang lain. Latihan sejati: takut pada ketakutan itu sendiri, bukan pada kematian atau pengasingan.","source_ids":["S373","S374","S377"]},{"text":"Yang memberatkan kita hanyalah opini: di laut lepas Epictetus sendiri terbayang harus meneguk seluruh laut, padahal tiga pint cukup. Kesedihan perpisahan seperti anak menangis ditinggal pengasuh — orang dewasa juga menangis untuk gimnasium, portikos, air Dirce, Akropolis; perlu 'disapih' ke makanan yang lebih padat. Hukum ilahi: jagakan milikmu, gunakan yang diberikan, serahkan kembali dengan senang hati.","source_ids":["S377","S379","S380","S383"]},{"text":"Membuang kembung diri (self-conceit) adalah tugas pertama filsuf: mustahil belajar apa yang sudah diyakini tahu. Preconception (prolepsis) tentang baik dan sehat sudah kita punya, tetapi tak bisa disesuaikan dengan kasus tanpa analisis dan definisi — sebab itu orang berdebat, seperti dokter terbelah sebelum Hippocrates. Bukti ketidakcocokan: keinginan yang tak terjadi. Medea punya opini benar bahwa keinginan gagal adalah sengsara, tapi salah tahu cara memenuhinya — jangan menginginkan yang di luar kuasa; serahkan desire/aversion kepada para dewa.","source_ids":["S389","S390","S392","S393","S394"]},{"text":"Melawan penampakan lewat kebiasaan: setiap tindakan memperkuat kebiasaannya — marah atau takabur menambah kebiasaan itu seperti menambah bahan bakar api; penyakit jiwa meninggalkan bekas (luka) yang bila tak dihapus total akan kambuh lebih parah. Obatnya: hitung hari tanpa marah, dan saat penampakan datang, tahan dulu — 'tunggu sedikit, biar aku lihat apa kamu' — lalu lawan dengan penampakan yang indah dan mulia. Kemenangan atas penampakan inilah atlet sejati, demi kerajaan, kebebasan, dan ketenangan.","source_ids":["S403","S404","S407","S409"]},{"text":"Kritik pada yang menerima filsafat hanya dalam kata-kata: mengetahui pembagian baik-buruk-indiferen dari Chrysippus atau Cleanthes tidak berbeda dari hafalan sejarah Homer; ujian sejati adalah apakah pembagian itu diingat saat badai di kapal atau saat dipanggil ke pengadilan Caesar. 'Tunjukkan aku seorang Stoik' — orang yang sakit, mati, diasingkan, dan tetap bahagia; bukan sekadar yang mengulang argumen kecil. Sekolah Epictetus bertujuan membuat murid bebas dan bahagia, dan satu-satunya yang dalam kuasa kita adalah penggunaan penampakan yang benar.","source_ids":["S420","S421","S422","S424"]},{"text":"Bantahan terhadap Epicurus dan Akademik: mereka yang menyangkal kebenaran justru memakainya — 'percayalah bahwa tak ada yang perlu dipercaya' adalah kontradiksi. Epicurus menyangkal persaudaraan alami manusia tetapi bangun tidur dan menulis buku untuk memperingatkan orang lain — sifat manusia yang tak terbantahkan memaksanya; seperti tanaman tak bisa tumbuh melawan jenisnya, manusia tak bisa menghapus afeksi kemanusiaan. Doktrin yang merusak kesalehan dan keadilan merusak negara, padahal Sparta dan Thermopylae dibangun dari opini yang sebaliknya.","source_ids":["S428","S429","S431","S434"]},{"text":"Ketidakkonsistenan orang dalam mengakui kesalahan: tak ada yang mengaku bodoh atau tidak adil, tetapi banyak yang mengaku penakut dan penyayang — karena kebingungan tentang baik-buruk; mereka menganggap ketakutan ciri watak baik dan tak mengakui kesalahan terhadap masyarakat.","source_ids":["S440"]},{"text":"Inkonsistensi moral: orang menganggap ketakutan, kasih sayang, cemburu, dan nafsu 'tidak disengaja' untuk membenarkan diri, tetapi ketidakadilan dianggap disengaja. Menghadapi murid yang datang ke sekolah hanya untuk menguasai syllogisme sambil bertengkar dengan budak di rumah; mereka membawa pulang persis yang mereka bawa—teorema tidak berguna bagi yang salah guna, seperti cuka tidak berguna bagi penderita disentri sebelum luka disembuhkan. Alasan mesti dibawa ke sekolah tenang dan bebas distraksi.","source_ids":["S441","S444","S445"]},{"text":"Persahabatan: hanya orang bijak yang mampu mencintai, karena cinta memerlukan pengetahuan tentang Baik. Setiap makhluk terikat pada kepentingannya sendiri; bila kepentingan diletakkan pada hal eksternal, saudara atau ayah pun bisa jadi musuh—seperti anjing yang bertengkar saat sepotong daging dilempar di antara mereka (Eteocles-Polynices, Alexander membakar kuil Aesculapius). Persahabatan sejati ada hanya bila kepentingan diletakkan pada will dan penggunaan penampakan yang benar.","source_ids":["S448","S454","S455"]},{"text":"Uji persahabatan: jangan percaya pada sumpah atau lahir dari orang tua sama—periksa di mana kepentingan orang itu diletakkan (hal luar atau will). 'Kamu menemani saya lama—tahu kamu tidak ia memperlakukanmu seperti membasuh sepatu dengan spons?'; kalung Eriphyle (opini tentang barang) merusak pernikahan Amphiaraus. Yang menempatkan diri pada will akan menjadi teman sejati dan memaafkan yang berbeda karena kebodohan (doktrin Plato: jiwa dirampas kebenaran dengan tak rela).","source_ids":["S456","S458","S459"]},{"text":"Kekuatan berbicara adalah hadiah Tuhan; menyangkalnya tidak syukur dan pengecut. Namun fakultas will adalah yang tertinggi: ia menggunakan semua fakultas lain sebagai pelayan, menilai nilai setiap fakultas, membuka-tutup mata dan telinga; hanya will sendiri yang bisa menghambat will—maka will itulah satu-satunya kebajikan atau kejahatan. Kritik Epicurus yang memposisikan daging sebagai yang terutama padahal daging tidak bisa menulis tentang tujuan hidup.","source_ids":["S462","S464","S466","S467"]},{"text":"Kekuatan bicara dan teorema hanyalah 'penginapan' di jalan pulang: jangan berhenti dan tinggal di sana seperti pelancong yang lupa tujuannya, terpikat pada ungkapan, syllogisme, atau sophisme seperti di antara Sirens. Tujuan sejati: menggunakan penampakan sesuai alam, desire tidak frustrasi, bebas, taat pada administrasi Zeus, tanpa menyalahkan siapa pun ('Lead me, O Zeus, and thou too Destiny'). Bicara seperti Demosthenes atau memecahkan syllogisme seperti Chrysippus tidak mencegah kecelakaan.","source_ids":["S472","S474","S476"]},{"text":"Ada juga seni mendengar: sebagaimana mendengar musik milik musisi dan menilai patung memerlukan seni, mendengar filsuf dengan bermanfaat memerlukan latihan khusus; tidak semua pendengar teruntung—yang mendengar terampil teruntung, yang tidak terampil merugi.","source_ids":["S479","S480"]}],"sources":[{"id":"S481","chapter":"XXIV: To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"Tell me then about what I should talk to you: about what matter are you able to listen? “About good and evil.” Good and evil in what? In a horse? “No.” Well, in an ox? “No.” What then? In a man? “Yes.” Do we know then what a man is, what the notion is which we have of him, or have we our ears in any degree practiced about this matter? But do you understand what nature is? or can you even in any degree understand me when I say I shall use demonstration to you? How? Do you understand this very thing, what demonstration is, or how anything is demonstrated, or by what means; or what things are like demonstration, but are not demonstration? Do you know what is true or what is false? What is consequent on a thing, what is repugnant to a thing, or not consistent, or inconsistent? But must I excite you to philosophy, and how? Shall I show to you the repugnance in the opinions of most men, through which they differ about things good and evil, and about things which are profitable and unprofitable, when you know not this very thing, what repugnance (contradiction) is? Show me then what I shall accomplish by discoursing with you —excite my inclination to do this. As the grass which is suitabl"},{"id":"S482","chapter":"XXIV: To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"e, when it is presented to a sheep, moves its inclination to eat, but if you present to it a stone or bread, it will not be moved to eat; so there are in us certain natural inclinations also to speak, when the hearer shall appear to be somebody, when he himself shall excite us: but when he shall sit by us like a stone or like grass, how can he excite a man’s desire (to speak)? Does the vine say to the husbandman, “Take care of me?” No, but the vine by showing in itself that it will be profitable to the husbandman, if he does take care of it, invites him to exercise care. When children are attractive and lively, whom do they not invite to play with them, and crawl with them, and lisp with them? But who is eager to play with an ass or to bray with it? for though it is small, it is still a little ass."},{"id":"S483","chapter":"XXIV: To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"Why then do you say nothing to me? I can only say this to you, that he who knows not who he is, and for what purpose he exists, and what is this world, and with whom he is associated, and what things are the good and the bad, and the beautiful and the ugly, and who neither understands discourse nor demonstration, nor what is true nor what is false, and who is not able to distinguish them, will neither desire according to nature nor turn away nor move towards, nor intend (to act), nor assent nor dissent, nor suspend his judgment: to say all in a few words, he will go about dumb and blind, thinking that he is somebody, but being nobody. Is this so now for the first time? Is it not the fact that ever since the human race existed, all errors and misfortunes have arisen through this ignorance? Why did Agamemnon and Achilles quarrel with one another? Was it not through not knowing what things are profitable and not profitable? Does not the one say it is profitable to restore Chryseis to her father, and does not the other say that it is not profitable? Does not the one say that he ought to take the prize of another, and does not the other say that he ought not? Did they not for these reas"},{"id":"S484","chapter":"XXIV: To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"ons forget, both who they were and for what purpose they had come there? Oh, man, for what purpose did you come? to gain mistresses or to fight? “To fight.” With whom? the Trojans or the Hellenes? “With the Trojans.” Do you then leave Hector alone and draw your sword against your own king? And do you, most excellent Sir, neglect the duties of the king, you who are the people’s guardian and have such cares? and are you quarrelling about a little girl with the most warlike of your allies, whom you ought by every means to take care of and protect? and do you become worse than (inferior to) a well behaved priest who treats you these fine gladiators with all respect? Do you see what kind of things ignorance of what is profitable does?"},{"id":"S485","chapter":"XXIV: To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"“But I also am rich.” Are you then richer than Agamemnon? “But I am also handsome.” Are you then more handsome than Achilles? “But I have also beautiful hair.” But had not Achilles more beautiful hair and gold colored? and he did not comb it elegantly nor dress it. “But I am also strong.” Can you then lift so great a stone as Hector or Ajax? “But I am also of noble birth.” Are you the son of a goddess mother? Are you the son of a father sprung from Zeus? What good then do these things do to him, when he sits and weeps for a girl? “But I am an orator.” And was he not? Do you not see how he handled the most skillful of the Hellenes in oratory, Odysseus and Phoenix? how he stopped their mouths?"},{"id":"S486","chapter":"XXIV: To (Or Against) a Person Who Was One of Those Who Were Not Valued (Esteemed) by Him","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"This is all that I have to say to you; and I say even this not willingly. Why? Because you have not roused me. For what must I look to in order to be roused, as men who are expert in riding are roused by generous horses? Must I look to your body? You treat it disgracefully. To your dress? That is luxurious. To your behavior, to your look? That is the same as nothing. When you would listen to a philosopher, do not say to him, “You tell me nothing;” but only show yourself worthy of hearing or fit for hearing; and you will see how you will move the speaker."},{"id":"S487","chapter":"XXV: That Logic Is Necessary","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"XXV"},{"id":"S488","chapter":"XXV: That Logic Is Necessary","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"That Logic Is Necessary"},{"id":"S489","chapter":"XXV: That Logic Is Necessary","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"When one of those who were present said, “Persuade me that logic is necessary,” he replied: Do you wish me to prove this to you? The answer was “Yes.” Then I must use a demonstrative form of speech. —This was granted. —How then will you know if I am cheating you by my argument? The man was silent. Do you see, said Epictetus, that you yourself are admitting that logic is necessary, if without it you cannot know so much as this, whether logic is necessary or not necessary?"},{"id":"S490","chapter":"XXVI: What Is the Property of Error","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"XXVI"},{"id":"S491","chapter":"XXVI: What Is the Property of Error","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"What Is the Property of Error"},{"id":"S492","chapter":"XXVI: What Is the Property of Error","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"Every error comprehends contradiction: for since he who errs does not wish to err, but to be right, it is plain that he does not do what he wishes. For what does the thief wish to do? That which is for his own interest. If then the theft is not for his interest, he does not do that which he wishes. But every rational soul is by nature offended at contradiction, and so long as it does not understand this contradiction, it is not hindered from doing contradictory things: but when it does understand the contradiction, it must of necessity avoid the contradiction and avoid it as much as a man must dissent from the false when he sees that a thing is false; but so long as this falsehood does not appear to him, he assents to it as to truth."},{"id":"S493","chapter":"XXVI: What Is the Property of Error","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"He then is strong in argument and has the faculty of exhorting and confuting, who is able to show to each man the contradiction through which he errs and clearly to prove how he does not do that which he wishes and does that which he does not wish. For if anyone shall show this, a man will himself withdraw from that which he does; but so long as you do not show this, do not be surprised if a man persists in his practice; for having the appearance of doing right, he does what he does. For this reason Socrates also trusting to this power used to say, I am used to call no other witness of what I say, but I am always satisfied with him with whom I am discussing, and I ask him to give his opinion and call him as a witness, and though he is only one, he is sufficient in the place of all. For Socrates knew by what the rational soul is moved, just like a pair of scales, and then it must incline, whether it chooses or not. Show the rational governing faculty a contradiction, and it will withdraw from it; but if you do not show it, rather blame yourself than him who is not persuaded."},{"id":"S494","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"I"},{"id":"S495","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"Of Finery in Dress"},{"id":"S496","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"A certain young man, a rhetorician, came to see Epictetus, with his hair dressed more carefully than was usual and his attire in an ornamental style; whereupon Epictetus said: Tell me if you do not think that some dogs are beautiful and some horses, and so of all other animals. “I do think so,” the youth replied. Are not then some men also beautiful and others ugly? “Certainly.” Do we then for the same reason call each of them in the same kind beautiful, or each beautiful for something peculiar? And you will judge of this matter thus: Since we see a dog naturally formed for one thing, and a horse for another, and for another still, as an example, a nightingale, we may generally and not improperly declare each of them to be beautiful then when it is most excellent according to its nature; but since the nature of each is different, each of them seems to me to be beautiful in a different way. Is it not so? He admitted that it was. That then which makes a dog beautiful, makes a horse ugly; and that which makes a horse beautiful, makes a dog ugly, if it is true that their natures are different. It seems to be so. For I think that what makes a Pancratiast beautiful, makes a wrestler to b"},{"id":"S497","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"e not good, and a runner to be most ridiculous; and he who is beautiful for the Pentathlon, is very ugly for wrestling. “It is so,” said he. What then makes a man beautiful? Is it that which in its kind makes both a dog and a horse beautiful? “It is,” he said. What then makes a dog beautiful? The possession of the excellence of a dog. And what makes a horse beautiful? The possession of the excellence of a horse. What then makes a man beautiful? Is it not the possession of the excellence of a man? And do you then, if you wish to be beautiful, young man, labor at this, the acquisition of human excellence. But what is this? Observe whom you yourself praise, when you praise many persons without partiality: do you praise the just or the unjust? The just. Whether do you praise the moderate or the immoderate? The moderate. And the temperate or the intemperate? The temperate. If then you make yourself such a person, you will know that you will make yourself beautiful: but so long as you neglect these things, you must be ugly (αἰσχρόν) even though you contrive all you can to appear beautiful. Further I do not know what to say to you: for if I say to you what I think, I shall offend you, and"},{"id":"S498","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":" you will perhaps leave the school and not return to it: and if I do not say what I think, see how I shall be acting, if you come to me to be improved, and I shall not improve you at all, and if you come to me as to a philosopher, and I shall say nothing to you as a philosopher. And how cruel it is to you to leave you uncorrected. If at any time afterwards you shall acquire sense, you will with good reason blame me and say, “What did Epictetus observe in me that when he saw me in such a plight coming to him in such a scandalous condition, he neglected me and never said a word? did he so much despair of me? was I not young? was I not able to listen to reason? and how many other young men at this age commit many like errors? I hear that a certain Polemon from being a most dissolute youth underwent such a great change. Well, suppose that he did not think that I should be a Polemon; yet he might have set my hair right, he might have stripped off my decorations, he might have stopped me from plucking the hair out of my body; but when he saw me dressed like —what shall I say? —he kept silent.” I do not say like what; but you will say when you come to your senses, and shall know what it i"},{"id":"S499","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"s, and what persons use such a dress."},{"id":"S500","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"If you bring this charge against me hereafter, what defense shall I make? Why, shall I say that the man will not be persuaded by me? Was Laius persuaded by Apollo? Did he not go away and get drunk and show no care for the oracle? Well then for this reason did Apollo refuse to tell him the truth? I indeed do not know whether you will be persuaded by me or not; but Apollo knew most certainly that Laius would not be persuaded and yet he spoke. But why did he speak? I say in reply: But why is he Apollo, and why does he deliver oracles, and why has he fixed himself in this place as a prophet and source of truth and for the inhabitants of the world to resort to him? and why are the words “Know yourself” written in front of the temple, though no person takes any notice of them?"},{"id":"S501","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"Did Socrates persuade all his hearers to take care of themselves? Not the thousandth part. But however, after he had been placed in this position by the deity, as he himself says, he never left it. But what does he say even to his judges? “If you acquit me on these conditions that I no longer do that which I do now, I will not consent and I will not desist; but I will go up both to young and to old, and, to speak plainly, to every man whom I meet, and I will ask the questions which I ask now; and most particularly will I do this to you my fellow citizens, because you are more nearly related to me.” —Are you so curious, Socrates, and such a busybody? and how does it concern you how we act? and what is it that you say? Being of the same community and of the same kin, you neglect yourself, and show yourself a bad citizen to the state, and a bad kinsman to your kinsmen, and a bad neighbour to your neighbours. Who then are you? —Here it is a great thing to say, “I am he whose duty it is to take care of men; for it is not every little heifer which dares to resist a lion; but if the bull comes up and resists him, say to the bull, if you choose, ‘and who are you, and what business have you"},{"id":"S502","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":" here?’ ” Man, in every kind there is, produced something which excels; in oxen, in dogs, in bees, in horses. Do not then say to that which excels, “Who then are you?” If you do, it will find a voice in some way and say, “I am such a thing as the purple in a garment: do not expect me to be like the others, or blame my nature that it has made me different from the rest of men.”"},{"id":"S503","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"What then? am I such a man? Certainly not. And are you such a man as can listen to the truth? I wish you were. But however since in a manner I have been condemned to wear a white beard and a cloak, and you come to me as to a philosopher, I will not treat you in a cruel way nor yet as if I despaired of you, but I will say: Young man, whom do you wish to make beautiful? In the first place, know who you are and then adorn yourself appropriately. You are a human being; and this is a mortal animal which has the power of using appearances rationally. But what is meant by “rationally”? Conformably to nature and completely. What then do you possess which is peculiar? Is it the animal part? No. Is it the condition of mortality? No. Is it the power of using appearances? No. You possess the rational faculty as a peculiar thing: adorn and beautify this; but leave your hair to him who made it as he chose. Come, what other appellations have you? Are you man or woman? Man. Adorn yourself then as man, not as woman. Woman is naturally smooth and delicate; and if she has much hair (on her body), she is a monster and is exhibited at Rome among monsters. And in a man it is monstrous not to have hair; "},{"id":"S504","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"and if he has no hair, he is a monster; but if he cuts off his hairs and plucks them out, what shall we do with him? where shall we exhibit him? and under what name shall we show him? I will exhibit to you a man who chooses to be a woman rather than a man. What a terrible sight! There is no man who will not wonder at such a notice. Indeed I think that the men who pluck out their hairs do what they do without knowing what they do. Man what fault have you to find with your nature? That it made you a man? What then was it fit that nature should make all human creatures women? and what advantage in that case would you have had in being adorned? for whom would you have adorned yourself, if all human creatures were women? But you are not pleased with the matter: set to work then upon the whole business. Take away —what is its name? —that which is the cause of the hairs: make yourself a woman in all respects, that we may not be mistaken: do not make one half man, and the other half woman. Whom do you wish to please? The women? Please them as a man. Well; but they like smooth men. Will you not hang yourself? and if women took delight in catamites, would you become one? Is this your busines"},{"id":"S505","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"s? were you born for this purpose, that dissolute women should delight in you? Shall we make such a one as you a citizen of Corinth and perchance a prefect of the city, or chief of the youth, or general or superintendent of the games? Well, and when you have taken a wife, do you intend to have your hairs plucked out? To please whom and for what purpose? And when you have begotten children, will you introduce them also into the state with the habit of plucking their hairs? A beautiful citizen, and senator, and rhetorician. We ought to pray that such young men be born among us and brought up."},{"id":"S506","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"Do not so, I entreat you by the Gods, young man: but when you have once heard these words, go away and say to yourself, “Epictetus has not said this to me; for how could he? but some propitious God through him: for it would never have come into his thoughts to say this, since he is not accustomed to talk thus with any person. Come then let us obey God, that we may not be subject to his anger.” You say, “No.” But (I say), if a crow by his croaking signifies anything to you, it is not the crow which signifies, but God through the crow; and if he signifies anything through a human voice, will he not cause the man to say this to you, that you may know the power of the divinity, that he signifies to some in this way, and to others in that way, and concerning the greatest things and the chief he signifies through the noblest messenger? What else is it which the poet says:"},{"id":"S507","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"For we ourselves have warned him, and have sent\nHermes the careful watcher, Argus’ slayer,\nThe husband not to kill nor wed the wife."},{"id":"S508","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":"Was Hermes going to descend from heaven to say this to him (Aegisthus)? And now the Gods say this to you and send the messenger, the slayer of Argus, to warn you not to pervert that which is well arranged, nor to busy yourself about it, but to allow a man to be a man, and a woman to be a woman, a beautiful man to be as a beautiful man, and an ugly man as an ugly man, for you are not flesh and hair, but you are will (προαίρεσις); and if your will is beautiful, then you will be beautiful. But up to the present time I dare not tell you that you are ugly, for I think that you are readier to hear anything than this. But see what Socrates says to the most beautiful and blooming of men Alcibiades: Try then to be beautiful. What does he say to him? Dress your hair and pluck the hairs from your legs? Nothing of that kind. But adorn your will, take away bad opinions. How with the body? Leave it as it is by nature. Another has looked after these things: entrust them to him. What then, must a man be uncleaned? Certainly not; but what you are and are made by nature, cleanse this. A man should be cleanly as a man, a woman as a woman, a child as a child. You say no: but let us also pluck out the "},{"id":"S509","chapter":"I: Of Finery in Dress","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":"lion’s mane, that he may not be uncleaned, and the cock’s comb for he also ought to be cleaned. Granted, but as a cock, and the lion as a lion, and the hunting dog as a hunting dog."},{"id":"S510","chapter":"II: In What a Man Ought to Be Exercised Who Has Made Proficiency; and That We Neglect the Chief Things","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"II"},{"id":"S511","chapter":"II: In What a Man Ought to Be Exercised Who Has Made Proficiency; and That We Neglect the Chief Things","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"In What a Man Ought to Be Exercised Who Has Made Proficiency; and That We Neglect the Chief Things"},{"id":"S512","chapter":"II: In What a Man Ought to Be Exercised Who Has Made Proficiency; and That We Neglect the Chief Things","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"There are three things (topics, τόποι) in which a man ought to exercise himself who would be wise and good. The first concerns the desires and the aversions, that a man may not fail to get what he desires, and that he may not fall into that which he does not desire. The second concerns the movements (towards an object) and the movements from an object, and generally in doing what a man ought to do, that he may act according to order, to reason, and not carelessly. The third thing concerns freedom from deception and rashness in judgment, and generally it concerns the assents (συγκαταθέσεις). Of these topics the chief and the most urgent is that which relates to the affects (τὰ πάθη, perturbations); for an affect is produced in no other way than by a failing to obtain that which a man desires or falling into that which a man would wish to avoid. This is that which brings in perturbations, disorders, bad fortune, misfortunes, sorrows, lamentations, and envy; that which makes men envious and jealous; and by these causes we are unable even to listen to the precepts of reason. The second topic concerns the duties of a man; for I ought not to be free from affects (ἀπαθῆ) like a statue, bu"},{"id":"S513","chapter":"II: In What a Man Ought to Be Exercised Who Has Made Proficiency; and That We Neglect the Chief Things","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"t I ought to maintain the relations (σχέσεις) natural and acquired, as a pious man, as a son, as a father, as a citizen."},{"id":"S514","chapter":"II: In What a Man Ought to Be Exercised Who Has Made Proficiency; and That We Neglect the Chief Things","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"The third topic is that which immediately concerns those who are making proficiency, that which concerns the security of the other two, so that not even in sleep any appearance unexamined may surprise us, nor in intoxication, nor in melancholy. This, it may be said, is above our power. But the present philosophers neglecting the first topic and the second (the affects and duties), employ themselves on the third, using sophistical arguments (μεταπίπτοντας), making conclusions from questioning, employing hypotheses, lying. For a man must, as it is said, when employed on these matters, take care that he is not deceived. Who must? The wise and good man. This then is all that is wanting to you. Have you successfully worked out the rest? Are you free from deception in the matter of money? If you see a beautiful girl, do you resist the appearance? If your neighbour obtains an estate by will, are you not vexed? Now is there nothing else wanting to you except unchangeable firmness of mind (ἀμεταπτωσία)? Wretch, you hear these very things with fear and anxiety that some person may despise you, and with inquiries about what any person may say about you. And if a man come and tell you that in "},{"id":"S515","chapter":"II: In What a Man Ought to Be Exercised Who Has Made Proficiency; and That We Neglect the Chief Things","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"a certain conversation in which the question was, “Who is the best philosopher,” a man who was present said that a certain person was the chief philosopher, your little soul which was only a finger’s length stretches out to two cubits. But if another who is present says, “You are mistaken; it is not worthwhile to listen to a certain person, for what does he know? he has only the first principles, and no more?” then you are confounded, you grow pale, you cry out immediately, “I will show him who I am, that I am a great philosopher.” It is seen by these very things: why do you wish to show it by others? Do you not know that Diogenes pointed out one of the sophists in this way: by stretching out his middle finger? And then when the man was wild with rage, “This,” he said, “is the certain person: I have pointed him out to you.” For a man is not shown by the finger, as a stone or a piece of wood; but when any person shows the man’s principles, then he shows him as a man."},{"id":"S516","chapter":"II: In What a Man Ought to Be Exercised Who Has Made Proficiency; and That We Neglect the Chief Things","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"Let us look at your principles also. For is it not plain that you value not at all your own will (προαίρεσις), but you look externally to things which are independent of your will? For instance, what will a certain person say? and what will people think of you? will you be considered a man of learning; have you read Chrysippus or Antipater? for if you have read Archedemus also, you have everything [that you can desire]. Why are you still uneasy lest you should not show us who you are? Would you let me tell you what manner of man you have shown us that you are? You have exhibited yourself to us as a mean fellow, querulous, passionate, cowardly, finding fault with everything, blaming everybody, never quiet, vain: this is what you have exhibited to us. Go away now and read Archedemus; then if a mouse should leap down and make a noise, you are a dead man. For such a death awaits you as it did —what was the man’s name? —Crinis; and he too was proud, because he understood Archedemus."},{"id":"S517","chapter":"II: In What a Man Ought to Be Exercised Who Has Made Proficiency; and That We Neglect the Chief Things","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"Wretch, will you not dismiss these things that do not concern you at all? These things are suitable to those who are able to learn them without perturbation, to those who can say: “I am not subject to anger, to grief, to envy: I am not hindered, I am not restrained. What remains for me? I have leisure, I am tranquil: let us see how we must deal with sophistical arguments; let us see how when a man has accepted a hypothesis he shall not be led away to anything absurd.” To them such things belong. To those who are happy it is appropriate to light a fire, to dine; if they choose, both to sing and to dance. But when the vessel is sinking, you come to me and hoist the sails."},{"id":"S518","chapter":"III: What Is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practice Ourselves","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"III"},{"id":"S519","chapter":"III: What Is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practice Ourselves","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"What Is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practice Ourselves"},{"id":"S520","chapter":"III: What Is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practice Ourselves","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"The material for the wise and good man is his own ruling faculty: and the body is the material for the physician and the aliptes (the man who oils persons); the land is the matter for the husbandman. The business of the wise and good man is to use appearances conformably to nature: and as it is the nature of every soul to assent to the truth, to dissent from the false, and to remain in suspense as to that which is uncertain; so it is its nature to be moved towards the desire of the good, and to aversion from the evil; and with respect to that which is neither good nor bad it feels indifferent. For as the money-changer (banker) is not allowed to reject Caesar’s coin, nor the seller of herbs, but if you show the coin, whether he chooses or not, he must give up what is sold for the coin; so it is also in the matter of the soul. When the good appears, it immediately attracts to itself; the evil repels from itself. But the soul will never reject the manifest appearance of the good, any more than persons will reject Caesar’s coin. On this principle depends every movement both of man and God."}],"newWindowIds":["S481","S482","S483","S484","S485","S486","S487","S488","S489","S490","S491","S492","S493","S494","S495","S496","S497","S498","S499","S500","S501","S502","S503","S504","S505","S506","S507","S508","S509","S510","S511","S512","S513","S514","S515","S516","S517","S518","S519","S520"]}
requests.raw: {"notes":[{"text":"Kesalahan (error) selalu mengandung kontradiksi: pencuri berpikir mencuri menguntungkan padahal tidak; jiwa rasional tak bisa menyetujui yang palsu bila kefalsahannya tampak. Maka sang pembaharu cukup menunjukkan kontradiksi itu—seperti Socrates yang cukup satu pembicara sebagai saksi—bila tak tampak, saling diri sendiri, bukan orangnya.","source_ids":["S492","S493"]},{"text":"Perawatan diri lewat penampilan (rambut berhias, mencabut bulu) dikritik: keindahan manusia ada pada keunggulan khasnya (keadilan, moderasi, kesederhanaan), bukan pada bagian hewani atau mortalitas; manusia adalah will (proairesis), bukan daging dan rambut. Socrates menasihati Alcibiades untuk menghiasi kemauan dan membuang opini buruk, bukan tubuh.","source_ids":["S496","S497","S508"]},{"text":"Filsuf wajib berkata benar meski pendengar tidak mau dipengaruhi: contoh Apollo tetap berbicara kepada Laius dan Socrates menolak berhenti mengajukan pertanyaan meski diadili; 'aku adalah orang yang bertugas merawat manusia'—yang unggul dalam setiap jenis (seperti ungu pada jubah, bulla melawan singa) tidak perlu membela diri atas keberbedaannya.","source_ids":["S500","S501","S502"]},{"text":"Tiga topik latihan orang yang berprogres: (1) desire/aversion—yang paling utama karena dari situ lahir gejolak; (2) tugas dan relasi alami (anak, ayah, warga) dengan afek yang tidak hampa seperti patung; (3) assent tanpa kekeliruan. Filsuf sezaman menelorkan topik ketiga (sophisme) sambil mengabaikan dua yang pertama—padahal bahkan terganggu oleh ketakutan diremehkan orang.","source_ids":["S512","S513","S514"]},{"text":"Nilai sejati tidak ditunjukkan dengan membaca Chrysippus/Archedemus: Diogenes menunjuk sophist dengan jari tengah—manusia ditunjukkan oleh prinsip-prinsipnya, bukan seperti batu. Yang kapalnya tenggelam tidak waktunya membahas argumen hipotetis; pembahasan logis hanya untuk yang sudah tenang, tanpa marah, duka, dan iri.","source_ids":["S515","S516","S517"]},{"text":"Materi kerja orang baik adalah fakultas penguasanya sendiri: menggunakan penampakan sesuai alam; jiwa tak bisa menolak penampakan baik yang jelas, seperti penukar uang tak bisa menolak koin Caesar—prinsip inilah dasar seluruh gerakan manusia dan Tuhan.","source_ids":["S520"]}]}
