requests.user: {"question":"apa gagasan utama buku ini?","book":"Discourses","examinedBefore":520,"totalWindows":957,"previousNotes":[{"text":"Tesis utama buku: hanya penggunaan yang benar atas penampakan (right use of appearances) yang berada dalam kuasa kita; fakultas rasional adalah satu-satunya yang dapat mengkontemplasi dirinya sendiri dan menilai fakultas lain. Segala hal lain (tubuh, harta, orang tercinta) di luar kuasa kita; manusia menderita karena terikat pada banyak hal eksternal.","source_ids":["S3","S5","S6"]},{"text":"Kunci ketenangan: selalu membedakan apa milikku dan bukan milikku. Kematian, penjara, pengasingan harus dihadapi tanpa ratapan — tubuh bisa dibelenggu, tetapi kemauan (will) tidak bisa ditaklukkan bahkan oleh Zeus. Contoh: Lateranus mengulurkan leher dengan tenang; Agrippinus tetap makan setelah dijatuhi hukuman pengasingan.","source_ids":["S9","S11","S12"]},{"text":"Menjaga karakter (proper character): yang rasional selalu diterima, yang irasional tak tertanggungkan — karena itu kita butuh disiplin. Agrippinus menolak ikut tontonan Nero: ia ingin menjadi 'ungu' pada jubah, bukan sekadar satu benang biasa; Priscus Helvidius tetap bersuara di senat meski Vespasian mengancam mati — tugas kaisar membunuh, tugasnya mati tanpa takut.","source_ids":["S15","S18","S19"]},{"text":"Allah adalah bapa semua manusia: manusia memiliki kekerabatan ganda — tubuh bersama hewan, nalar bersama dewa. Yang banyak condong pada daging dan menjadi seperti serigala, singa, atau rubah; sebagian kecil yang mengenali asal ilahiah tidak memiliki pikiran rendah tentang dirinya.","source_ids":["S27","S29"]},{"text":"Kemajuan (progres) bukan menguasai banyak buku filsafat, tetapi melatih desire dan aversion agar tidak gagal memperoleh yang diinginkan atau jatuh pada yang dihindari; bukti kemajuan adalah keadaan kemauan yang bebas, setia, dan sederhana dalam tindakan sehari-hari. Tragedi adalah gambaran gejolak orang yang menghargai hal eksternal.","source_ids":["S32","S36","S37"]},{"text":"Gagasan utama: manusia adalah makhluk rasional, kerabat/kepunyaan Tuhan; tujuan hidup adalah menggunakan akal dengan benar — memahami penggunaan penampakan, bukan sekadar memakainya seperti hewan. Alam berakhir pada kontemplasi dan hidup sesuai alam; memulai dan berakhir seperti hewan adalah memalukan.","source_ids":["S48","S49"]},{"text":"Providence: dari segala yang ada dan terjadi mudah memuji providensi bila memiliki dua hal — kemampuan melihat kegunaan segala hal dan watak bersyukur. Kesesuaian struktur dunia (mata, cahaya, warna) membuktikan Sang Pencipta.","source_ids":["S46","S47"]},{"text":"Kesulitan hidup adalah sarana latihan kebajikan: seperti Hercules membutuhkan singa dan hydra, manusia diberi kebesaran jiwa, keberanian, dan ketahanan untuk menanggung apa pun yang terjadi; mengeluh dan menyalahkan dewa adalah kekufuran akibat jiwa yang hina.","source_ids":["S52","S53"]},{"text":"Kekerasan kepalaan (menolak kebenaran yang jelas) ada dua macam: pada akal dan pada rasa malu. Orang yang melihat kontradiksi tetapi tidak berubah lebih buruk dari orang yang tidak melihat — akalnya tidak hilang melainkan dibinatangkan; itu bukan kekuatan budi.","source_ids":["S42","S43"]},{"text":"Logika dan argumen dialektis adalah kewajiban hidup: cukup tidak hanya mengetahui prinsip membedakan benar-salah, tetapi harus ada kemahiran seperti membedakan drachma asli-palsu. Namun bila premis berubah makna, kita boleh menarik persetujuan dari konsekuensinya.","source_ids":["S57","S60"]},{"text":"Kerabat dengan Tuhan: jangan menyebut diri warga Athena melainkan warga dunia (kosmopolites); komunitas tertinggi adalah manusia dan Tuhan. Contoh Socrates yang memilih mati daripada meninggalkan tugas yang Tuhan tempatkan; tubuh dan harta bukan kekuatan tiran atas kita.","source_ids":["S72","S78"]},{"text":"Gagasan utama: manusia berkerabat dengan Tuhan sehingga memiliki dari dalam dirinya sendiri hal-hal terpenting (kemuliaan jiwa); orang penakut dan hina hanyalah 'mayat dan segayung darah', dan tidak ada orang yang membuat orang lain sengsara—yang benar-benar berharga tidak diperoleh dari orang lain (tanah, uang, jabatan).","source_ids":["S81"]},{"text":"Epictetus mengkritik mereka yang mengejar jabatan di Roma: orang tua yang bersumpah akan hidup tenang setelah pengasingan langsung melupakan segalanya begitu menerima surat dari Caesar. Manusia memang dibuat untuk bekerja, tetapi pekerjaan yang benar adalah mempelajari administrasi dunia dan siapa diri kita, bukan urusan biji gandum dan tanah.","source_ids":["S84","S86"]},{"text":"Dialog tentang kasih sayang alami: meninggalkan anak yang sakit bukanlah tindakan penyayang—kasih sayang harus konsisten dengan rasio; yang keduanya penyayang dan rasional itulah yang benar dan baik. Kita butuh kriteria (bukan sekadar 'semua orang melakukannya') untuk menilai baik-buruk, seperti penglihatan untuk warna.","source_ids":["S92","S93","S94"]},{"text":"Sebab segala tindakan adalah will/opini (dogma) kita sendiri, bukan hal luar: bukan kematian Patroklus yang membuat Achilles meratap, tetapi pilihannya. Kematian, pengasingan, atau rasa sakit tidak menyebabkan kita berbuat apa pun; kita harus membuang opini salah seperti membuang tumor, dan hanya memeriksa opini, bukan tanah, budak, atau kuda.","source_ids":["S96","S97","S98"]},{"text":"Kebahagiaan (contentment): manusia harus meneliti pendapat tentang para dewa lalu menundukkan pikirannya kepada Yang mengatur semuanya seperti warga yang taat pada hukum. Kebebasan adalah belajar menginginkan segala sesuatu terjadi sebagaimana terjadi; yang tidak menerima hukumannya adalah menjadi dirinya sendiri—di mana ia berada dengan tidak rela, di situ ia dipenjara (Socrates tidak dipenjara karena ada dengan rela).","source_ids":["S103","S104","S107"]},{"text":"Tuhan mengawasi segala hal: jiwa kita adalah bagian dan potongan dari Tuhan, dan setiap manusia diberi penjaga (daimon) yang tidak pernah tidur; kita harus bersumpah kepada Tuhan—tidak pernah membangkang, tidak mencela apa yang diberikan, dan tidak dengan enggan melakukan atau menderita apa yang perlu—sumpah yang menghormati diri sendiri, bukan Caesar.","source_ids":["S115","S117","S118"]},{"text":"Filosofi tidak menjanjikan hal eksternal apa pun; materinya adalah hidup orang itu sendiri. Angka saudara marah bukan wilayahnya — ia hanya menjamin bagian penguasa (governing part) selalu sesuai alam. Kebenaran besar tidak terbentuk tiba-tiba, seperti buah ara butuh waktu matang.","source_ids":["S121","S123"]},{"text":"Providence terlihat bahkan dalam hal kecil: susu dari rumput, keju dari susu, rambut dagu sebagai tanda pembeda pria-wanita. Hymn kepada Tuhan harus dinyanyikan terus — Epictetus menyebut dirinya makhluk rasional yang tugasnya memuji Tuhan; 'jika aku burungNightangle aku menyanyi seperti nightangle, tetapi aku makhluk rasional, maka aku memuji Tuhan.'","source_ids":["S127","S128","S129"]},{"text":"Seni logis diperlukan karena akal menganalisis fakultas lain dan harus menganalisis dirinya sendiri; tanpa kriteria (seperti modius untuk gandum) tidak ada pengukuran akurat. Kita tidak butuh Chrysippus karena dirinya, tetapi untuk memahami kehendak alam.","source_ids":["S133","S136"]},{"text":"Kebebasan will terbukti: tak ada yang bisa memaksa assent pada yang palsu atau menghalangi assent pada yang benar. Yang memaksa bukan yang diletakkan di depan (ketakutan akan mati), melainkan opini kita sendiri — will memaksa will. Jika memilih, kita bebas, tidak menyalahkan siapa pun; segala jadi sesuai kehendak kita dan Tuhan.","source_ids":["S137","S138"]},{"text":"Jangan marah pada kesalahan orang lain: pelaku salah adalah yang keliru tentang baik-buruk, seperti buta — layak dikasihani bukan dibenci. Kita marah karena menghargai hal yang dicuri; jangan menghargai pakaian, tak akan marah pada pencuri. Latih diri dari hal kecil (sakit kepala tanpa 'alas!') menuju yang besar.","source_ids":["S141","S143","S145"]},{"text":"Tiran hanya menguasai tubuh (kaki, leher), tidak akan (will). Yang membuat orang takut bukan tiran dan pengawalnya, melainkan opini sendiri. Manusia yang ditunjuk Caesar jadi tukang sepatunya langsung tampak bijak di mata orang — nilai yang salah. Bakat dirinya mencakup memikirkan diri sendiri, dan karena manusia rasional tak bisa memperoleh kepentingannya sendiri tanpa berkontribusi pada kepentingan bersama, mementingkan diri tidak kontrasosial.","source_ids":["S151","S152","S154"]},{"text":"Akal sendiri berasal dari penampakan (system of appearances) sehingga bisa mengkhawati dirinya sendiri; tugas pertama filosof adalah memeriksa penampakan tanpa menerima tanpa ujian. Doktrin filosof sangat singkat: tujuan manusia mengikuti para dewa, dan baik adalah penggunaan penampakan yang tepat; kata-kata panjang hanya perlu menjelaskan apa Tuhan, penampakan, dan alam.","source_ids":["S158","S160"]},{"text":"Kritik terhadap Epicurus: kendati mengakui manusia bersifat sosial, ia menempatkan kebaikan pada 'kulitnya' sehingga menyarankan orang bijak tidak membesarkan anak—padahal begitu anak lahir, sayang padanya di luar kuasa kita; bahkan domba dan serigala tidak meninggalkan anaknya. Orang bijak seharusnya terlibat urusan publik, bukan memperlakukan manusia seperti sekawanan lalat.","source_ids":["S174","S175"]},{"text":"Kesulitan adalah lawan sparring dari Tuhan: seperti pelatih gulat mencocokkan kita dengan pemuda tangguh agar menjadi juara Olimpiade. Diogenes adalah penembak ronda teladan—melaporkan kematian bukan jahat, ketenaran gemuruh orang gila, hidup telanjang dan tidur di tanah lebih baik, dengan bukti ketenangan dan kebebasannya sendiri; penembak ronda penakut yang lapor musuh dekat hanya layak disuruh pulang.","source_ids":["S178","S179"]},{"text":"Hidup seperti berperan: manusia hanya boleh membawa yang miliknya (kirimannya), bukan kemudi atau dayung kapal—hal luar boleh dicabut satu per satu (toga, tubuh) tanpa takut. Harta seperti tempat tidur di penginapan; tragedi hanya terjadi pada orang kaya dan raja, orang miskin tidak punya peran tragis; bila permainan tidak menyenangkan, 'aku tidak bermain lagi'—pintu terbuka.","source_ids":["S180","S181","S182"]},{"text":"Perintah Zeus sudah cukup: jaga apa milikmu (integritas, rasa malu yang baik), jangan menginginkan milik orang lain; bila memegangnya tidak perlu arahan lain. Hidup itu permainan Saturnalia: patuh raja yang ditunjuk agar permainan tidak kacau, tetapi tidak ada yang memaksa kita berpikir menderita—seperti hipotesis logika, boleh menyanggupi 'sial', tetapi Zeus melarang menganggap diri hina.","source_ids":["S186","S187","S188"]},{"text":"Kita yang menghimpit diri sendiri lewat opini: ingin duduk di tempat senator menghimpit; hinaan hanya efektif lewat kelemahan orang yang dihinakan—jika mendengar seperti batu, tidak ada untungnya. Yang dijaga itulah yang diserang: bila menaruh hormat pada tubuh atau harta kecil, di situlah kita jadi budak. Socrates selalu satu wajah karena mempraktikkan kebebasan tanpa hambatan.","source_ids":["S189","S190","S191","S192"]},{"text":"Hukum hidup mendahului hukum hipotesis logis: bertindak sesuai alam adalah hukum dasar; filsuf melatih teori dulu (lebih mudah) baru urusan hidup yang lebih sulit. Awal filsafat adalah menyadari kelemahan fakultas penuntun—yang tak bisa menelan sepotong pun membeli seluruh jilid lalu memuntahkannya; orang membaca argumen hipotetis hanya untuk dipuji orang senatori (contoh: pengeluh punya 1,5 juta denarii yang membuat Epaphroditus tercengang, bukan mentertawakan).","source_ids":["S195","S196","S199"]},{"text":"Empat cara penampakan muncul; tugas orang terdidik menilai dengan benar. Ramuan melawan kebiasaan adalah kebiasaan yang berlawanan; melawan penampakan menipu adalah prekognisi yang bersih; melawan kematian—ia perlu dan bukan kejahatan, jadi tanpa rasa takut. Ketiadaan kesalehan lahir karena piety dan kepentingan pribadi dianggap terpisah.","source_ids":["S202","S205"]},{"text":"Jangan marah kepada orang lain: jiwa hanya menyetujui yang tampak benar (Plato: jiwa kehilangan kebenaran dengan tak rela); Medea terlilit karena mengira balas dendam lebih menguntungkan. Orang sesat pada fakultas tertinggi patut dikasihani seperti orang buta, bukan dibenci. Segala tindakan diukur oleh penampakan.","source_ids":["S210","S212","S213"]},{"text":"Iliad hanyalah penampakan dan penggunaannya: pembakaran Troya tidak lebih dahsyat dari sarang bangau yang terbakar—bedanya manusia memiliki kejujuran, kemoderatan, kesetiaan, kecerdasan. Kehancuran sejati adalah kehancuran opini benar: Alexander hancur saat kehilangan karakter, Achilles saat marah dan lupa tugasnya.","source_ids":["S214","S216","S217"]},{"text":"Esensi Baik adalah kemauan; hal luar hanya bahan bagi kemauan. Hukum Allah: ambil kebaikan dari dirimu sendiri. Tirani hanya mengancam tubuh; tidak ada yang lebih kuat daripada kemauan kecuali kemauan sendiri—sepuluh orang lebih kuat dalam mengekang, tetapi tidak dalam opini yang benar.","source_ids":["S222","S224"]},{"text":"Socrates menafsir ulang: yang dibawa ke penjara hanyalah 'tubuh miskinnya'; 'Anytus dan Melitus dapat membunuhku, tetapi tidak menyakitiku.' Kesulitan adalah ujian pembelajaran: seperti atlet yang ingin lawan berat, orang terdidik harus menunjukkan ajarannya dalam praktik, bukan argumen kecil di sudut sekolah; jadilah saksi Allah bahwa yang eksternal bukan baik atau jahat.","source_ids":["S226","S232","S235"]},{"text":"Pelayan yang baik menghormati semua orang sesuai 'relasi': ayah, saudara, keabadian—mengingat bahwa adalah watak dewata mempertahankan diri dari mimpi dan kecenderungan; putusan orang yang belum terdidik tentang kesalehan tidak lebih penting daripada seorang musisi yang salah menilai tali lyre. Hamba yang lari menikmati teater dengan ketakutan; membebaskan diri dari 'majikan' (kematian, kesenangan, sakit) menghapus seluruh ketakutan.","source_ids":["S236","S238","S239"]},{"text":"Sikap yang harus disiapkan dalam kesulitan: saat menghadapi orang besar, ingat ada yang melihat dari atas; pengasingan, penjara, mati, aib tetap hal indiferen yang tak berubah — hanya hal di luar kemauan yang 'tak ada bagiku'; Baik adalah kemauan sebagaimana mestinya dan penggunaan penampakan; tujuan hidup adalah mengikuti Tuhan. YAng begitu belajar akan berani karena tahu semua persiapan gelar-gelar kuasa 'bukanlah apa-apa'.","source_ids":["S243","S244"]},{"text":"Percaya diri dan kehati-hatian tidak bertentangan bila diterapkan pada objek berbeda: kehati-hatian pada hal dalam kemauan (satu-satunya jahat), keberanian pada hal di luar kemauan. Manusia terbalik seperti rusa yang takut pada bulu pemburu lalu lari ke jaring: takut pada kematian, sakit, aib (hal luar) tetapi gegabah pada tipu, nafsu, aib tindakan (hal will). Bukan kematian yang menakutkan, melainkan ketakutan pada kematian.","source_ids":["S247","S248","S249"]},{"text":"Kematian dan sakit adalah 'topeng tragedi': putar dan periksa — tidak menggigit; pintu selalu terbuka bila tak tertahankan. Kebebasan sejati adalah milik yang terdidik: hidup tanpa kesalahan, takut, duka, dan gejolak adalah bebas; budak yang dibebaskan di pengadilan tetap tak bebas bila uang, kekasih, atau tiran jadi majikannya. Socrates menulis untuk menguji dirinya sendiri dalam praktik, bukan karya-karya kosong; pamer sejati pemuda terdidik adalah 'sajikan kematian, penjara, siksaan — aku tak kecewa dan tak jatuh'.","source_ids":["S252","S254","S257","S258"]},{"text":"Ketenangan dalam perkara (contoh: ke pengadilan): bila tujuannya mempertahankan will sesuai alam, aman penuh — tak ada yang menguasainya; bila ingin mempertahankan hal luar, siaplah jadi budak penuh (berlutut, menangis). Socrates seumur hidup bersiap menghadapi sidang karena tak pernah berbuat zalim. Minta 'saran untuk setiap kejadian' seperti orang buta huruf minta tahu nama apa yang akan ditulis; latihan membuat siap untuk semua, dan yang mengejar hal luar pasti terombang-ambing pada kehendak majikannya.","source_ids":["S262","S263","S264","S267"]},{"text":"Magnanimitas konsisten dengan kehati-hatian lewat analogi meja judi: keping dan dadanya indiferen, tetapi penggunaan lemparan harus cermat — hal luar tak milik kita, will milik kita; gunakan hal luar dengan hati-hati karena penggunaannya bukan indiferen, sambil tetap tenang karena materinya indiferen. Seperti pelayaran: pilih kapten, pelaut, waktu; datang badai, tugas kita selesai — bila kapal tenggelam, lakukan satu-satunya yang bisa: tidak tenggelam.","source_ids":["S279","S280"]},{"text":"Manusia dibentuk untuk kesetiaan (fidelity); perusaknya meruntuhkan ciri khas manusia: kesopanan, kesucian, hubungan tetangga, persahabatan, komunitas — jadilah serigala atau kera, dan layak dibuang seperti peralatan rusak ke tumpukan kotoran. Argumen 'wanita memang bersifat umum secara alam' dibantah dengan analogi: babi dan teater juga umum bagi semua, tetapi setelah dibagikan, mencuri porsi orang lain adalah perampokan.","source_ids":["S274","S276"]},{"text":"Metafora permainan bola: keahlian ada pada melempar dan menangkap, bukan pada bola itu sendiri — bola (hal eksternal) harus dianggap tak berharga. Socrates bermain bola di pengadilannya: omongannya yang menyenangkan pada Anytus adalah lemparan; bolanya adalah hidup, belenggu, racun. Kita harus mengerahkan seluruh keahlian pada materi eksternal tanpa menghargai materinya, seperti tukang tenun yang mengerjakan wol apa pun yang diterimanya.","source_ids":["S282","S283"]},{"text":"Foot analogy: manusia adalah bagian dari keseluruhan, bukan makhluk terpisah — kaki yang menjejak lumpur atau dipotong demi tubuh masih sesuai alam sebagai kaki; manusia yang sakit, miskin, atau mati muda tetap sesuai alam sebagai bagian dari negara yang pertama (dewa dan manusia). Hidup seperti satu jam dalam sehari: hadir lalu lewat; bagaimana cara berlalunya tak penting.","source_ids":["S281","S285"]},{"text":"Hal indiferen vs penilaiannya: proposisi hipotetis indiferen, tetapi penilaian tentangnya tidak (pengetahuan, opini, atau kekelirian); hidup indiferen, penggunaannya tidak. Maka jangan lalai karenanya, tetapi juga jangan tunduk pada materi. Ingatlah pembagian milikku/bukan milikku — jangan mengklaim milik orang lain (misal: hasil pembicaraan dengan orang lain bukan tanggung jawabmu).","source_ids":["S289","S293"]},{"text":"Kematian itu kutukan bila dihindari: padi yang tidak pernah dipanen adalah kutukan; manusia yang tidak mati seperti tidak matang. Chrysantas menuruti terompet mundur daripada kehendaknya sendiri, sedangkan kita meratap menyebutnya 'keadaan' — padahal semua cara menuju Hades setara, bahkan jalan tiran lebih singkat daripada demam.","source_ids":["S290","S291"]},{"text":"Ramalan/divinasi sering dipakai karena pengecut — ketakutan pada masa depan — hingga melalaikan kewajiban (contoh: perempuan mengirim bantuan ke Gratilla yang diasingkan meski risiko disita Domitian). Konsultasi dengan Tuhan harus tanpa desire/aversion, seperti bertanya arah jalan kepada penumpang atau memakai mata; yang sejati adalah ramal internal dalam diri yang tanda baik-buruk.","source_ids":["S297","S298","S300"]},{"text":"Hakikat Baik: Tuhan bermanfaat, maka Baik ada di mana hakikat Tuhan ada — yaitu nalar benar dan kecerdasan dalam makhluk rasional, bukan pada tumbuhan atau hewan. Manusia adalah bagian terpisah dari dewa, 'membawa Tuhan di dalam dirinya' dan merusaknya dengan pikiran kotor; Tuhan menitipkan diri kita pada diri kita sendiri seperti titipan — jaganya agar sederhana, setia, bebas gejolak. Orang bijak mati dan sakit 'sebagaimana layaknya dewa'.","source_ids":["S303","S305","S307"]},{"text":"Kritik filsuf yang hanya bicara: menempatkan doktrin seperti roti di gudang, bukan yang telah dicerna menjadi daging dan tulang — hanya muncul bila kebisingan atau tawa mengganggu. Gagasan harus dipraktikkan setelah dipelajari; yang gagal memenuhi janji watak manusia (rasional) lalu menambahkan profesi filsuf seperti orang tak mampu mengangkat beban 10 pon mencoba mengangkat batu Ajax. Analogi: disebut Yahudi bukan dengan nama melainkan dengan pemilihan dan afek yang nyata.","source_ids":["S314","S316","S317"]},{"text":"Man adalah warga dunia yang rasional, yang tugasnya adalah bertindak sesuai dengan konstitusi alam dan tatanan ilahi (S321, S322). Karakter yang baik adalah tidak menganggap apa pun menguntungkan bagi diri sendiri dan bertindak sesuai peran (S321).","source_ids":["S321"]},{"text":"Kerusakan sejati bagi manusia bukanlah kehilangan harta atau tubuh, melainkan hilangnya karakter (seperti kesopanan atau ketenangan) yang merupakan bagian dari kehendak (will) (S324, S326).","source_ids":["S324","S326"]},{"text":"Filsafat dimulai dari kesadaran akan kelemahan diri dan ketidakmampuan untuk secara sempurna menyesuaikan prasangka bawaan (seperti baik/buruk) dengan kasus nyata. Tujuannya adalah menemukan aturan (kanonos) yang melampaui sekadar 'tampakan' atau 'perasaan' (S330, S333).","source_ids":["S330","S333"]},{"text":"Kecemasan (anxiety) muncul karena manusia menginginkan hal-hal yang berada di luar kekuasaannya (seperti pujian atau kehendak Caesar). Kepercayaan sejati hanya ada dalam penguasaan keadaan internal (keinginan dan keengganannya) (S347, S348).","source_ids":["S347","S348"]},{"text":"Tujuan praktis filsafat adalah menyesuaikan kehendak (will) dengan apa yang terjadi, sehingga seseorang dapat menjalani hidup tanpa ketakutan atau gangguan, baik dalam urusan pribadi maupun sosial (S358, S359).","source_ids":["S358","S359"]},{"text":"Langkah awal dalam filsafat adalah mempelajari providensi Tuhan dan berusaha meniru sifat-sifat ilahi (seperti kesetiaan dan kebebasan) dalam tindakan dan perkataan (S360).","source_ids":["S360"]},{"text":"Membedakan 'menggunakan' dan 'memahami': orang banyak memakai kata baik-buruk seperti buta huruf memakai tulisan atau hewan memakai penampakan. Seseorang yang kaya, punya keluarga dan teman Caesar, tetapi tak tahu apa itu Tuhan, manusia, baik dan jahat — bahkan tak tahu tentang dirinya sendiri. Kebenaran seperti cermin atau dokter: bukan penghinaan, meski orang mengeluh dihina bila dikatakan keinginannya menyala dan opiniannya gegabah.","source_ids":["S361","S362"]},{"text":"Mayoritas manusia seperti hewan di pasar: hanya sibuk dengan 'pakan' (harta, tanah, budak, jabatan). Sedikit yang datang untuk memperhatikan tatanan dunia — siapa yang mengaturnya, apa relasi kita dengan pengatur itu — dan karena itu ditertawakan banyak orang, seperti penonton ditertawakan pedagang di pasar.","source_ids":["S363","S364"]},{"text":"Kekerasan kepalaan pada keputusan bukanlah keteguhan: yang tetap dipegang hanyalah keputusan yang benar, seperti otot yang sehat, bukan kejang orang gila. Contoh teman yang memutuskan mati kelaparan tanpa alasan; jiwa sakit yang menambah keputusan gegabah jadi tak terbantu — 'orang bodoh tak bisa diyakinkan maupun dipecahkan'.","source_ids":["S367","S368","S370"]},{"text":"Baik ada di kemauan, jahat di kemauan, keduanya tidak ada di luar kemauan — tetapi kita tak pernah berlatih memberi jawaban benar di luar sekolah (ketika uang ditunjukkan: uang bukan baik). Rhetorician dan pemain lute gemetar di atas panggung karena tak dilatih tentang pujian dan cemoohan; ketakutan dan kecemasan bukan pekerjaan orang lain. Latihan sejati: takut pada ketakutan itu sendiri, bukan pada kematian atau pengasingan.","source_ids":["S373","S374","S377"]},{"text":"Yang memberatkan kita hanyalah opini: di laut lepas Epictetus sendiri terbayang harus meneguk seluruh laut, padahal tiga pint cukup. Kesedihan perpisahan seperti anak menangis ditinggal pengasuh — orang dewasa juga menangis untuk gimnasium, portikos, air Dirce, Akropolis; perlu 'disapih' ke makanan yang lebih padat. Hukum ilahi: jagakan milikmu, gunakan yang diberikan, serahkan kembali dengan senang hati.","source_ids":["S377","S379","S380","S383"]},{"text":"Membuang kembung diri (self-conceit) adalah tugas pertama filsuf: mustahil belajar apa yang sudah diyakini tahu. Preconception (prolepsis) tentang baik dan sehat sudah kita punya, tetapi tak bisa disesuaikan dengan kasus tanpa analisis dan definisi — sebab itu orang berdebat, seperti dokter terbelah sebelum Hippocrates. Bukti ketidakcocokan: keinginan yang tak terjadi. Medea punya opini benar bahwa keinginan gagal adalah sengsara, tapi salah tahu cara memenuhinya — jangan menginginkan yang di luar kuasa; serahkan desire/aversion kepada para dewa.","source_ids":["S389","S390","S392","S393","S394"]},{"text":"Melawan penampakan lewat kebiasaan: setiap tindakan memperkuat kebiasaannya — marah atau takabur menambah kebiasaan itu seperti menambah bahan bakar api; penyakit jiwa meninggalkan bekas (luka) yang bila tak dihapus total akan kambuh lebih parah. Obatnya: hitung hari tanpa marah, dan saat penampakan datang, tahan dulu — 'tunggu sedikit, biar aku lihat apa kamu' — lalu lawan dengan penampakan yang indah dan mulia. Kemenangan atas penampakan inilah atlet sejati, demi kerajaan, kebebasan, dan ketenangan.","source_ids":["S403","S404","S407","S409"]},{"text":"Kritik pada yang menerima filsafat hanya dalam kata-kata: mengetahui pembagian baik-buruk-indiferen dari Chrysippus atau Cleanthes tidak berbeda dari hafalan sejarah Homer; ujian sejati adalah apakah pembagian itu diingat saat badai di kapal atau saat dipanggil ke pengadilan Caesar. 'Tunjukkan aku seorang Stoik' — orang yang sakit, mati, diasingkan, dan tetap bahagia; bukan sekadar yang mengulang argumen kecil. Sekolah Epictetus bertujuan membuat murid bebas dan bahagia, dan satu-satunya yang dalam kuasa kita adalah penggunaan penampakan yang benar.","source_ids":["S420","S421","S422","S424"]},{"text":"Bantahan terhadap Epicurus dan Akademik: mereka yang menyangkal kebenaran justru memakainya — 'percayalah bahwa tak ada yang perlu dipercaya' adalah kontradiksi. Epicurus menyangkal persaudaraan alami manusia tetapi bangun tidur dan menulis buku untuk memperingatkan orang lain — sifat manusia yang tak terbantahkan memaksanya; seperti tanaman tak bisa tumbuh melawan jenisnya, manusia tak bisa menghapus afeksi kemanusiaan. Doktrin yang merusak kesalehan dan keadilan merusak negara, padahal Sparta dan Thermopylae dibangun dari opini yang sebaliknya.","source_ids":["S428","S429","S431","S434"]},{"text":"Ketidakkonsistenan orang dalam mengakui kesalahan: tak ada yang mengaku bodoh atau tidak adil, tetapi banyak yang mengaku penakut dan penyayang — karena kebingungan tentang baik-buruk; mereka menganggap ketakutan ciri watak baik dan tak mengakui kesalahan terhadap masyarakat.","source_ids":["S440"]},{"text":"Inkonsistensi moral: orang menganggap ketakutan, kasih sayang, cemburu, dan nafsu 'tidak disengaja' untuk membenarkan diri, tetapi ketidakadilan dianggap disengaja. Menghadapi murid yang datang ke sekolah hanya untuk menguasai syllogisme sambil bertengkar dengan budak di rumah; mereka membawa pulang persis yang mereka bawa—teorema tidak berguna bagi yang salah guna, seperti cuka tidak berguna bagi penderita disentri sebelum luka disembuhkan. Alasan mesti dibawa ke sekolah tenang dan bebas distraksi.","source_ids":["S441","S444","S445"]},{"text":"Persahabatan: hanya orang bijak yang mampu mencintai, karena cinta memerlukan pengetahuan tentang Baik. Setiap makhluk terikat pada kepentingannya sendiri; bila kepentingan diletakkan pada hal eksternal, saudara atau ayah pun bisa jadi musuh—seperti anjing yang bertengkar saat sepotong daging dilempar di antara mereka (Eteocles-Polynices, Alexander membakar kuil Aesculapius). Persahabatan sejati ada hanya bila kepentingan diletakkan pada will dan penggunaan penampakan yang benar.","source_ids":["S448","S454","S455"]},{"text":"Uji persahabatan: jangan percaya pada sumpah atau lahir dari orang tua sama—periksa di mana kepentingan orang itu diletakkan (hal luar atau will). 'Kamu menemani saya lama—tahu kamu tidak ia memperlakukanmu seperti membasuh sepatu dengan spons?'; kalung Eriphyle (opini tentang barang) merusak pernikahan Amphiaraus. Yang menempatkan diri pada will akan menjadi teman sejati dan memaafkan yang berbeda karena kebodohan (doktrin Plato: jiwa dirampas kebenaran dengan tak rela).","source_ids":["S456","S458","S459"]},{"text":"Kekuatan berbicara adalah hadiah Tuhan; menyangkalnya tidak syukur dan pengecut. Namun fakultas will adalah yang tertinggi: ia menggunakan semua fakultas lain sebagai pelayan, menilai nilai setiap fakultas, membuka-tutup mata dan telinga; hanya will sendiri yang bisa menghambat will—maka will itulah satu-satunya kebajikan atau kejahatan. Kritik Epicurus yang memposisikan daging sebagai yang terutama padahal daging tidak bisa menulis tentang tujuan hidup.","source_ids":["S462","S464","S466","S467"]},{"text":"Kekuatan bicara dan teorema hanyalah 'penginapan' di jalan pulang: jangan berhenti dan tinggal di sana seperti pelancong yang lupa tujuannya, terpikat pada ungkapan, syllogisme, atau sophisme seperti di antara Sirens. Tujuan sejati: menggunakan penampakan sesuai alam, desire tidak frustrasi, bebas, taat pada administrasi Zeus, tanpa menyalahkan siapa pun ('Lead me, O Zeus, and thou too Destiny'). Bicara seperti Demosthenes atau memecahkan syllogisme seperti Chrysippus tidak mencegah kecelakaan.","source_ids":["S472","S474","S476"]},{"text":"Ada juga seni mendengar: sebagaimana mendengar musik milik musisi dan menilai patung memerlukan seni, mendengar filsuf dengan bermanfaat memerlukan latihan khusus; tidak semua pendengar teruntung—yang mendengar terampil teruntung, yang tidak terampil merugi.","source_ids":["S479","S480"]}],"sources":[{"id":"S521","chapter":"III: What Is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practice Ourselves","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"For this reason the good is preferred to every intimate relationship (obligation). There is no intimate relationship between me and my father, but there is between me and the good. Are you so hard-hearted? Yes, for such is my nature; and this is the coin which God has given me. For this reason if the good is something different from the beautiful and the just, both father is gone (neglected), and brother and country, and everything. But shall I overlook my own good, in order that you may have it, and shall I give it up to you? Why? I am your father. But you are not my good. I am your brother. But you are not my good. But if we place the good in a right determination of the will, the very observance of the relations of life is good, and accordingly he who gives up any external things, obtains that which is good. Your father takes away your property. But he does not injure you. Your brother will have the greater part of the estate in land. Let him have as much as he chooses. Will he then have a greater share of modesty, of fidelity, of brotherly affection? For who will eject you from this possession? Not even Zeus, for neither has he chosen to do so; but he has made this in my own po"},{"id":"S522","chapter":"III: What Is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practice Ourselves","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"wer, and he has given it to me just as he possessed it himself, free from hindrance, compulsion, and impediment. When then the coin which another uses is a different coin, if a man presents this coin, he receives that which is sold for it. Suppose that there comes into the province a thievish proconsul, what coin does he use? Silver coin. Show it to him, and carry off what you please. Suppose one comes who is an adulterer: what coin does he use? Little girls. Take, a man says, the coin, and sell me the small thing. Give, says the seller, and buy [what you want]. Another is eager to possess boys. Give him the coin, and receive what you wish. Another is fond of hunting: give him a fine nag or a dog. Though he groans and laments, he will sell for it that which you want. For another compels him from within, he who has fixed determined) this coin."},{"id":"S523","chapter":"III: What Is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practice Ourselves","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"Against (or with respect to) this kind of thing chiefly a man should exercise himself. As soon as you go out in the morning, examine every man whom you see, every man whom you hear; answer as to a question: What have you seen? A handsome man or woman? Apply the rule. Is this independent of the will, or dependent? Independent. Take it away. What have you seen? A man lamenting over the death of a child. Apply the rule. Death is a thing independent of the will. Take it away. Has the proconsul met you? Apply the rule. What kind of thing is a proconsul’s office? Independent of the will, or dependent on it? Independent. Take this away also. It does not stand examination. Cast it away; it is nothing to you."},{"id":"S524","chapter":"III: What Is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practice Ourselves","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"If we practiced this and exercised ourselves in it daily from morning to night, something indeed would be done. But now we are forthwith caught half asleep by every appearance, and it is only, if ever, that in the school we are roused a little. Then when we go out, if we see a man lamenting, we say, “He is undone.” If we see a consul, we say, “He is happy.” If we see an exiled man, we say, “He is miserable.” If we see a poor man, we say, “He is wretched: he has nothing to eat.”"},{"id":"S525","chapter":"III: What Is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practice Ourselves","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"We ought then to eradicate these bad opinions, and to this end we should direct all our efforts. For what is weeping and lamenting? Opinion. What is bad fortune? Opinion. What is civil sedition, what is divided opinion, what is blame, what is accusation, what is impiety, what is trifling? All these things are opinions, and nothing more, and opinions about things independent of the will, as if they were good and bad. Let a man transfer these opinions to things dependent on the will, and I engage for him that he will be firm and constant, whatever may be the state of things around him. Such as is a dish of water, such is the soul. Such as is the ray of light which falls on the water, such are the appearances. When the water is moved, the ray also seems to be moved, yet it is not moved. And when then a man is seized with giddiness, it is not the arts and the virtues which are confounded, but the spirit (the nervous power) on which they are impressed; but if the spirit be restored to its settled state, those things also are restored."},{"id":"S526","chapter":"IV: Against a Person Who Showed His Partisanship in an Unseemly Way in a Theatre","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"IV"},{"id":"S527","chapter":"IV: Against a Person Who Showed His Partisanship in an Unseemly Way in a Theatre","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"Against a Person Who Showed His Partisanship in an Unseemly Way in a Theatre"},{"id":"S528","chapter":"IV: Against a Person Who Showed His Partisanship in an Unseemly Way in a Theatre","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"The governor of Epirus having shown his favor to an actor in an unseemly way and being publicly blamed on this account, and afterwards having reported to Epictetus that he was blamed and that he was vexed at those who blamed him, Epictetus said: What harm have they been doing? These men also were acting as partisans, as you were doing. The governor replied, “Does then any person show his partisanship in this way?” When they see you, said Epictetus, who are their governor, a friend of Caesar and his deputy, showing partisanship in this way, was it not to be expected that they also should show their partisanship in the same way? for if it is not right to show partisanship in this way, do not do so yourself; and if it is right, why are you angry if they followed your example? For whom have the many to imitate except you, who are their superiors? to whose example should they look when they go to the theatre except yours? See how the deputy of Caesar looks on: he has cried out, and I too then will cry out. He springs up from his seat, and I will spring up. His slaves sit in various parts of the theatre and call out. I have no slaves, but I will myself cry out as much as I can and as lou"},{"id":"S529","chapter":"IV: Against a Person Who Showed His Partisanship in an Unseemly Way in a Theatre","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"d as all of them together. You ought then to know when you enter the theatre that you enter as a rule and example to the rest how they ought to look at the acting. Why then did they blame you? Because every man hates that which is a hindrance to him. They wished one person to be crowned; you wished another. They were a hindrance to you, and you were a hindrance to them. You were found to be the stronger; and they did what they could: they blamed that which hindered them. What then would you have? That you should do what you please, and they should not even say what they please? And what is the wonder? Do not the husbandmen abuse Zeus when they are hindered by him? do not the sailors abuse him? do they ever cease abusing Caesar? What then? does not Zeus know? is not what is said reported to Caesar? What then does he do? he knows that if he punished all who abuse him, he would have nobody to rule over. What then? when you enter the theatre, you ought to say not, “Let Sophron (some actor) be crowned,” but you ought to say this: “Come let me maintain my will in this matter so that it shall be conformable to nature: no man is dearer to me than myself. It would be ridiculous then for me "},{"id":"S530","chapter":"IV: Against a Person Who Showed His Partisanship in an Unseemly Way in a Theatre","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"to be hurt (injured) in order that another who is an actor may be crowned. Whom then do I wish to gain the prize? Why the actor who does gain the prize; and so he will always gain the prize whom I wish to gain it.” “But I wish Sophron to be crowned.” Celebrate as many games as you choose in your own house, Nemean, Pythian, Isthmian, Olympian, and proclaim him victor. But in public do not claim more than your due, nor attempt to appropriate to yourself what belongs to all. If you do not consent to this, bear being abused: for when you do the same as the many, you put yourself on the same level with them."},{"id":"S531","chapter":"V: Against Those Who on Account of Sickness Go Away Home","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"V"},{"id":"S532","chapter":"V: Against Those Who on Account of Sickness Go Away Home","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"Against Those Who on Account of Sickness Go Away Home"},{"id":"S533","chapter":"V: Against Those Who on Account of Sickness Go Away Home","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"“I am sick here,” said one of the pupils, “and I wish to return home.” At home, I suppose, you were free from sickness. Do you not consider whether you are doing anything here which may be useful to the exercise of your will, that it may be corrected? For if you are doing nothing towards this end, it was to no purpose that you came. Go away. Look after your affairs at home. For if your ruling power cannot be maintained in a state conformable to nature, it is possible that your land can, that you will be able to increase your money, you will take care of your father in his old age, frequent the public place, hold magisterial office: being bad you will do badly anything else that you have to do. But if you understand yourself, and know that you are casting away certain bad opinions and adopting others in their place, and if you have changed your state of life from things which are not within your will to things which are within your will, and if you ever say, “Alas!” you are not saying what you say on account of your father, or your brother, but on account of yourself, do you still allege your sickness? Do you not know that both disease and death must surprise us while we are doing s"},{"id":"S534","chapter":"V: Against Those Who on Account of Sickness Go Away Home","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"omething? the husbandman while he is tilling the ground, the sailor while he is on his voyage? what would you be doing when death surprises you, for you must be surprised when you are doing something? If you can be doing anything better than this when you are surprised, do it. For I wish to be surprised by disease or death when I am looking after nothing else than my own will, that I may be free from perturbation, that I may be free from hindrance, free from compulsion, and in a state of liberty. I wish to be found practicing these things that I may be able to say to God, “Have I in any respect transgressed thy commands? have I in any respect wrongly used the powers which thou gavest me? have I misused my perceptions or my preconceptions (προλήψεσι)? have I ever blamed thee? have I ever found fault with thy administration? I have been sick, because it was thy will, and so have others, but I was content to be sick. I have been poor because it was thy will, but I was content also. I have not filled a magisterial office, because it was not thy pleasure that I should: I have never desired it. Hast thou ever seen me for this reason discontented? have I not always approached thee with a "},{"id":"S535","chapter":"V: Against Those Who on Account of Sickness Go Away Home","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"cheerful countenance, ready to do thy commands and to obey thy signals? Is it now thy will that I should depart from the assemblage of men? I depart. I give thee all thanks that thou hast allowed me to join in this thy assemblage of men and to see thy works, and to comprehend this thy administration.” May death surprise me while I am thinking of these things, while I am thus writing and reading."},{"id":"S536","chapter":"V: Against Those Who on Account of Sickness Go Away Home","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"“But my mother will not hold my head when I am sick.” Go to your mother then; for you are a fit person to have your head held when you are sick. “But at home I used to lie down on a delicious bed.” Go away to your bed: indeed you are fit to lie on such a bed even when you are in health: do not then lose what you can do there (at home)."},{"id":"S537","chapter":"V: Against Those Who on Account of Sickness Go Away Home","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"But what does Socrates say? As one man, he says, is pleased with improving his land, another with improving his horse, so I am daily pleased in observing that I am growing better. “Better in what? in using nice little words?” Man, do not say that. “In little matters of speculation (θεωρήματα)?” what are you saying? “And indeed I do not see what else there is on which philosophers employ their time.” Does it seem nothing to you to have never found fault with any person, neither with God nor man? to have blamed nobody? to carry the same face always in going out and coming in? This is what Socrates knew, and yet he never said that he knew anything or taught anything. But if any man asked for nice little words or little speculations, he would carry him to Protagoras or to Hippias; and if any man came to ask for potherbs, he would carry him to the gardener. Who then among you has this purpose (motive to action)? for if indeed you had it, you would both be content in sickness, and in hunger, and in death. If any among you has been in love with a charming girl, he knows that I say what is true."},{"id":"S538","chapter":"VI: Miscellaneous","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"VI"},{"id":"S539","chapter":"VI: Miscellaneous","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"Miscellaneous"},{"id":"S540","chapter":"VI: Miscellaneous","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"When some person asked him how it happened that since reason has been more cultivated by the men of the present age, the progress made in former times was greater. In what respect, he answered, has it been more cultivated now, and in what respect was the progress greater then? For in that in which it has now been more cultivated, in that also the progress will now be found. At present it has been cultivated for the purpose of resolving syllogisms, and progress is made. But in former times it was cultivated for the purpose of maintaining the governing faculty in a condition conformable to nature, and progress was made. Do not then mix things which are different, and do not expect, when you are laboring at one thing, to make progress in another. But see if any man among us when he is intent upon this, the keeping himself in a state conformable to nature and living so always, does not make progress. For you will not find such a man."},{"id":"S541","chapter":"VI: Miscellaneous","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"The good man is invincible, for he does not enter the contest where he is not stronger. If you (his adversary) want to have his land and all that is on it, take the land; take his slaves, take his magisterial office, take his poor body. But you will not make his desire fail in that which it seeks, nor his aversion fall into that which he would avoid. The only contest into which he enters is that about things which are within the power of his will; how then will he not be invincible?"},{"id":"S542","chapter":"VI: Miscellaneous","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"Some person having asked him what is common sense, Epictetus replied: As that may be called a certain common hearing which only distinguishes vocal sounds, and that which distinguishes musical sounds is not common, but artificial; so there are certain things which men, who are not altogether perverted, see by the common notions which all possess. Such a constitution of the mind is named common sense."},{"id":"S543","chapter":"VI: Miscellaneous","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"It is not easy to exhort weak young men; for neither is it easy to hold (soft) cheese with a hook. But those who have a good natural disposition, even if you try to turn them aside, cling still more to reason. Wherefore Rufus generally attempted to discourage (his pupils), and he used this method as a test of those who had a good natural disposition and those who had not. For it was his habit to say, “as a stone, if you cast it upwards, will be brought down to the earth by its own nature, so the man whose mind is naturally good, the more you repel him, the more he turns towards that to which he is naturally inclined.”"},{"id":"S544","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"VII"},{"id":"S545","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean"},{"id":"S546","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"When the administrator came to visit him, and the man was an Epicurean, Epictetus said: It is proper for us who are not philosophers to inquire of you who are philosophers, as those who come to a strange city inquire of the citizens and those who are acquainted with it, what is the best thing in the world, in order that we also after inquiry may go in quest of that which is best and look at it, as strangers do with the things in cities. For that there are three things which relate to man —soul, body, and things external —scarcely any man denies. It remains for you philosophers to answer what is the best. What shall we say to men? Is the flesh the best? and was it for this that Maximus sailed as far as Cassiope in winter (or bad weather) with his son, and accompanied him that he might be gratified in the flesh? When the man said that it was not, and added, “Far be that from him.” Is it not fit then, Epictetus said, to be actively employed about the best? “It is certainly of all things the most fit.” What then do we possess which is better than the flesh? “The soul,” he replied. And the good things of the best, are they better, or the good things of the worse? “The good things of the"},{"id":"S547","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":" best.” And are the good things of the best within the power of the will or not within the power of the will? “They are within the power of the will.” Is then the pleasure of the soul a thing within the power of the will? “It is,” he replied. And on what shall this pleasure depend? On itself? But that cannot be conceived: for there must first exist a certain substance or nature (οὐσία) of good, by obtaining which we shall have pleasure in the soul. He assented to this also. On what then shall we depend for this pleasure of the soul? for if it shall depend on things of the soul, the substance (nature) of the good is discovered; for good cannot be one thing, and that at which we are rationally delighted another thing; nor if that which precedes is not good, can that which comes after be good, for in order that the thing which comes after may be good, that which precedes must be good. But you would not affirm this, if you are in your right mind, for you would then say what is inconsistent both with Epicurus and the rest of your doctrines. It remains then that the pleasure of the soul is in the pleasure from things of the body: and again that those bodily things must be the things whic"},{"id":"S548","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"h precede and the substance (nature) of the good."},{"id":"S549","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"For this reason Maximus acted foolishly if he made the voyage for any other reason than for the sake of the flesh, that is, for the sake of the best. And also a man acts foolishly if he abstains from that which belongs to others, when he is a judge (δικαστής) and able to take it. But, if you please, let us consider this only: how this thing may be done secretly, and safely, and so that no man will know it. For not even does Epicurus himself declare stealing to be bad, but he admits that detection is; and because it is impossible to have security against detection, for this reason he says, “Do not steal.” But I say to you that if stealing is done cleverly and cautiously, we shall not be detected: further also we have powerful friends in Rome both men and women, and the Hellenes (Greeks) are weak, and no man will venture to go up to Rome for the purpose (of complaining). Why do you refrain from your own good? This is senseless, foolish. But even if you tell me that you do refrain, I will not believe you. For as it is impossible to assent to that which appears false, and to turn away from that which is true, so it is impossible to abstain from that which appears good. But wealth is a "},{"id":"S550","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"good thing, and certainly most efficient in producing pleasure. Why will you not acquire wealth? And why should we not corrupt our neighbor’s wife, if we can do it without detection? and if the husband foolishly prates about the matter, why not pitch him out of the house? If you would be a philosopher such as you ought to be, if a perfect philosopher, if consistent with your own doctrines, [you must act thus]. If you would not, you will not differ at all from us who are called Stoics; for we also say one thing, but we do another: we talk of the things which are beautiful (good), but we do what is base. But you will be perverse in the contrary way, teaching what is bad, practicing what is good."},{"id":"S551","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"In the name of God, are you thinking of a city of Epicureans? [One man says], “I do not marry.” —“Nor I, for a man ought not to marry; nor ought we to beget children, nor engage in public matters.” What then will happen? whence will the citizens come? who will bring them up? who will be governor of the youth, who preside over gymnastic exercises? and in what also will the teacher instruct them? will he teach them what the Lacedaemonians were taught, or what the Athenians were taught? Come take a young man, bring him up according to your doctrines. The doctrines are bad, subversive of a state, pernicious to families, and not becoming to women. Dismiss them, man. You live in a chief city: it is your duty to be a magistrate, to judge justly, to abstain from that which belongs to others; no woman ought to seem beautiful to you except your own wife, and no youth, no vessel of silver, no vessel of gold (except your own). Seek for doctrines which are consistent with what I say, and by making them your guide you will with pleasure abstain from things which have such persuasive power to lead us and overpower us. But if to the persuasive power of these things, we also devise such a philosoph"},{"id":"S552","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"y as this which helps to push us on towards them and strengthens us to this end, what will be the conesquence? In a piece of toreutic art which is the best part? the silver or the workmanship? The substance of the hand is the flesh; but the work of the hand is the principal part (that which precedes and leads the rest). The duties then are also three: those which are directed towards the existence of a thing; those which are directed towards its existence in a particular kind; and third, the chief or leading things themselves. So also in man we ought not to value the material, the poor flesh, but the principal (leading things, τὰ προηγούμενα). What are these? Engaging in public business, marrying, begetting children, venerating God, taking care of parents, and generally, having desires, aversions (ἐκκλίνειν), pursuits of things, and avoidances, in the way in which we ought to do these things, and according to our nature. And how are we constituted by nature? Free, noble, modest: for what other animal blushes? what other is capable of receiving the appearance (the impression) of shame? and we are so constituted by nature as to subject pleasure to these things, as a minister, a serva"},{"id":"S553","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"nt, in order that it may call forth our activity, in order that it may keep us constant in acts which are conformable to nature."},{"id":"S554","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"“But I am rich and I want nothing.” Why then do you pretend to be a philosopher? Your golden and your silver vessels are enough for you. What need have you of principles (opinions)? “But I am also a judge (κριτής) of the Greeks.” Do you know how to judge? Who taught you to know? “Caesar wrote to me a codicil.” Let him write and give you a commission to judge of music; and what will be the use of it to you? Still how did you become a judge? whose hand did you kiss? the hand of Symphorus or Numenius? Before whose bedchamber have you slept? To whom have you sent gifts? Then do you not see that to be a judge is just of the same value as Numenius is? “But I can throw into prison any man whom I please.” So you can do with a stone. “But I can beat with sticks whom I please.” So you may an ass. This is not a governing of men. Govern us as rational animals: show us what is profitable to us, and we will follow it: show us what is unprofitable, and we will turn away from it. Make us imitators of yourself, as Socrates made men imitators of himself. For he was like a governor of men, who made them subject to him their desires, their aversion, their movements towards an object and their turning "},{"id":"S555","chapter":"VII: To the Administrator of the Free Cities Who Was an Epicurean","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"away from it. —Do this: do not do this: if you do not obey, I will throw you into prison. —This is not governing men like rational animals. But I (say): As Zeus has ordained, so act: if you do not act so, you will feel the penalty, you will be punished. —What will be the punishment? Nothing else than not having done your duty: you will lose the character of fidelity, modesty, propriety. Do not look for greater penalties than these."},{"id":"S556","chapter":"VIII: How We Must Exercise Ourselves Against Appearances (Φαντασίας)","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"VIII"},{"id":"S557","chapter":"VIII: How We Must Exercise Ourselves Against Appearances (Φαντασίας)","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"How We Must Exercise Ourselves Against Appearances (Φαντασίας)"},{"id":"S558","chapter":"VIII: How We Must Exercise Ourselves Against Appearances (Φαντασίας)","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"As we exercise ourselves against sophistical questions, so we ought to exercise ourselves daily against appearances; for these appearances also propose questions to us. A certain person’s son is dead. Answer: the thing is not within the power of the will; it is not an evil. A father has disinherited a certain son. What do you think of it? It is a thing beyond the power of the will, not an evil. Caesar has condemned a person. It is a thing beyond the power of the will, not an evil. The man is afflicted at this. Affliction is a thing which depends on the will: it is an evil. He has borne the condemnation bravely. That is a thing within the power of the will: it is a good. If we train ourselves in this manner, we shall make progress, for we shall never assent to anything of which there is not an appearance capable of being comprehended. Your son is dead. What has happened? Your son is dead. Nothing more? Nothing. Your ship is lost. What has happened? Your ship is lost. A man has been led to prison. What has happened? He has been led to prison. But that herein he has fared badly, every man adds from his own opinion. But Zeus, you say, does not do right in these matters. Why? because he"},{"id":"S559","chapter":"VIII: How We Must Exercise Ourselves Against Appearances (Φαντασίας)","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":" has made you capable of endurance? because he has made you magnanimous? because he has taken, from that which befalls you, the power of being evils? because it is in your power to be happy while you are suffering what you suffer; because he has opened the door to you, when things do not please you? Man, go out and do not complain."},{"id":"S560","chapter":"VIII: How We Must Exercise Ourselves Against Appearances (Φαντασίας)","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"Hear how the Romans feel towards philosophers, if you would like to know. Italicus, who was the most in repute of the philosophers, once when I was present being vexed with his own friends and as if he was suffering something intolerable said, “I cannot bear it, you are killing me: you will make me such as that man is;” pointing to me."}],"newWindowIds":["S521","S522","S523","S524","S525","S526","S527","S528","S529","S530","S531","S532","S533","S534","S535","S536","S537","S538","S539","S540","S541","S542","S543","S544","S545","S546","S547","S548","S549","S550","S551","S552","S553","S554","S555","S556","S557","S558","S559","S560"]}
requests.raw: {"notes":[{"text":"Baik lebih diutamakan daripada relasi terdekat: tidak ada relasi antara aku dan ayah, tetapi antara aku dan Baik. Bila Baik diletakkan pada penentuan kemauan yang benar, justru pemenuhan relasi hidup menjadi baik; ayah yang mengambil harta tidak melukai — kesopanan dan kesetiaan tak dapat dirampas bahkan oleh Zeus. Setiap orang punya 'koin' sendiri dari Tuhan (proconsul dibayar perak, pezina dengan gadis) yang menentukan apa yang ia beli.","source_ids":["S521","S522"]},{"text":"Latihan harian melawan penampakan: setiap pagi uji setiap penampakan dengan aturan — apakah dalam kuasa kemauan atau tidak; bila tidak, buang ('tidak ada bagimu'). Ratapan, sial, perpecahan sipil, celaan, kekufuran semuanya hanyalah opini tentang hal di luar kemauan seolah baik-buruk; pindahkan opini itu ke hal dalam kemauan maka orang akan teguh. Seperti cahaya di atas air yang bergoyang: jiwa yang terganggu tampak mengacaukan kebajikan, tetapi sebenarnya hanya roh yang perlu dikembalikan tenang.","source_ids":["S523","S524","S525"]},{"text":"Gubernur Epirus yang berseberangan di teater ditegur: banyak orang meniru contoh orang berkuasa; bila berseberangan itu salah, jangan lakukan sendiri; bila benar, jangan marah ditiru. Di teater masuklah dengan tujuan menjaga kemauan sesuai alam — 'tak ada yang lebih kusayang daripada diriku sendiri'; di rumah boleh menggelar permainan sendiri dan menobatkan Sophron, tetapi di publik jangan mengklaim milik semua orang; bila menolak, tanggunglah cemoohan.","source_ids":["S528","S529","S530"]},{"text":"Murid yang ingin pulang karena sakit ditegur: penyakit dan kematian pasti mengejutkan kita saat sedang melakukan sesuatu — berharap dikejutkan saat menjaga kemauan sendiri, agar bisa berkata kepada Tuhan: aku sakit dan miskin karena kehendak-Mu dan tetap pasrah, tak pernah mencela administrasi-Mu. Socrates bahagia karena tiap hari melihat dirinya bertumbuh lebih baik: tak pernah mencela siapa pun, Tuhan maupun manusia, dan selalu berwajah sama.","source_ids":["S533","S534","S537"]},{"text":"Orang baik tak terkalahkan karena tak masuk pertarungan di mana ia lebih lemah: tanah, budak, jabatan, tubuh boleh diambil, tetapi desire dan aversion-nya tak bisa digagalkan — satu-satunya pertarungan yang ia masuki adalah tentang hal dalam kuasa kemauannya. Kemajuan kini terhambat karena akal dilatih untuk memecahkan syllogisme, bukan untuk menjaga fakultas penguasa sesuai alam; jangan mencampur hal yang berbeda.","source_ids":["S540","S541"]},{"text":"Dialog dengan administrator Epicurean: jika daging yang terbaik, maka Maximus berlayar demi daging; tetapi kenikmatan jiwa harus bergantung pada sesuatu yang mendahuluinya — jika bukan hal jiwa, maka hal tubuh, dan substansi Baik jatuh ke tubuh. Konsekuensi logis Epicurean: mencuri dan berzina boleh bila tak terdeteksi — doktrin yang merusak negara dan keluarga. Tugas utama manusia: urusan publik, menikah, membesarkan anak, menghormati Tuhan, merawat orang tua; manusia terbawa bebas, mulia, dan mampu malu — kenikmatan harus jadi pelayan, bukan tuan.","source_ids":["S546","S549","S552","S553"]},{"text":"Kekuasaan menghukum bukan pemerintahan manusia: memenjarakan seperti batu, memukul seperti keledai. Pemerintahan sejati menunjukkan apa yang menguntungkan sebagai makhluk rasional, seperti Socrates. Hukuman bagi yang tak patuh bukan penjara, melainkan kehilangan watak: kesetiaan, kesopanan, kepatutan — jangan cari hukuman lebih besar dari itu.","source_ids":["S554","S555"]},{"text":"Latihan melawan penampakan seperti melawan soal sophistik: anakmu mati — apa yang terjadi? Anakmu mati, tidak lebih; 'ia sengsara' adalah tambahan opini sendiri. Bila menyalahkan Zeus, ingat: ia menjadimu mampu menanggung, menjadimu magnanimous, mengambil kuasa hal-hal menjadi kejahatan, dan membukakan pintu keluar — 'keluarlah dan jangan meratap'.","source_ids":["S558","S559"]}]}

Yang dijaga itulah yang diserang: bila menaruh hormat pada tubuh atau harta kecil, di situlah kita jadi budak.
