Segala tindakan diukur oleh penampakan.","source_ids":["S210","S212","S213"]},{"text":"Iliad hanyalah penampakan dan penggunaannya: pembakaran Troya tidak lebih dahsyat dari sarang bangau yang terbakar—bedanya manusia memiliki kejujuran, kemoderatan, kesetiaan, kecerdasan. Kehancuran sejati adalah kehancuran opini benar: Alexander hancur saat kehilangan karakter, Achilles saat marah dan lupa tugasnya.","source_ids":["S214","S216","S217"]},{"text":"Esensi Baik adalah kemauan; hal luar hanya bahan bagi kemauan. Hukum Allah: ambil kebaikan dari dirimu sendiri. Tirani hanya mengancam tubuh; tidak ada yang lebih kuat daripada kemauan kecuali kemauan sendiri—sepuluh orang lebih kuat dalam mengekang, tetapi tidak dalam opini yang benar.","source_ids":["S222","S224"]},{"text":"Socrates menafsir ulang: yang dibawa ke penjara hanyalah 'tubuh miskinnya'; 'Anytus dan Melitus dapat membunuhku, tetapi tidak menyakitiku.' Kesulitan adalah ujian pembelajaran: seperti atlet yang ingin lawan berat, orang terdidik harus menunjukkan ajarannya dalam praktik, bukan argumen kecil di sudut sekolah; jadilah saksi Allah bahwa yang eksternal bukan baik atau jahat.","source_ids":["S226","S232","S235"]},{"text":"Pelayan yang baik menghormati semua orang sesuai 'relasi': ayah, saudara, keabadian—mengingat bahwa adalah watak dewata mempertahankan diri dari mimpi dan kecenderungan; putusan orang yang belum terdidik tentang kesalehan tidak lebih penting daripada seorang musisi yang salah menilai tali lyre. Hamba yang lari menikmati teater dengan ketakutan; membebaskan diri dari 'majikan' (kematian, kesenangan, sakit) menghapus seluruh ketakutan.","source_ids":["S236","S238","S239"]},{"text":"Sikap yang harus disiapkan dalam kesulitan: saat menghadapi orang besar, ingat ada yang melihat dari atas; pengasingan, penjara, mati, aib tetap hal indiferen yang tak berubah — hanya hal di luar kemauan yang 'tak ada bagiku'; Baik adalah kemauan sebagaimana mestinya dan penggunaan penampakan; tujuan hidup adalah mengikuti Tuhan. YAng begitu belajar akan berani karena tahu semua persiapan gelar-gelar kuasa 'bukanlah apa-apa'.","source_ids":["S243","S244"]},{"text":"Percaya diri dan kehati-hatian tidak bertentangan bila diterapkan pada objek berbeda: kehati-hatian pada hal dalam kemauan (satu-satunya jahat), keberanian pada hal di luar kemauan. Manusia terbalik seperti rusa yang takut pada bulu pemburu lalu lari ke jaring: takut pada kematian, sakit, aib (hal luar) tetapi gegabah pada tipu, nafsu, aib tindakan (hal will). Bukan kematian yang menakutkan, melainkan ketakutan pada kematian.","source_ids":["S247","S248","S249"]},{"text":"Kematian dan sakit adalah 'topeng tragedi': putar dan periksa — tidak menggigit; pintu selalu terbuka bila tak tertahankan. Kebebasan sejati adalah milik yang terdidik: hidup tanpa kesalahan, takut, duka, dan gejolak adalah bebas; budak yang dibebaskan di pengadilan tetap tak bebas bila uang, kekasih, atau tiran jadi majikannya. Socrates menulis untuk menguji dirinya sendiri dalam praktik, bukan karya-karya kosong; pamer sejati pemuda terdidik adalah 'sajikan kematian, penjara, siksaan — aku tak kecewa dan tak jatuh'.","source_ids":["S252","S254","S257","S258"]},{"text":"Ketenangan dalam perkara (contoh: ke pengadilan): bila tujuannya mempertahankan will sesuai alam, aman penuh — tak ada yang menguasainya; bila ingin mempertahankan hal luar, siaplah jadi budak penuh (berlutut, menangis). Socrates seumur hidup bersiap menghadapi sidang karena tak pernah berbuat zalim. Minta 'saran untuk setiap kejadian' seperti orang buta huruf minta tahu nama apa yang akan ditulis; latihan membuat siap untuk semua, dan yang mengejar hal luar pasti terombang-ambing pada kehendak majikannya.","source_ids":["S262","S263","S264","S267"]},{"text":"Magnanimitas konsisten dengan kehati-hatian lewat analogi meja judi: keping dan dadanya indiferen, tetapi penggunaan lemparan harus cermat — hal luar tak milik kita, will milik kita; gunakan hal luar dengan hati-hati karena penggunaannya bukan indiferen, sambil tetap tenang karena materinya indiferen. Seperti pelayaran: pilih kapten, pelaut, waktu; datang badai, tugas kita selesai — bila kapal tenggelam, lakukan satu-satunya yang bisa: tidak tenggelam.","source_ids":["S279","S280"]},{"text":"Manusia dibentuk untuk kesetiaan (fidelity); perusaknya meruntuhkan ciri khas manusia: kesopanan, kesucian, hubungan tetangga, persahabatan, komunitas — jadilah serigala atau kera, dan layak dibuang seperti peralatan rusak ke tumpukan kotoran. Argumen 'wanita memang bersifat umum secara alam' dibantah dengan analogi: babi dan teater juga umum bagi semua, tetapi setelah dibagikan, mencuri porsi orang lain adalah perampokan.","source_ids":["S274","S276"]},{"text":"Metafora permainan bola: keahlian ada pada melempar dan menangkap, bukan pada bola itu sendiri — bola (hal eksternal) harus dianggap tak berharga. Socrates bermain bola di pengadilannya: omongannya yang menyenangkan pada Anytus adalah lemparan; bolanya adalah hidup, belenggu, racun. Kita harus mengerahkan seluruh keahlian pada materi eksternal tanpa menghargai materinya, seperti tukang tenun yang mengerjakan wol apa pun yang diterimanya.","source_ids":["S282","S283"]},{"text":"Foot analogy: manusia adalah bagian dari keseluruhan, bukan makhluk terpisah — kaki yang menjejak lumpur atau dipotong demi tubuh masih sesuai alam sebagai kaki; manusia yang sakit, miskin, atau mati muda tetap sesuai alam sebagai bagian dari negara yang pertama (dewa dan manusia). Hidup seperti satu jam dalam sehari: hadir lalu lewat; bagaimana cara berlalunya tak penting.","source_ids":["S281","S285"]},{"text":"Hal indiferen vs penilaiannya: proposisi hipotetis indiferen, tetapi penilaian tentangnya tidak (pengetahuan, opini, atau kekelirian); hidup indiferen, penggunaannya tidak. Maka jangan lalai karenanya, tetapi juga jangan tunduk pada materi. Ingatlah pembagian milikku/bukan milikku — jangan mengklaim milik orang lain (misal: hasil pembicaraan dengan orang lain bukan tanggung jawabmu).","source_ids":["S289","S293"]},{"text":"Kematian itu kutukan bila dihindari: padi yang tidak pernah dipanen adalah kutukan; manusia yang tidak mati seperti tidak matang. Chrysantas menuruti terompet mundur daripada kehendaknya sendiri, sedangkan kita meratap menyebutnya 'keadaan' — padahal semua cara menuju Hades setara, bahkan jalan tiran lebih singkat daripada demam.","source_ids":["S290","S291"]},{"text":"Ramalan/divinasi sering dipakai karena pengecut — ketakutan pada masa depan — hingga melalaikan kewajiban (contoh: perempuan mengirim bantuan ke Gratilla yang diasingkan meski risiko disita Domitian). Konsultasi dengan Tuhan harus tanpa desire/aversion, seperti bertanya arah jalan kepada penumpang atau memakai mata; yang sejati adalah ramal internal dalam diri yang tanda baik-buruk.","source_ids":["S297","S298","S300"]},{"text":"Hakikat Baik: Tuhan bermanfaat, maka Baik ada di mana hakikat Tuhan ada — yaitu nalar benar dan kecerdasan dalam makhluk rasional, bukan pada tumbuhan atau hewan. Manusia adalah bagian terpisah dari dewa, 'membawa Tuhan di dalam dirinya' dan merusaknya dengan pikiran kotor; Tuhan menitipkan diri kita pada diri kita sendiri seperti titipan — jaganya agar sederhana, setia, bebas gejolak. Orang bijak mati dan sakit 'sebagaimana layaknya dewa'.","source_ids":["S303","S305","S307"]},{"text":"Kritik filsuf yang hanya bicara: menempatkan doktrin seperti roti di gudang, bukan yang telah dicerna menjadi daging dan tulang — hanya muncul bila kebisingan atau tawa mengganggu. Gagasan harus dipraktikkan setelah dipelajari; yang gagal memenuhi janji watak manusia (rasional) lalu menambahkan profesi filsuf seperti orang tak mampu mengangkat beban 10 pon mencoba mengangkat batu Ajax. Analogi: disebut Yahudi bukan dengan nama melainkan dengan pemilihan dan afek yang nyata.","source_ids":["S314","S316","S317"]},{"text":"Man adalah warga dunia yang rasional, yang tugasnya adalah bertindak sesuai dengan konstitusi alam dan tatanan ilahi (S321, S322). Karakter yang baik adalah tidak menganggap apa pun menguntungkan bagi diri sendiri dan bertindak sesuai peran (S321).","source_ids":["S321"]},{"text":"Kerusakan sejati bagi manusia bukanlah kehilangan harta atau tubuh, melainkan hilangnya karakter (seperti kesopanan atau ketenangan) yang merupakan bagian dari kehendak (will) (S324, S326).","source_ids":["S324","S326"]},{"text":"Filsafat dimulai dari kesadaran akan kelemahan diri dan ketidakmampuan untuk secara sempurna menyesuaikan prasangka bawaan (seperti baik/buruk) dengan kasus nyata. Tujuannya adalah menemukan aturan (kanonos) yang melampaui sekadar 'tampakan' atau 'perasaan' (S330, S333).","source_ids":["S330","S333"]},{"text":"Kecemasan (anxiety) muncul karena manusia menginginkan hal-hal yang berada di luar kekuasaannya (seperti pujian atau kehendak Caesar). Kepercayaan sejati hanya ada dalam penguasaan keadaan internal (keinginan dan keengganannya) (S347, S348).","source_ids":["S347","S348"]},{"text":"Tujuan praktis filsafat adalah menyesuaikan kehendak (will) dengan apa yang terjadi, sehingga seseorang dapat menjalani hidup tanpa ketakutan atau gangguan, baik dalam urusan pribadi maupun sosial (S358, S359).","source_ids":["S358","S359"]},{"text":"Langkah awal dalam filsafat adalah mempelajari providensi Tuhan dan berusaha meniru sifat-sifat ilahi (seperti kesetiaan dan kebebasan) dalam tindakan dan perkataan (S360).","source_ids":["S360"]},{"text":"Membedakan 'menggunakan' dan 'memahami': orang banyak memakai kata baik-buruk seperti buta huruf memakai tulisan atau hewan memakai penampakan. Seseorang yang kaya, punya keluarga dan teman Caesar, tetapi tak tahu apa itu Tuhan, manusia, baik dan jahat — bahkan tak tahu tentang dirinya sendiri. Kebenaran seperti cermin atau dokter: bukan penghinaan, meski orang mengeluh dihina bila dikatakan keinginannya menyala dan opiniannya gegabah.","source_ids":["S361","S362"]},{"text":"Mayoritas manusia seperti hewan di pasar: hanya sibuk dengan 'pakan' (harta, tanah, budak, jabatan). Sedikit yang datang untuk memperhatikan tatanan dunia — siapa yang mengaturnya, apa relasi kita dengan pengatur itu — dan karena itu ditertawakan banyak orang, seperti penonton ditertawakan pedagang di pasar.","source_ids":["S363","S364"]},{"text":"Kekerasan kepalaan pada keputusan bukanlah keteguhan: yang tetap dipegang hanyalah keputusan yang benar, seperti otot yang sehat, bukan kejang orang gila. Contoh teman yang memutuskan mati kelaparan tanpa alasan; jiwa sakit yang menambah keputusan gegabah jadi tak terbantu — 'orang bodoh tak bisa diyakinkan maupun dipecahkan'.","source_ids":["S367","S368","S370"]},{"text":"Baik ada di kemauan, jahat di kemauan, keduanya tidak ada di luar kemauan — tetapi kita tak pernah berlatih memberi jawaban benar di luar sekolah (ketika uang ditunjukkan: uang bukan baik). Rhetorician dan pemain lute gemetar di atas panggung karena tak dilatih tentang pujian dan cemoohan; ketakutan dan kecemasan bukan pekerjaan orang lain. Latihan sejati: takut pada ketakutan itu sendiri, bukan pada kematian atau pengasingan.","source_ids":["S373","S374","S377"]},{"text":"Yang memberatkan kita hanyalah opini: di laut lepas Epictetus sendiri terbayang harus meneguk seluruh laut, padahal tiga pint cukup. Kesedihan perpisahan seperti anak menangis ditinggal pengasuh — orang dewasa juga menangis untuk gimnasium, portikos, air Dirce, Akropolis; perlu 'disapih' ke makanan yang lebih padat. Hukum ilahi: jagakan milikmu, gunakan yang diberikan, serahkan kembali dengan senang hati.","source_ids":["S377","S379","S380","S383"]},{"text":"Membuang kembung diri (self-conceit) adalah tugas pertama filsuf: mustahil belajar apa yang sudah diyakini tahu. Preconception (prolepsis) tentang baik dan sehat sudah kita punya, tetapi tak bisa disesuaikan dengan kasus tanpa analisis dan definisi — sebab itu orang berdebat, seperti dokter terbelah sebelum Hippocrates. Bukti ketidakcocokan: keinginan yang tak terjadi. Medea punya opini benar bahwa keinginan gagal adalah sengsara, tapi salah tahu cara memenuhinya — jangan menginginkan yang di luar kuasa; serahkan desire/aversion kepada para dewa.","source_ids":["S389","S390","S392","S393","S394"]},{"text":"Melawan penampakan lewat kebiasaan: setiap tindakan memperkuat kebiasaannya — marah atau takabur menambah kebiasaan itu seperti menambah bahan bakar api; penyakit jiwa meninggalkan bekas (luka) yang bila tak dihapus total akan kambuh lebih parah. Obatnya: hitung hari tanpa marah, dan saat penampakan datang, tahan dulu — 'tunggu sedikit, biar aku lihat apa kamu' — lalu lawan dengan penampakan yang indah dan mulia. Kemenangan atas penampakan inilah atlet sejati, demi kerajaan, kebebasan, dan ketenangan.","source_ids":["S403","S404","S407","S409"]},{"text":"Kritik pada yang menerima filsafat hanya dalam kata-kata: mengetahui pembagian baik-buruk-indiferen dari Chrysippus atau Cleanthes tidak berbeda dari hafalan sejarah Homer; ujian sejati adalah apakah pembagian itu diingat saat badai di kapal atau saat dipanggil ke pengadilan Caesar. 'Tunjukkan aku seorang Stoik' — orang yang sakit, mati, diasingkan, dan tetap bahagia; bukan sekadar yang mengulang argumen kecil. Sekolah Epictetus bertujuan membuat murid bebas dan bahagia, dan satu-satunya yang dalam kuasa kita adalah penggunaan penampakan yang benar.","source_ids":["S420","S421","S422","S424"]},{"text":"Bantahan terhadap Epicurus dan Akademik: mereka yang menyangkal kebenaran justru memakainya — 'percayalah bahwa tak ada yang perlu dipercaya' adalah kontradiksi. Epicurus menyangkal persaudaraan alami manusia tetapi bangun tidur dan menulis buku untuk memperingatkan orang lain — sifat manusia yang tak terbantahkan memaksanya; seperti tanaman tak bisa tumbuh melawan jenisnya, manusia tak bisa menghapus afeksi kemanusiaan. Doktrin yang merusak kesalehan dan keadilan merusak negara, padahal Sparta dan Thermopylae dibangun dari opini yang sebaliknya.","source_ids":["S428","S429","S431","S434"]},{"text":"Ketidakkonsistenan orang dalam mengakui kesalahan: tak ada yang mengaku bodoh atau tidak adil, tetapi banyak yang mengaku penakut dan penyayang — karena kebingungan tentang baik-buruk; mereka menganggap ketakutan ciri watak baik dan tak mengakui kesalahan terhadap masyarakat.","source_ids":["S440"]},{"text":"Inkonsistensi moral: orang menganggap ketakutan, kasih sayang, cemburu, dan nafsu 'tidak disengaja' untuk membenarkan diri, tetapi ketidakadilan dianggap disengaja. Menghadapi murid yang datang ke sekolah hanya untuk menguasai syllogisme sambil bertengkar dengan budak di rumah; mereka membawa pulang persis yang mereka bawa—teorema tidak berguna bagi yang salah guna, seperti cuka tidak berguna bagi penderita disentri sebelum luka disembuhkan. Alasan mesti dibawa ke sekolah tenang dan bebas distraksi.","source_ids":["S441","S444","S445"]},{"text":"Persahabatan: hanya orang bijak yang mampu mencintai, karena cinta memerlukan pengetahuan tentang Baik. Setiap makhluk terikat pada kepentingannya sendiri; bila kepentingan diletakkan pada hal eksternal, saudara atau ayah pun bisa jadi musuh—seperti anjing yang bertengkar saat sepotong daging dilempar di antara mereka (Eteocles-Polynices, Alexander membakar kuil Aesculapius). Persahabatan sejati ada hanya bila kepentingan diletakkan pada will dan penggunaan penampakan yang benar.","source_ids":["S448","S454","S455"]},{"text":"Uji persahabatan: jangan percaya pada sumpah atau lahir dari orang tua sama—periksa di mana kepentingan orang itu diletakkan (hal luar atau will). 'Kamu menemani saya lama—tahu kamu tidak ia memperlakukanmu seperti membasuh sepatu dengan spons?'; kalung Eriphyle (opini tentang barang) merusak pernikahan Amphiaraus. Yang menempatkan diri pada will akan menjadi teman sejati dan memaafkan yang berbeda karena kebodohan (doktrin Plato: jiwa dirampas kebenaran dengan tak rela).","source_ids":["S456","S458","S459"]},{"text":"Kekuatan berbicara adalah hadiah Tuhan; menyangkalnya tidak syukur dan pengecut. Namun fakultas will adalah yang tertinggi: ia menggunakan semua fakultas lain sebagai pelayan, menilai nilai setiap fakultas, membuka-tutup mata dan telinga; hanya will sendiri yang bisa menghambat will—maka will itulah satu-satunya kebajikan atau kejahatan. Kritik Epicurus yang memposisikan daging sebagai yang terutama padahal daging tidak bisa menulis tentang tujuan hidup.","source_ids":["S462","S464","S466","S467"]},{"text":"Kekuatan bicara dan teorema hanyalah 'penginapan' di jalan pulang: jangan berhenti dan tinggal di sana seperti pelancong yang lupa tujuannya, terpikat pada ungkapan, syllogisme, atau sophisme seperti di antara Sirens. Tujuan sejati: menggunakan penampakan sesuai alam, desire tidak frustrasi, bebas, taat pada administrasi Zeus, tanpa menyalahkan siapa pun ('Lead me, O Zeus, and thou too Destiny'). Bicara seperti Demosthenes atau memecahkan syllogisme seperti Chrysippus tidak mencegah kecelakaan.","source_ids":["S472","S474","S476"]},{"text":"Ada juga seni mendengar: sebagaimana mendengar musik milik musisi dan menilai patung memerlukan seni, mendengar filsuf dengan bermanfaat memerlukan latihan khusus; tidak semua pendengar teruntung—yang mendengar terampil teruntung, yang tidak terampil merugi.","source_ids":["S479","S480"]},{"text":"Kesalahan (error) selalu mengandung kontradiksi: pencuri berpikir mencuri menguntungkan padahal tidak; jiwa rasional tak bisa menyetujui yang palsu bila kefalsahannya tampak. Maka sang pembaharu cukup menunjukkan kontradiksi itu—seperti Socrates yang cukup satu pembicara sebagai saksi—bila tak tampak, saling diri sendiri, bukan orangnya.","source_ids":["S492","S493"]},{"text":"Perawatan diri lewat penampilan (rambut berhias, mencabut bulu) dikritik: keindahan manusia ada pada keunggulan khasnya (keadilan, moderasi, kesederhanaan), bukan pada bagian hewani atau mortalitas; manusia adalah will (proairesis), bukan daging dan rambut. Socrates menasihati Alcibiades untuk menghiasi kemauan dan membuang opini buruk, bukan tubuh.","source_ids":["S496","S497","S508"]},{"text":"Filsuf wajib berkata benar meski pendengar tidak mau dipengaruhi: contoh Apollo tetap berbicara kepada Laius dan Socrates menolak berhenti mengajukan pertanyaan meski diadili; 'aku adalah orang yang bertugas merawat manusia'—yang unggul dalam setiap jenis (seperti ungu pada jubah, bulla melawan singa) tidak perlu membela diri atas keberbedaannya.","source_ids":["S500","S501","S502"]},{"text":"Tiga topik latihan orang yang berprogres: (1) desire/aversion—yang paling utama karena dari situ lahir gejolak; (2) tugas dan relasi alami (anak, ayah, warga) dengan afek yang tidak hampa seperti patung; (3) assent tanpa kekeliruan. Filsuf sezaman menelorkan topik ketiga (sophisme) sambil mengabaikan dua yang pertama—padahal bahkan terganggu oleh ketakutan diremehkan orang.","source_ids":["S512","S513","S514"]},{"text":"Nilai sejati tidak ditunjukkan dengan membaca Chrysippus/Archedemus: Diogenes menunjuk sophist dengan jari tengah—manusia ditunjukkan oleh prinsip-prinsipnya, bukan seperti batu. Yang kapalnya tenggelam tidak waktunya membahas argumen hipotetis; pembahasan logis hanya untuk yang sudah tenang, tanpa marah, duka, dan iri.","source_ids":["S515","S516","S517"]},{"text":"Materi kerja orang baik adalah fakultas penguasanya sendiri: menggunakan penampakan sesuai alam; jiwa tak bisa menolak penampakan baik yang jelas, seperti penukar uang tak bisa menolak koin Caesar—prinsip inilah dasar seluruh gerakan manusia dan Tuhan.","source_ids":["S520"]},{"text":"Baik lebih diutamakan daripada relasi terdekat: tidak ada relasi antara aku dan ayah, tetapi antara aku dan Baik. Bila Baik diletakkan pada penentuan kemauan yang benar, justru pemenuhan relasi hidup menjadi baik; ayah yang mengambil harta tidak melukai — kesopanan dan kesetiaan tak dapat dirampas bahkan oleh Zeus. Setiap orang punya 'koin' sendiri dari Tuhan (proconsul dibayar perak, pezina dengan gadis) yang menentukan apa yang ia beli.","source_ids":["S521","S522"]},{"text":"Latihan harian melawan penampakan: setiap pagi uji setiap penampakan dengan aturan — apakah dalam kuasa kemauan atau tidak; bila tidak, buang ('tidak ada bagimu'). Ratapan, sial, perpecahan sipil, celaan, kekufuran semuanya hanyalah opini tentang hal di luar kemauan seolah baik-buruk; pindahkan opini itu ke hal dalam kemauan maka orang akan teguh. Seperti cahaya di atas air yang bergoyang: jiwa yang terganggu tampak mengacaukan kebajikan, tetapi sebenarnya hanya roh yang perlu dikembalikan tenang.","source_ids":["S523","S524","S525"]},{"text":"Gubernur Epirus yang berseberangan di teater ditegur: banyak orang meniru contoh orang berkuasa; bila berseberangan itu salah, jangan lakukan sendiri; bila benar, jangan marah ditiru. Di teater masuklah dengan tujuan menjaga kemauan sesuai alam — 'tak ada yang lebih kusayang daripada diriku sendiri'; di rumah boleh menggelar permainan sendiri dan menobatkan Sophron, tetapi di publik jangan mengklaim milik semua orang; bila menolak, tanggunglah cemoohan.","source_ids":["S528","S529","S530"]},{"text":"Murid yang ingin pulang karena sakit ditegur: penyakit dan kematian pasti mengejutkan kita saat sedang melakukan sesuatu — berharap dikejutkan saat menjaga kemauan sendiri, agar bisa berkata kepada Tuhan: aku sakit dan miskin karena kehendak-Mu dan tetap pasrah, tak pernah mencela administrasi-Mu. Socrates bahagia karena tiap hari melihat dirinya bertumbuh lebih baik: tak pernah mencela siapa pun, Tuhan maupun manusia, dan selalu berwajah sama.","source_ids":["S533","S534","S537"]},{"text":"Orang baik tak terkalahkan karena tak masuk pertarungan di mana ia lebih lemah: tanah, budak, jabatan, tubuh boleh diambil, tetapi desire dan aversion-nya tak bisa digagalkan — satu-satunya pertarungan yang ia masuki adalah tentang hal dalam kuasa kemauannya. Kemajuan kini terhambat karena akal dilatih untuk memecahkan syllogisme, bukan untuk menjaga fakultas penguasa sesuai alam; jangan mencampur hal yang berbeda.","source_ids":["S540","S541"]},{"text":"Dialog dengan administrator Epicurean: jika daging yang terbaik, maka Maximus berlayar demi daging; tetapi kenikmatan jiwa harus bergantung pada sesuatu yang mendahuluinya — jika bukan hal jiwa, maka hal tubuh, dan substansi Baik jatuh ke tubuh. Konsekuensi logis Epicurean: mencuri dan berzina boleh bila tak terdeteksi — doktrin yang merusak negara dan keluarga. Tugas utama manusia: urusan publik, menikah, membesarkan anak, menghormati Tuhan, merawat orang tua; manusia terbawa bebas, mulia, dan mampu malu — kenikmatan harus jadi pelayan, bukan tuan.","source_ids":["S546","S549","S552","S553"]},{"text":"Kekuasaan menghukum bukan pemerintahan manusia: memenjarakan seperti batu, memukul seperti keledai. Pemerintahan sejati menunjukkan apa yang menguntungkan sebagai makhluk rasional, seperti Socrates. Hukuman bagi yang tak patuh bukan penjara, melainkan kehilangan watak: kesetiaan, kesopanan, kepatutan — jangan cari hukuman lebih besar dari itu.","source_ids":["S554","S555"]},{"text":"Latihan melawan penampakan seperti melawan soal sophistik: anakmu mati — apa yang terjadi? Anakmu mati, tidak lebih; 'ia sengsara' adalah tambahan opini sendiri. Bila menyalahkan Zeus, ingat: ia menjadimu mampu menanggung, menjadimu magnanimous, mengambil kuasa hal-hal menjadi kejahatan, dan membukakan pintu keluar — 'keluarlah dan jangan meratap'.","source_ids":["S558","S559"]},{"text":"Opini adalah sebab segala tindakan: Epictetus tak punya aturan apakah seseorang akan menang di Rome, hanya bahwa dengan opini benar ia berjalan baik. Filsuf yang ditemui hanya sekilas seperti batu bukan pertemuan sejati — bertukar dan menguji opini itulah maknanya. Yang kaya justru lebih miskin: butuh keteguhan, ketenangan, kebebasan dari kecemasan; keinginan yang banyak seperti tangan penuh buah dalam guci leher sempit — buang sebagian agar bisa keluar.","source_ids":["S563","S566","S567","S568"]},{"text":"Sakit adalah bagian hidup seperti berjalan dan berlayar; filosofi adalah persiapan menghadapi peristiwa — menyerah saat demam seperti mundur dari Pancratium setelah dipukul. Menanggung demam dengan baik: tak menyalahkan Tuhan atau manusia, menghadapi kematian dengan mulut, tak gentar atau gembira berlebihan pada kabar dokter. Dua prinsip siap sedia: selain will tak ada baik atau jahat, dan kita harus mengikuti peristiwa, bukan memimpinnya.","source_ids":["S573","S575","S576","S577"]},{"text":"Latihan (exercise) tidak boleh bertentangan dengan alam demi kekaguman (berjalan di tali, memeluk patung) — itu bedahara pesulap. Tujuannya: desire tak frustrasi dan aversion tak jatuh pada yang dihindari; lawan kebiasaan dengan kebiasaan sebaliknya. Pemula harus menjauhi yang lebih kuat darinya (gadis cantik vs pemula filosofi). Tiga topik latihan: desire/aversion, tindakan sesuai alasan, dan assent — periksa setiap penampakan seperti penjaga malam memeriksa izin.","source_ids":["S586","S587","S589","S590"]},{"text":"Kesendirian (solitude) adalah kondisi tak berdaya, bukan sekadar sendiri — bahkan Zeus sendiri di konflagrasi tak menyendiri. Manusia harus mampu jadi teman dirinya sendiri seperti Zeus: memperhatikan administrasi ilahi dan relasi dirinya dengan segala hal. Damai dari Caesar tak melindungi dari demam, kapal karam, cinta, duka; doktrin filosof menjanjikan ketenangan dari semuanya — dan kematian adalah pintu pulang ke unsur-unsur, penuh dewa, bukan Hades.","source_ids":["S594","S595","S596","S597"]},{"text":"Kekuatan besar berbahaya bagi pemula: berlatih menahan diri (makan sedikit, air, menahan desire) agar kelak menginginkan sesuai alasan; berbuat baik lewat contoh hidup, bukan ceramah. Penalti ilahi bagi yang menempatkan baik di luar will: ia akan iri, menyanjung, gelisah; yang menempatkan jahat di luar will akan berduka dan menangis. Setiap relasi (ayah, saudara) diawasi Zeus.","source_ids":["S580","S583","S599"]},{"text":"Lakukan segala tindakan dengan pertimbangan matang: pertimbangkan apa yang mendahului dan mengikuti, seperti atlet Olimpiade harus menerima latihan ketat, diet, dan kekalahan. Tanpa pertimbangan manusia seperti anak kecil atau kera yang meniru apa saja — kadang atlet, kadang gladiator, kadang filsuf — tanpa pernah satu hal pun dikerjakan dengan seluruh jiwa; harus memilih jadi satu orang: filosof atau orang biasa.","source_ids":["S609","S610","S611"]},{"text":"Pilih lingkungan pergaulan dengan hati-hati: bila bersosialisasi, kita pasti menyerupai orang lain atau mengubah mereka — seperti arang padam dekat arang menyala. Pendapat orang biasa kuat karena keluar dari keyakinan sungguhan, sementara exhortasi filosofis kita hanya kata-kata 'dari bibir' yang mati; hingga prinsip baik menjadi teguh, jauhi kebiasaan lama dan pergaulan umum, bahkan meninggalkan kampung halaman seperti dokter mengirim pasien ke udara berbeda.","source_ids":["S616","S618","S619"]},{"text":"Tentang providence: tidak perlu terganggu bila orang tidak adil 'menang' dalam uang — unggul di sana karena tanpa malu dan suciapapun; hukum alam: yang lebih unggul unggul dalam hal kemampuannya sendiri. Jangan katakan 'kekasihku memperlakukanku buruk adalah kejahatan' — cukup laporkan fakta; yang perlu dibuang bukan kemiskinan melainkan opini tentang kemiskinan.","source_ids":["S622","S624"]},{"text":"Berita yang mengganggu selalu tentang hal di luar will: tak ada yang bisa melaporkan bahwa kamu beropini buruk atau menginginkan hal buruk. Pemakzulan hakim terhadap Socrates tak menyentuh dirinya; kejahatan hakim adalah milik hakim — tangkiskanlah dengan pembelaan yang tegas dan sopan tanpa marah.","source_ids":["S627","S628"]},{"text":"Perbedaan utama orang biasa vs filosof: orang biasa berkata 'dedih aku karena anakku', filosof berkata 'dedih aku karena diriku sendiri' — sebab hanya will yang bisa merusak will. Kita terbiasa sejak kecil menyalahkan batu (dipukul pengasuh) atau koki, padahal harusnya anak yang dikoreksi; yang tak terlatih adalah anak dalam hidup.","source_ids":["S631","S632"]},{"text":"Keuntungan bisa diperoleh dari segala hal luar, bahkan dari yang menghina: orang jahat baginya sendiri, bagiku ia 'pemukul latihan' yang melatih ketahanan dan kesabaran — tongkat Hermes yang mengubah apa saja jadi emas: bawa penyakit, kematian, kemiskinan, dan aku jadikan semuanya terhormat. Menoeceus memperoleh banyak dengan mati mempertahankan cinta tanah air.","source_ids":["S635","S637","S638"]},{"text":"Kritik terhadap para 'sophist' yang hanya menghafal teorema lalu 'memuntahkannya' tanpa mencerna: bukti belajar filsafat adalah perubahan pada fakultas penguasa dalam hidup nyata — makan, menikah, menanggung makian, saudara, tetangga. Menjelaskan Chrysippus tanpa memiliki ketenangan sendiri hanya membawa nama buruk bagi filsafat; jangan menyebut diri filsuf bila desire dan penggunaan penampakan belum berubah.","source_ids":["S642","S647"]},{"text":"Ajaran harus diberikan dengan fit, waktu, dan bimbingan Tuhan — seperti misteri Eleusis yang butuh penyucian, bukan kata-kata saja; tanpa itu berarti membuka toko obat tanpa tahu kapan dan kepada siapa obat dipakai. Terbuka tanpa pertimbangan hanya membongkar misteri dan menghina yang sakral.","source_ids":["S645","S646"]},{"text":"Sinisme sejati bukan gaya (tas, tongkat, menggertak siapa saja), melainkan purnawirawan ilahi: tanpa God tidak ada yang berhak mencoba — seperti tak ada yang memberontak pada penguasa rumah. Sinikus adalah utusan, mata-mata, dan penyuruh Zeus tentang baik-buruk; seperti Diogenes yang jadi mata-mata Philip dan laporan harusnya jujur tanpa takut.","source_ids":["S650","S652","S656"]},{"text":"Syarat Sinis: fakultas penguasa murni, tanpa desire/aversion pada hal luar, tak bisa malu pada hal apa pun karena tak perlu menutupi apa pun — malulah tembok dan pintunya. Bila ia menakuti dirinya dengan malu, ia tak mampu berani mengawasi manusia.","source_ids":["S653","S654"]},{"text":"Sinikus harus memikul satu tugas dan tidak menikah, sebab menikah menuntut perhatian penuh (bedak bayi, peralatan, dana pendidikan) dan mengurangi kemampuan mengawasi semua manusia; ia justru menjadi bapak semua orang, sementara kaum tak menikah (Epaminondas, Homer) bisa lebih berjasa bagi kota daripada Priamus yang beranak lima puluh.","source_ids":["S673","S678","S679"]},{"text":"Analogi Agamemnon dipakai untuk menunjukkan bahwa stresnya berasal dari menaruh baik di luar will — seperti Gubernur menangisi perihal yang bukan miliknya, bukan karena hilang kemauan (Greeks bisa mati). Baik ditemukan di mana penilaian benar berada: tak bisa dipaksa menyetujui yang palsu atau tak bisa dicegah menyetujui yang benar — kebebasan bawaan.","source_ids":["S664","S667"]}],"sources":[{"id":"S761","chapter":"XXVI: To Those Who Fear Want","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"Does any good man fear that he shall fail to have food? To the blind it does not fail, to the lame it does not: shall it fail to a good man? And to a good soldier there does not fail to be one who gives him pay, nor to a laborer, nor to a shoemaker: and to the good man shall there be wanting such a person? Does God thus neglect the things that he has established, his ministers, his witnesses, whom alone he employs as examples to the uninstructed, both that he exists, and administers well the whole, and does not neglect human affairs, and that to a good man there is no evil either when he is living or when he is dead? What then when he does not supply him with food? What else does he do than like a good general he has given me the signal to retreat? I obey, I follow, assenting to the words of the commander, praising his acts: for I came when it pleased him, and I will also go away when it pleases him; and while I lived, it was my duty to praise God both by myself, and to each person severally and to many. He does not supply me with many things, nor with abundance, he does not will me to live luxuriously; for neither did he supply Hercules who was his own son; but another (Eurystheus"},{"id":"S762","chapter":"XXVI: To Those Who Fear Want","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":") was king of Argos and Mycenae, and Hercules obeyed orders, and labored, and was exercised. And Eurystheus was what he was, neither king of Argos nor of Mycenae, for he was not even king of himself; but Hercules was ruler and leader of the whole earth and sea, who purged away lawlessness, and introduced justice and holiness; and he did these things both naked and alone. And when Ulysses was cast out shipwrecked, did want humiliate him, did it break his spirit? but how did he go off to the virgins to ask for necessaries, to beg which is considered most shameful?"},{"id":"S763","chapter":"XXVI: To Those Who Fear Want","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"As a lion bred in the mountains trusting in his strength."},{"id":"S764","chapter":"XXVI: To Those Who Fear Want","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":"— Odyssey vi 130."},{"id":"S765","chapter":"XXVI: To Those Who Fear Want","paragraphStart":9,"paragraphEnd":9,"text":"Relying on what? Not on reputation nor on wealth nor on the power of a magistrate, but on his own strength, that is, on his opinions about the things which are in our power and those which are not. For these are the only things which make men free, which make them escape from hindrance, which raise the head (neck) of those who are depressed, which make them look with steady eyes on the rich and on tyrants. And this was (is) the gift given to the philosopher. But you will not come forth bold, but trembling about your trifling garments and silver vessels. Unhappy man, have you thus wasted your time till now?"},{"id":"S766","chapter":"XXVI: To Those Who Fear Want","paragraphStart":10,"paragraphEnd":10,"text":"“What then, if I shall be sick?” You will be sick in such a way as you ought to be. —“Who will take care of me?” —God; your friends —“I shall lie down on a hard bed.” —But you will lie down like a man. —“I shall not have a convenient chamber.” —You will be sick in an inconvenient chamber —“Who will provide for me the necessary food?” —Those who provide for others also. You will be sick like Manes. —And what also will be the end of the sickness? Any other than death? —Do you then consider that this the chief of all evils to man and the chief mark of mean spirit and of cowardice is not death, but rather the fear of death? Against this fear then I advise you to exercise yourself: to this let all your reasoning tend, your exercises, and reading; and you will know that thus only are men made free."},{"id":"S767","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":0,"paragraphEnd":0,"text":"I"},{"id":"S768","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":1,"paragraphEnd":1,"text":"About Freedom"},{"id":"S769","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":2,"paragraphEnd":2,"text":"He is free who lives as he wishes to live; who is neither subject to compulsion nor to hindrance, nor to force; whose movements to action (ὁρμαί) are not impeded, whose desires attain their purpose, and who does not fall into that which he would avoid (ἐκκλίσεις ἀπερίπτωτοι). Who then chooses to live in error? No man. Who chooses to live deceived, liable to mistake, unjust, unrestrained, discontented, mean? No man. Not one then of the bad lives as he wishes; nor is he then free. And who chooses to live in sorrow, fear, envy, pity, desiring and failing in his desires, attempting to avoid something and falling into it? Not one. Do we then find any of the bad free from sorrow, free from fear, who does not fall into that which he would avoid, and does not obtain that which he wishes? Not one; nor then do we find any bad man free."},{"id":"S770","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":3,"paragraphEnd":3,"text":"If then a man who has been twice consul should hear this, if you add, “But you are a wise man; this is nothing to you,” he will pardon you. But if you tell him the truth, and say, “You differ not at all from those who have been thrice sold as to being yourself not a slave,” what else ought you to expect than blows? For he says, “What, I a slave, I whose father was free, whose mother was free? I whom no man can purchase? I am also of senatorial rank, and a friend of Caesar, and I have been a consul, and I own many slaves.” —In the first place, most excellent senatorial man, perhaps your father also was a slave in the same kind of servitude, and your mother, and your grandfather, and all your ancestors in an ascending series. But even if they were as free as it is possible, what is this to you? What if they were of a noble nature, and you of a mean nature; if they were fearless, and you a coward; if they had the power of self-restraint, and you are not able to exercise it."},{"id":"S771","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":4,"paragraphEnd":4,"text":"“And what,” you may say, “has this to do with being a slave?” Does it seem to you to be nothing to do a thing unwillingly, with compulsion, with groans, has this nothing to do with being a slave? “It is something,” you say: “but who is able to compel me, except the lord of all, Caesar?” Then even you yourself have admitted that you have one master. But that he is the common master of all, as you say, let not this console you at all: but know that you are a slave in a great family. So also the people of Nicopolis are used to exclaim, “By the fortune of Caesar, we are free.”"},{"id":"S772","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":"However, if you please, let us not speak of Caesar at present. But tell me this: did you never love any person, a young girl, or slave, or free? “What then is this with respect to being a slave or free?” Were you never commanded by the person beloved to do something which you did not wish to do? have you never flattered your little slave? have you never kissed her feet? And yet if any man compelled you to kiss Caesar’s feet, you would think it an insult and excessive tyranny. What else then is slavery? Did you never go out by night to some place whither you did not wish to go, did you not expend that you did not wish to expend, did you not utter words with sighs and groans, did you not submit to abuse and to be excluded? But if you are ashamed to confess your own acts, see what Thrasonides says and does, who having seen so much military service as perhaps not even you have, first of all went out by night, when Geta (a slave) does not venture out, but if he were compelled by his master would have cried out much and would have gone out lamenting his bitter slavery. Next, what does Thrasonides say? “A worthless girl has enslaved me, me whom no enemy ever did.” Unhappy man, who are the"},{"id":"S773","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":5,"paragraphEnd":5,"text":" slave even of a girl, and a worthless girl. Why then do you still call yourself free? and why do you talk of your service in the army? Then he calls for a sword and is angry with him who out of kindness refuses it; and he sends presents to her who hates him, and entreats and weeps, and on the other hand having had a little success he is elated. But even then how? was he free enough neither to desire nor to fear?"},{"id":"S774","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":"Now consider in the case of animals, how we employ the notion of liberty. Men keep tame lions shut up, and feed them, and some take them about; and who will say that this lion is free? Is it not the fact that the more he lives at his ease, so much the more he is in a slavish condition? and who if he had perception and reason would wish to be one of these lions? Well, these birds when they are caught and are kept shut up, how much do they suffer in their attempts to escape? and some of them die of hunger rather than submit to such a kind of life. And as many of them as live, hardly live and with suffering pine away; and if they ever find any opening, they make their escape. So much do they desire their natural liberty, and to be independent and free from hindrance. And what harm is there to you in this? What do you say? I am formed by nature to fly where I choose, to live in the open air, to sing when I choose: you deprive me of all this, and say, what harm is it to you? For this reason we shall say that those animals only are free which cannot endure capture, but as soon as they are caught escape from captivity by death. So Diogenes also somewhere says that there is only one way to"},{"id":"S775","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":6,"paragraphEnd":6,"text":" freedom, and that is to die content: and he writes to the Persian king. “You cannot enslave the Athenian state any more than you can enslave fishes.” How is that? cannot I catch them? “If you catch them,” says Diogenes, “they will immediately leave you, as fishes do; for if you catch a fish, it dies; and if these men that are caught shall die, of what use to you is the preparation for war?” These are the words of a free man who had carefully examined the thing, and, as was natural, had discovered it. But if you look for it in a different place from where it is, what wonder if you never find it?"},{"id":"S776","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"The slave wishes to be set free immediately. Why? Do you think that he wishes to pay money to the collectors of twentieths? No; but because he imagines that hitherto, through not having obtained this, he is hindered and unfortunate. If I shall be set free, immediately it is all happiness, I care for no man, I speak to all as an equal and like to them, I go where I choose, I come from any place I choose, and go where I choose. Then he is set free; and forthwith having no place where he can eat, he looks for some man to flatter, someone with whom he shall sup: then he either works with his body and endures the most dreadful things; and if he can obtain a manger, he falls into a slavery much worse than his former slavery; or even if he is become rich, being a man without any knowledge of what is good, he loves some little girl, and in his unhappiness laments and desires to be a slave again. He says, “what evil did I suffer in my state of slavery? Another clothed me, another supplied me with shoes, another fed me, another looked after me in sickness; and I did only a few services for him. But now a wretched man, what things I suffer, being a slave to many instead of to one. But however"},{"id":"S777","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":",” he says, “if I shall acquire rings then I shall live most prosperously and happily.” First, in order to acquire these rings, he submits to that which he is worthy of; then when he has acquired them, it is again all the same. Then he says, “If I shall be engaged in military service, I am free from all evils.” He obtains military service. He suffers as much as a flogged slave, and nevertheless he asks for a second service and a third. After this, when he has put the finishing stroke (the colophon) to his career, and is become a senator, then he becomes a slave by entering into the assembly, then he serves the finer and most splendid slavery —not to be a fool, but to learn what Socrates taught, what is the nature of each thing that exists, and that a man should not rashly adapt preconceptions (προλήψεις) to the several things which are. For this is the cause to men of all their evils, the not being able to adapt the general preconceptions to the several things. But we have different opinions (about the cause of our evils). One man thinks that he is sick: not so however, but the fact is that he does not adapt his preconceptions right. Another thinks that he is poor; another that he "},{"id":"S778","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"has a severe father or mother; and another again that Caesar is not favorable to him. But all this is one and only one thing, the not knowing how to adapt the preconceptions. For who has not a preconception of that which is bad: that it is hurtful, that it ought to be avoided, that it ought in every way to be guarded against? One preconception is not repugnant to another, only where it comes to the matter of adaptation. What then is this evil, which is both hurtful, and a thing to be avoided? He answers, “not to be Caesar’s friend.” —He is gone far from the mark, he has missed the adaptation, he is embarrassed, he seeks the things which are not at all pertinent to the matter; for when he has succeeded in being Caesar’s friend, nevertheless he has failed in finding what he sought. For what is that which every man seeks? To live secure, to be happy, to do everything as he wishes, not to be hindered, nor compelled. When then he is become the friend of Caesar, is he free from hindrance? free from compulsion? is he tranquil, is he happy? Of whom shall we inquire? What more trustworthy witness have we than this very man who is become Caesar’s friend? Come forward and tell us when did you"},{"id":"S779","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":" sleep more quietly, now or before you became Caesar’s friend? Immediately you hear the answer, “Stop, I entreat you, and do not mock me: you know not what miseries I suffer, and sleep does not come to me; but one comes and says, ‘Caesar is already awake, he is now going forth:’ then come troubles and cares.” —Well, when did you sup with more pleasure, now or before? Hear what he says about this also. He says that if he is not invited, he is pained: and if he is invited, he sups like a slave with his master, all the while being anxious that he does not say or do anything foolish. And what do you suppose that he is afraid of; lest he should be lashed like a slave? How can he expect anything so good? No, but as befits so great a man, Caesar’s friend, he is afraid that he may lose his head. And when did you bathe more free from trouble, and take your gymnastic exercise more quietly? In fine, which kind of life did you prefer? your present or your former life? I can swear that no man is so stupid or so ignorant of truth as not to bewail his own misfortunes the nearer he is in friendship to Caesar. Since then neither those who are called kings live as they choose, nor the friends of kin"},{"id":"S780","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":7,"paragraphEnd":7,"text":"gs, who finally are those who are free? Seek, and you will find; for you have aids from nature for the discovery of truth. But if you are not able yourself by going along these ways only to discover that which follows, listen to those who have made the inquiry. What do they say? Does freedom seem to you a good thing? “The greatest good.” Is it possible then that he who obtains the greatest good can be unhappy or fare badly? “No.” Whomsoever then you shall see unhappy, unfortunate, lamenting, confidently declare that they are not free. “I do declare it.” We have now then got away from buying and selling and from such arrangements about matters of property: for if you have rightly assented to these matters, if the great king (the Persian king) is unhappy, he cannot be free, nor can a little king, nor a man of consular rank, nor one who has been twice consul. —Be it so."},{"id":"S781","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":"Further then answer me this question also: does freedom seem to you to be something great and noble and valuable? —“How should it not seem so?” Is it possible then when a man obtains anything so great and valuable and noble to be mean? —“It is not possible.” —When then you see any man subject to another or flattering him contrary to his own opinion, confidently affirm that this man also is not free; and not only if he do this for a bit of supper, but also if he does it for a government (province) or a consulship. And call these men little slaves who for the sake of little matters do these things, and those who do so for the sake of great things call great slaves, as they deserve to be. —“This is admitted also.” —Do you think that freedom is a thing independent and self-governing? —“Certainly.” —Whomsoever then it is in the power of another to hinder and compel, declare that he is not free. And do not look, I entreat you, after his grandfathers and great grandfathers, or inquire about his being bought or sold; but if you hear him saying from his heart and with feeling, “Master,” even if the twelve fasces precede him (as consul), call him a slave. And if you hear him say, “Wretch tha"},{"id":"S782","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":"t I am, how much I suffer,” call him a slave. If finally you see him lamenting, complaining, unhappy, call him a slave though he wears a praetexta. If then he is doing nothing of this kind, do not yet say that he is free, but learn his opinions, whether they are subject to compulsion, or may produce hindrance, or to bad fortune; and if you find him such, call him a slave who has a holiday in the Saturnalia: say that his master is from home; he will return soon, and you will know what he suffers. “Who will return?” Whoever has in himself the power over anything which is desired by the man, either to give it to him or to take it away. “Thus then have we many masters?” We have: for we have circumstances as masters prior to our present masters; and these circumstances are many. Therefore it must of necessity be that those who have the power over any of these circumstances must be our masters. For no man fears Caesar himself, but he fears death, banishment, deprivation of his property, prison, and disgrace. Nor does any man love Caesar, unless Caesar is a person of great merit, but he loves wealth, the office of tribune, praetor, or consul. When we love, and hate, and fear these things,"},{"id":"S783","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":8,"paragraphEnd":8,"text":" it must be that those who have the power over them must be our masters. Therefore we adore them even as gods; for we think that what possesses the power of conferring the greatest advantage on us is divine. Then we wrongly assume (ὑποτάσσομεν) that a certain person has the power of conferring the greatest advantages; therefore he is something divine. For if we wrongly assume that a certain person has the power of conferring the greatest advantages, it is a necessary consequence that the conclusion from these premises must be false."},{"id":"S784","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":9,"paragraphEnd":9,"text":"What then is that which makes a man free from hindrance and makes him his own master? For wealth does not do it, nor consulship, nor provincial government, nor royal power; but something else must be discovered. What then is that which when we write makes us free from hindrance and unimpeded? The knowledge of the art of writing. What then is it in playing the lute? The science of playing the lute. Therefore in life also it is the science of life. You have then heard in a general way: but examine the thing also in the several parts. Is it possible that he who desires any of the things which depend on others can be free from hindrance? No. —Is it possible for him to be unimpeded? No. —Therefore he cannot be free. Consider then: whether we have nothing which is in our own power only, or whether we have all things, or whether some things are in our own power, and others in the power of others. —“What do you mean?” —When you wish the body to be entire (sound), is it in your power or not? —“It is not in my power.” —When you wish it to be healthy? —“Neither is this in my power.” —When you wish it to be handsome? —“Nor is this.” —Life or death? —“Neither is this in my power.” —Your body th"},{"id":"S785","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":9,"paragraphEnd":9,"text":"en is another’s, subject to every man who is stronger than yourself —“It is.” —But your estate, is it in your power to have it when you please, and as long as you please, and such as you please? —“No.” —And your slaves? —“No.” —And your clothes? —“No.” —And your house? —“No.” —And your horses? —“Not one of these things.” —And if you wish by all means your children to live, or your wife, or your brother, or your friends, is it in your power? —“This also is not in my power.”"},{"id":"S786","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":10,"paragraphEnd":10,"text":"Whether then have you nothing which is in your own power, which depends on yourself only and cannot be taken from you, or have you anything of the kind? —“I know not.” —Look at the thing then thus, and examine it. Is any man able to make you assent to that which is false —“No man.” —In the matter of assent then you are free from hindrance and obstruction. —“Granted.” —Well; and can a man force you to desire to move towards that to which you do not choose? —“He can, for when he threatens me with death or bonds, he compels me to desire to move towards it.” If then, you despise death and bonds, do you still pay any regard to him? —“No.” —Is then the despising of death an act of your own or is it not yours? —“It is my act.” —It is your own act then also to desire to move towards a thing: or is it not so? —“It is my own act.” —But to desire to move away from a thing, whose act is that? This also is your act. —“What then if I have attempted to walk, suppose another should hinder me.” —What part of you does he hinder? does he hinder the faculty of assent? —“No: but my poor body.” —Yes, as he would do with a stone. —“Granted; but I no longer walk.” —And who told you that walking is your ow"},{"id":"S787","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":10,"paragraphEnd":10,"text":"n act free from hindrance? for I said that this only was free from hindrance: to desire to move; but where there is need of body and its cooperation, you have heard long ago that nothing is your own. —“Granted this also.” —And who can compel you to desire what you do not wish? —“No man.” —And to propose or intend, or in short to make use of the appearances which present themselves, can any man compel you? —“He cannot do this: but he will hinder me when I desire from obtaining what I desire.” —If you desire anything which is your own, and one of the things which cannot be hindered, how will he hinder you? —“He cannot in any way.” —Who then tells you that he who desires the things that belong to another is free from hindrance?"},{"id":"S788","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":11,"paragraphEnd":11,"text":"“Must I then not desire health?” By no means, nor anything else that belongs to another: for what is not in your power to acquire or to keep when you please, this belongs to another. Keep then far from it not only your hands, but more than that, even your desires. If you do not, you have surrendered yourself as a slave; you have subjected your neck, if you admire anything not your own, to everything that is dependent on the power of others and perishable, to which you have conceived a liking. —“Is not my hand my own?” —It is a part of your own body; but it is by nature earth, subject to hindrance, compulsion, and the slave of everything which is stronger. And why do I say your hand? You ought to possess your whole body as a poor ass loaded, as long as it is possible, as long as you are allowed. But if there be a press, and a soldier should lay hold of it, let it go, do not resist, nor murmur; if you do, you will receive blows, and nevertheless you will also lose the ass. But when you ought to feel thus with respect to the body, consider what remains to be done about all the rest which is provided for the sake of the body. When the body is an ass, all the other things are bits belon"},{"id":"S789","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":11,"paragraphEnd":11,"text":"ging to the ass: packsaddles, shoes, barley, fodder. Let these also go: get rid of them quicker and more readily than of the ass."},{"id":"S790","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":12,"paragraphEnd":12,"text":"When you have made this preparation, and have practiced this discipline —to distinguish that which belongs to another from that which is your own, the things which are subject to hindrance from those which are not, to consider the things free from hindrance to concern yourself, and those which are not free not to concern yourself, to keep your desire steadily fixed to the things which do concern yourself, and turned from the things which do not concern yourself —do you still fear any man? No one. For about what will you be afraid? about the things which are your own, in which consists the nature of good and evil? and who has power over these things? who can take them away? who can impede them? No man can, no more than he can impede God. But will you be afraid about your body and your possessions, about things which are not yours, about things which in no way concern you? and what else have you been studying from the beginning than to distinguish between your own and not your own, the things which are in your power and not in your power, the things subject to hindrance and not subject? and why have you come to the philosophers? was it that you may nevertheless be unfortunate and unh"},{"id":"S791","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":12,"paragraphEnd":12,"text":"appy? You will then in this way, as I have supposed you to have done, be without fear and disturbance. And what is grief to you? for fear comes from what you expect, but grief from that which is present. But what further will you desire? For of the things which are within the power of the will, as being good and present, you have a proper and regulated desire: but of the things which are not in the power of the will you do not desire any one, and so you do not allow any place to that which is irrational, and impatient, and above measure hasty."},{"id":"S792","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":13,"paragraphEnd":13,"text":"When then you are thus affected towards things, what man can any longer be formidable to you? For what has a man which is formidable to another, either when you see him or speak to him or finally are conversant with him? Not more than one horse has with respect to another, or one dog to another, or one bee to another bee. Things indeed are formidable to every man; and when any man is able to confer these things on another or to take them away, then he too becomes formidable. How then is an acropolis (a stronghold or fortress, the seat of tyranny) demolished? Not by the sword, not by fire, but by opinion. For if we abolish the acropolis which is in the city, can we abolish also that of fever, and that of beautiful women? Can we in a word abolish the acropolis which is in us and cast out the tyrants within us, whom we have daily over us, sometimes the same tyrants, at other times different tyrants? But with this we must begin, and with this we must demolish the acropolis and eject the tyrants, by giving up the body, the parts of it, the faculties of it, the possessions, the reputation, magisterial offices, honors, children, brothers, friends, by considering all these things as belong"},{"id":"S793","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":13,"paragraphEnd":13,"text":"ing to others. And if tyrants have been ejected from us, why do I still shut in the acropolis by a wall of circumvallation, at least on my account; for if it still stands, what does it do to me? why do I still eject (the tyrant’s) guards? For where do I perceive them? against others they have their fasces, and their spears and their swords. But I have never been hindered in my will, nor compelled when I did not will. And how is this possible? I have placed my movements towards action (ὁρμήν) in obedience to God. Is it his will that I shall have fever? It is my will also. Is it his will that I should move towards anything? It is my will also. Is it his will that I should obtain anything? It is my wish also. Does he not will? I do not wish. Is it his will that I die, is it his will that I be put to the rack? It is my will then to die, it is my will then to be put to the rack. Who then is still able to hinder me contrary to my own judgment, or to compel me? No more than he can hinder or compel Zeus."},{"id":"S794","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":14,"paragraphEnd":14,"text":"Thus the more cautious of travellers also act. A traveller has heard that the road is infested by robbers; he does not venture to enter on it alone, but he waits for the companionship on the road either of an ambassador, or of a quaestor, or of a proconsul, and when he has attached himself to such persons he goes along the road safely. So in the world the wise man acts. There are many companies of robbers, tyrants, storms, difficulties, losses of that which is dearest. Where is there any place of refuge? how shall he pass along without being attacked by robbers? what company shall he wait for that he may pass along in safety? to whom shall he attach himself? To what person generally? to the rich man, to the man of consular rank? and what is the use of that to me? Such a man is stripped himself, groans and laments. But what if the fellow companion himself turns against me and becomes my robber, what shall I do? I will be a friend of Caesar: when I am Caesar’s companion no man will wrong me. In the first place, that I may become illustrious, what things must I endure and suffer? how often and by how many must I be robbed? Then, if I become Caesar’s friend, he also is mortal. And if C"},{"id":"S795","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":14,"paragraphEnd":14,"text":"aesar from any circumstance becomes my enemy, where is it best for me to retire? Into a desert? Well, does fever not come there? What shall be done then? Is it not possible to find a safe fellow traveller, a faithful one, strong, secure against all surprises? Thus he considers and perceives that if he attaches himself to God, he will make his journey in safety."},{"id":"S796","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":15,"paragraphEnd":15,"text":"How do you understand “attaching yourself to God?” In this sense: that whatever God wills, a man also shall will; and what God does not will, a man also shall not will. How then shall this be done? In what other way than by examining the movements (ὁρμάς, the acts) of God and his administration? What has he given to me as my own and in my own power? what has he reserved to himself? He has given to me the things which are in the power of the will (τὰ προαιρετικὰ): he has put them in my power free from impediment and hindrance. How was he able to make the earthy body free from hindrance? [He could not], and accordingly he has subjected to the revolution of the whole (τῇ τῶν ὅλων περιόδῳ) possessions, household things, house, children, wife. Why then do I fight against God? why do I will what does not depend on the will? why do I will to have absolutely what is not granted to me? But how ought I to will to have things? In the way in which they are given and as long as they are given. But he who has given takes away. Why then do I resist? I do not say that I shall be a fool if I use force to one who is stronger, but I shall first be unjust. For whence had I things when I came into the "},{"id":"S797","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":15,"paragraphEnd":15,"text":"world? —My father gave them to me. —And who gave them to him? and who made the sun? and who made the fruits of the earth? and who the seasons? and who made the connection of men with one another and their fellowship?"},{"id":"S798","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":16,"paragraphEnd":16,"text":"Then after receiving everything from another and even yourself, are you angry and do you blame the giver if he takes anything from you? Who are you, and for what purpose did you come into the world? Did not he (God) introduce you here, did he not show you the light, did he not give you fellow workers, and perceptions and reason? and as whom did he introduce you here? did he not introduce you as subject to death, and as one to live on the earth with a little flesh, and to observe his administration, and to join with him in the spectacle and the festival for a short time? Will you not then, as long as you have been permitted, after seeing the spectacle and the solemnity, when he leads you out, go with adoration of him and thanks for what you have heard and seen? —“No; but I would still enjoy the feast.” —The initiated too would wish to be longer in the initiation: and perhaps also those at Olympia to see other athletes; but the solemnity is ended: go away like a grateful and modest man; make room for others: others also must be born, as you were, and being born they must have a place, and houses and necessary things. And if the first do not retire, what remains? Why are you insatiabl"},{"id":"S799","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":16,"paragraphEnd":16,"text":"e? Why are you not content? why do you contract the world? —“Yes, but I would have my little children with me and my wife.” —What, are they yours? do they not belong to the giver, and to him who made you? then will you not give up what belongs to others? will you not give way to him who is superior? —“Why then did he introduce me into the world on these conditions?” —And if the conditions do not suit you, depart. He has no need of a spectator who is not satisfied. He wants those who join in the festival, those who take part in the chorus, that they may rather applaud, admire, and celebrate with hymns the solemnity. But those who can bear no trouble, and the cowardly, he will not unwillingly see absent from the great assembly (πανήγυρις); for they did not when they were present behave as they ought to do at a festival nor fill up their place properly, but they lamented, found fault with the deity, fortune, their companions; not seeing both what they had, and their own powers, which they received for contrary purposes, the powers of magnanimity, of a generous mind, manly spirit, and what we are now inquiring about, freedom. —“For what purpose then have I received these things?” —To u"},{"id":"S800","chapter":"I: About Freedom","paragraphStart":16,"paragraphEnd":16,"text":"se them. —“How long?” —So long as he who has lent them chooses. —“What if they are necessary to me?” —Do not attach yourself to them and they will not be necessary: do not say to yourself that they are necessary, and then they are not necessary."}],"newWindowIds":["S761","S762","S763","S764","S765","S766","S767","S768","S769","S770","S771","S772","S773","S774","S775","S776","S777","S778","S779","S780","S781","S782","S783","S784","S785","S786","S787","S788","S789","S790","S791","S792","S793","S794","S795","S796","S797","S798","S799","S800"]}
